Breaks must be given during (in the middle of) working hours and, as a rule, simultaneously to all workers. Staggered/shift breaks require a labor-management agreement (労使協定).
Break time must be complete liberation from work. If a worker is made to wait for phone calls or visitors during a break, that time is hand-waiting time (手待時間) and constitutes working hours.

Statutory working hours (法定労働時間) under Japan's Labor Standards Act: excluding break times, an employer shall not make a worker work more than 40 hours per week and shall not make a worker work more than 8 hours per day.

Statutory working hours (法定労働時間) in Japan include a weekly limit of 40 hours; in practice, confirmation of hours exceeding 1 week / 40 hours is often missed during attendance management and payroll calculation, so this must be checked carefully.

所定労働時間 (prescribed/scheduled working hours) is a term frequently confused with statutory working hours. It refers to the working hours stipulated in the work rules (就業規則) of each company or workplace, not the legal maximum.
Example of 所定労働時間: If start time is 10:00, end time is 18:00, and break time is 1 hour, prescribed working hours equal 7 hours.
The next section (ツボ 022) covers the 36 Agreement (36協定), which relates to overtime work beyond statutory limits.

Labor hours (労働時間) are the time a worker is placed under the employer's command and control (使用者の指揮命令下に置かれている時間), including time spent engaging in work pursuant to the employer's explicit or implicit instructions (使用者の明示または黙示の指示により労働者が業務に従事する時間).

Rest periods (休憩時間) must be given during working hours (in the middle of the work period). When working hours exceed 6 hours but are 8 hours or less, at least 45 minutes of rest is required; when working hours exceed 8 hours, at least 1 hour of rest is required.
Time not counted as labor hours includes travel time for direct commute/return (直行直帰) or associated with business trips, but only when free use of that time is guaranteed (自由な利用が保障されている場合のみ).
Voluntary training or education (自由参加の研修・教育訓練) is generally not labor time; however, if participation is de facto compulsory (事実上参加が強制されている場合), it constitutes labor time.
The content is based on the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) guidance on the concept of labor hours, including handling of training and education.
Whether rest/break time (休憩), travel/moving time (移動時間), or training (研修) counts as working hours (労働時間) is determined by the actual circumstances (実態), not by labels or formal designations.
In labor-law analysis, classification of time as working hours depends on the reality of how the time is spent rather than its official name.

The 36 Agreement (36協定 or サブロク協定) is a labor-management agreement that makes otherwise illegal overtime or statutory holiday work lawful when concluded and filed with the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署).

Unlike work rules (就業規則), a 36 Agreement must be concluded even if there is only one regularly employed worker whenever statutory overtime or holiday work will be performed; missed filings have led to increasing document-based prosecutorial referrals (書類送検).
A 36 Agreement has two stages: a general clause and a special clause.
Under the general clause the extension limits are in principle 45 hours per month and 360 hours per year; annual overtime counting leaks are common, so a confirmation system should be built.
A special clause may be used only for temporary, unforeseeable large increases in workload; it cannot be used for constant, foreseeable overtime.

With a special clause the upper limits become: (1) 720 hours of overtime per year; (2) including holiday work, a monthly average of 80 hours or less in every 2-, 3-, 4-, 5- and 6-month period; (3) including holiday work, less than 100 hours in any single month; (4) months exceeding 45 hours allowed for at most 6 months per year.
A 36 Agreement must be concluded, made known to workers, and filed on a per-establishment (事業場単位) basis; each factory, branch, etc. requires its own agreement, notice and filing.
Two copies of the notification form are submitted to the Labor Standards Inspection Office; one copy is returned with a receipt stamp and kept as the establishment’s record.
The content of the 36 Agreement must be made known to workers by one of the methods prescribed by law.

The 36 agreement (労使協定) must be made known to workers by one of three methods: (1) always posting it in an easily visible place at each workplace or keeping it available there; (2) delivering the written document to workers; or (3) recording it on magnetic tape, magnetic disk, or equivalent media and installing equipment at each workplace so workers can always confirm the recorded content.
The validity period of a labor-management agreement (労使協定 / 36協定) is preferably set at one year.
Ordering employees to perform statutory overtime work or holiday work after the agreement’s validity period has expired is illegal.

As a practical rule, select the majority representative about one month before the expiration date, and complete conclusion, workplace notification, and filing of the next year’s 36 agreement with the Labor Standards Inspection Office while the current agreement is still valid.
When requiring overtime work (時間外労働) or holiday work (休日出勤), a 36 Agreement (三六協定, Article 36 of the Labor Standards Act) is required.
Prescribed working hours (所定労働時間) are 8 hours per day as stipulated in work rules (就業規則) or individual labor contracts (個別の労働契約).
Under the 36 Agreement general provisions (一般条項), the overtime upper limit is 45 hours per month.
Special provisions of the 36 Agreement can be used only in temporary/extraordinary cases (臨時的な場合にしか利用できない).

Special-provision overtime limits: (1) annual overtime within 720 hours; (2) including holiday work, a monthly average of 80 hours or less over any 2-, 3-, 4-, 5-, or 6-month period; (3) including holiday work, less than 100 hours in any single month; (4) months exceeding 45 hours of overtime are limited to 6 months per year.
In Japanese labor law, work that exceeds statutory working hours (法定労働時間) is illegal.
Such overtime can be legally exempted (免責) if a 36 Agreement (36協定) is in place between the employer and employees.
The 36 Agreement refers to an agreement under Article 36 of Japan's Labor Standards Act that permits overtime beyond statutory limits.
Properly grasping and managing working hours is a prerequisite for correctly carrying out various labor affairs such as payroll calculation and health management.
Working hours management must follow the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare guideline titled 'Guidelines on Measures Employers Should Take to Properly Grasp Working Hours'.
The guideline explicitly states that it is the employer's duty to confirm and record each worker's start and end times for every workday in order to properly grasp working hours.
There are principally two methods for confirming start and end times: (1) the employer personally confirms them (visual confirmation), and (2) basing them on objective records.
It is desirable to operate using objective records (method 2) as much as possible.

Examples of objective-record operations include linking time cards or office IC-card entry/exit logs to an attendance system as start/end times, counting PC usage logs as working hours, and correcting for non-working periods based on applications.
When objective records are unavoidably difficult to use, a self-declaration system may be introduced.

A self-declaration system requires: (1) sufficient explanation to both workers who self-declare and their managers regarding proper operation of the system and the guideline-based measures; (2) conducting an actual-condition survey whenever a significant discrepancy exists between self-reported working hours and in-office time grasped from entry/exit records or PC usage time.
When using a self-declaration system for working hours, necessary labor time must be corrected so that recorded hours match actual work.
Employers must not hinder proper self-reporting of working hours, including by setting an upper limit on the number of hours a worker is allowed to self-report.

Employers should check whether it has become customary for workers to report hours as if they are complying with the 36 Agreement (Article 36 overtime agreement) upper limits even when they are actually working beyond those limits.

Break-time recording is a common source of unpaid wages: if an attendance system automatically records a statutory 1-hour break every day even when the break was not actually taken, large unpaid-wage liabilities can arise.
Statutory break times must be thoroughly taken; if a break could not be taken, that time must be added to working hours, and this correct operation must be clearly communicated to workers.
The next related topic (ツボ024) covers working hours of managerial employees.
Working hours must be confirmed in accordance with Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) guidelines.
Objective confirmation methods are preferred; a self-declaration system (自己申告制) is permitted only when methods 1 and 2 are inevitably difficult.

When a self-declaration system is used, required initiatives include recording computer (パソコン) usage time, providing sufficient explanation (十分な説明), and eliminating obstructive/hindrance measures (阻害措置の排除).
Working hours (労働時間) are in principle calculated in 1-minute units.
Pay close attention to the initial settings of the attendance/timekeeping system (勤怠システム) so that rounding or other defaults do not violate the 1-minute calculation principle.

In Japanese labor practice, many companies refuse overtime pay to 'managers' (管理職) based on internal titles, but a company-defined management position is a different legal concept from a 'supervisory manager' (管理監督者) under the Labor Standards Act.

Even if work rules state that department heads and above are supervisory managers exempt from working-hour rules, classification is determined by actual working conditions (実態), not by title or internal rank.

Four concrete elements are used to determine whether someone is a true 管理監督者: (1) job content, (2) responsibility and authority, (3) working style/aspects of attendance, and (4) treatment/compensation.

Job-content element: the person must have important duties that inherently require activity beyond the statutory framework of working hours, breaks and holidays. For playing-managers, the ratio of individual contributor work versus actual supervisory work is a key practical issue.

Responsibility-and-authority element: the person must possess important responsibilities and powers that likewise require activity beyond those statutory limits. Practical indicators include personnel-evaluation authority, hiring authority, and mandatory attendance at important meetings.

Working-style element: the actual manner of work must be incompatible with ordinary working-hour regulation. Indicators include discretion over arrival/departure times, whether lateness or early departure results in wage deduction or performance-evaluation impact, and whether the person is included in shift schedules.

Treatment element: wages and other conditions must be commensurate with the status. Practical red flags include annual-income reversal versus the highest-paid non-supervisory employees and the presence or absence of a position allowance.

The overall ratio of supervisory managers among all employees should also be considered. There is no statutory quantitative threshold, but in practice a ratio of 10 % or more of the entire workforce tends to be viewed as excessively high.

Even a person who qualifies as a 管理監督者 is exempt only from the Labor Standards Act provisions on working hours, rest periods and holidays; the employer’s obligation to pay late-night (midnight) premium wages continues to apply.

管理監督者 (managers/supervisors) are not excluded from several labor-law obligations that companies often assume do not apply to them; many firms have unpaid-wage problems as a result, so internal operations should be reviewed.

Provisions on 年次有給休暇 (annual paid leave) are not an exemption for 管理監督者; the 年休5日の時季指定義務 (employer’s duty to designate the timing of five days of annual leave) must still be complied with (see ツボ029).

Under the 労働安全衛生法 (Industrial Safety and Health Act), the employer must provide 医師による面接指導 (physician interview guidance) to a worker who has performed more than 80 hours of overtime/holiday work in a month, has accumulated fatigue, and has requested an interview.
管理監督者 are not excluded from that physician-interview obligation either.
Even for 管理監督者, working hours must be grasped from the standpoint of 健康管理 (health management) and 安全配慮義務 (the employer’s duty of care for safety).
The next section (ツボ025) covers operation of the フレックスタイム制 (flextime system).
Even employees in managerial positions (管理職) must have their working hours tracked and grasped.
Company-defined managerial positions (管理職) are distinct from Labor Standards Act supervisory managers (管理監督者); only the latter receive certain exemptions.
Criteria for recognizing 管理監督者 include: (1) important job content, (2) responsibility and authority, (3) working style that does not fit ordinary regulations, and (4) treatment befitting the status.
管理監督者 are exempt from Labor Standards Act provisions on working hours, rest periods, and holidays.
Exemptions do not apply to: late-night work premium pay obligations, annual paid leave provisions, or the Industrial Safety and Health Act duty of physician interview guidance.
From the standpoint of health management and the employer’s duty of care for safety (安全配慮義務), working-hour tracking remains necessary even for managers and 管理監督者.
In Japanese labor law, designation as a 管理監督者 (kanri kantokusha / managerial supervisor exempt from certain working-hour rules) faces a considerably high hurdle for recognition.
Even after an employee is certified as a 管理監督者, the employer is still required to grasp/monitor that person's working hours (労働時間の把握).

Japan's Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) sets a principle of 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week, but also provides various other working-hour systems including the variable working hours system (変形労働時間制) and the deemed working hours system (みなし労働時間制).
The variable working hours system (変形労働時間制) allows working hours to be set elastically provided that total hours within a defined period stay within the statutory total working-hours cap.

The deemed working hours system (みなし労働時間制) treats workers as having worked a number of hours specified in a labor-management agreement (労使協定), regardless of actual hours, when certain legal conditions are met.

Annual, monthly, and weekly variable working-hour systems as well as the discretionary labor system (裁量労働制) have demanding legal requirements and operational difficulty, so only a limited number of companies can introduce them.
For most companies seeking flexible working hours, the flextime system (フレックスタイム制) is the most realistic and practical option.

Flextime works by first fixing a total working-hours quota (総労働時間) for a settlement period (清算期間, normally one month and at most three months); workers then freely decide daily start/end times and daily hours.
Because flextime is advantageous to workers, its legal requirements are less strict and it is easier to operate than other special working-hour regimes.

Introduction of flextime requires (1) a provision in the work rules (就業規則) stating that start and finish times are left to the worker's decision and (2) a labor-management agreement covering the prescribed items.
Flextime may optionally include core time (コアタイム)—hours during which attendance is mandatory—and flexible time (フレキシブルタイム)—hours the worker may choose.
Flexible time is customarily set between 5:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m. so that it does not constitute late-night work (深夜労働).
Core time should be scheduled for periods when the entire staff must be present (e.g., morning assembly or regular meetings).
To increase worker autonomy, some companies now omit core time altogether and allow work solely within the flexible-time window.
An increasing number of companies are adopting flextime rules that allow employees to work at any time (no core hours required).
Under Japan's flextime system (フレックスタイム制), if actual working hours (実労働時間) during the settlement period (清算期間) exceed the total statutory working hours (法定労働時間の総枠), premium wages (割増賃金) must be paid.
Premium wages are also required for late-night work (深夜労働) even when flextime is used.
Statutory holiday work (法定休日労働) is excluded from the flextime system and requires separate payment of premium wages.
Flextime (フレックスタイム制) is presented as an effective option for introduction in Japanese workplaces.
Under flextime, employees have flexible time bands (いつ出社しても良い時間帯) in which they may choose their start and end times, plus a core time during which they must be present and working (必ず勤務しなくてはならない).
The settlement/liquidation period (清算期間) is usually one month and may be set arbitrarily as long as it does not exceed three months.
Total actual working hours within the settlement period must not exceed the statutory working-hours total for that period; if they do, premium overtime wages must be paid.
For a one-month settlement period the statutory working-hours totals are: 31-day month 177.1 hours, 30-day month 171.4 hours, 29-day month 165.7 hours, 28-day month 160.0 hours.
The explanation and figures are based on the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) guide “フレックスタイム制のわかりやすい解説と導入の手引き”.
From the perspective of talent recruitment and retention (人材の採用・定着), introducing a flextime system (フレックスタイム制) is recommended.
When both a main job and a side/concurrent job are based on employment contracts, the key legal issue is aggregation (通算) of working hours under Japanese labor law.

Provisions that apply to aggregated working hours across jobs: the statutory 8 hours per day / 40 hours per week limits; the multiple-month average of 80 hours or less; and the monthly limit of under 100 hours.
Provisions that do NOT apply to aggregated working hours: the monthly 45-hour and annual 360-hour overtime limits, and the annual 720-hour overtime limit.

Working hours are not aggregated when the Labor Standards Act does not apply, such as freelance, independent work, entrepreneurship, joint management, advisor, consultant, counselor, director, or auditor roles.
Whether someone is a 'worker' under the Labor Standards Act is judged by actual working conditions (実態), not by the name or form of the contract; consult an expert when in doubt.
Aggregation of hours is performed by combining the company's own recorded working hours with hours at other employers that the worker self-reports.
It is generally not realistic for an employer to constantly monitor attendance and hours at a worker's side-job workplace.
The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) permits a simplified 'management model' (管理モデル) for labor-time tracking in its Guidelines for Promoting Side Jobs and Concurrent Employment.

In Japan's management model (管理モデル) for side jobs/concurrent employment (副業・兼業), each workplace sets its own working-hour upper limits so that statutory overtime at the main job (先契約の使用者; including statutory holiday work) plus all working hours at the side job (後契約の使用者) total under 100 hours in a single month and an average of 80 hours or less over multiple months.
Under the management model, the side-job employer pays premium wages (割増賃金) for hours worked at its own workplace regardless of the employee's actual hours at the main job.
As long as work stays within the pre-set hour limits, neither employer is required to track actual working hours at the other employer's workplace (実態把握不要).

The main employer proposes adoption of the management model to the side employer via the employee rather than through direct employer-to-employer contact; related explanation and proposal forms are available for download from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) website.
A workplace may adopt the management model as its default/principle rule for permitting side jobs and concurrent employment.

The 管理モデル (management model) is a framework for aggregating (通算) working hours of workers who perform 副業・兼業 (side jobs or concurrent employment) at multiple employers, enabling compliance with the Labor Standards Act without continuous cross-employer hour tracking.

When a worker is employed at 使用者A (first-contract employer) and 使用者B (later-contract employer), each workplace sets its own working-hour upper limits so that the sum of 法定外労働時間 (overtime including statutory holiday work) at A plus all 労働時間 at B stays under 100 hours in any single month and averages 80 hours or less over multiple months.
Statutory working hours used as the baseline in the model are 40 hours per week and 8 hours per day.

After the management model is introduced, 使用者B treats its entire workplace working hours as 法定外労働時間 and pays 割増賃金 (premium/overtime wages) on that basis, irrespective of the actual hours worked at 使用者A.

Once the pre-set upper limits are in place, neither employer is required to grasp (実態把握) the other employer’s actual working hours; as long as each keeps the worker within its own agreed limit, both remain in compliance with the 労働基準法.
The model therefore shifts the compliance burden from real-time mutual monitoring of hours to ex-ante allocation of monthly and multi-month overtime caps between the two employers.

双方向雇用契約の副業・兼業は、管理モデルで行うことを就業規則で定めましょう (For bidirectional/two-way employment contracts, side jobs and concurrent employment should be carried out under a management model, and this should be stipulated in the work rules/employment regulations.)

休日 (holiday) means a day on which a worker has no labor obligation at all. 休暇 (leave) means a scheduled workday on which the worker is entitled to be exempted from work (e.g. annual paid leave / 年次有給休暇, special leave / 特別休暇). Leave days do not count toward annual holiday totals. Many companies confuse the two terms; employment rules should be checked.

The Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) requires at least one holiday per week. These legally required holidays are called 法定休日 (statutory holidays). They need not be Sundays; they may be designated in the employment rules (就業規則).

Holidays other than statutory holidays are 所定休日 (prescribed/company holidays). Example: in a Sat–Sun two-day weekend firm, if Sunday is the statutory holiday, Saturday is a prescribed holiday. Holiday premium pay is required only for work on statutory holidays, not prescribed holidays.

A 変形週休制 (variable weekly holiday system) is also allowed: at least 4 holidays in each 4-week period. In that case the employment rules must clearly state the starting day of the 4-week calculation period.

At the start of each year, create an annual calendar that clearly distinguishes 法定休日, 所定休日, and 所定労働日 (prescribed workdays), and count how many days of each type are set. Verify that a statutory holiday is provided at least once every week.

When calculating premium wages for statutory overtime or statutory holiday work, an hourly wage must be derived. For monthly-salaried workers, to keep the hourly rate from fluctuating every month, use: (annual prescribed workdays × prescribed hours per day) ÷ 12 = average prescribed work hours per month. Premium-wage calculation is covered in ツボ 033.
For monthly-salary workers, hourly wage is derived as monthly salary divided by one month’s average prescribed working hours (月給 ÷ 1か月の平均所定労働時間 = 1時間あたりの賃金).
Annual prescribed working days equal 365 days (366 in a leap year) minus the number of annual holidays.
The annual holiday count therefore changes the hourly unit price used for premium (overtime) pay under a monthly-salary system.
Paying premium wages below the legally required hourly unit price is a Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) violation and can trigger guidance from the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署).
Employers should prepare an annual calendar at the start of the year and calculate the figures carefully.
The next topic (ツボ 028) covers the distinction between 振替休日 (transferred/substitute holiday) and 代休 (compensatory leave).
At the beginning of each year, always create and establish an annual calendar (年間カレンダー) to define working days, holidays, and related schedules.
An annual calendar example (図表 027) maps all 12 months with days of the week and marks for working days, holidays, and other designations to support yearly labor planning.

Hourly wage from monthly salary is calculated in two steps: (1) (annual prescribed working days × prescribed working hours per day) ÷ 12 = average monthly prescribed working hours; (2) monthly salary ÷ average monthly prescribed working hours = hourly wage rate.
Rounding rule for the resulting hourly wage: amounts less than 50 sen are discarded; 50 sen or more are rounded up to 1 yen.

Example calculation for a worker with 240,000 yen monthly salary: statutory holidays 52 days, prescribed holidays 70 days, prescribed working days 244 days, yielding 162 average monthly prescribed hours and an hourly wage of 1,481 yen.

Prescribed working days (所定労働日数) of 244, statutory holidays (法定休日) of 52, and prescribed holidays (所定休日) of 70 are used as inputs when converting monthly pay into an hourly rate under labor-standards rules.
A method for setting work calendars is to first fix the annual number of holidays (年間休日数) in the employment rules/work regulations (就業規則), and then create the calendar every year.

振替休日 (休日の振替) is the advance swapping of a predetermined holiday and a working day: a day set as a holiday is changed to a working day, and a specific working day before or after it is instead made a holiday. This is a rearrangement of prescribed working days and holidays on the annual calendar.

Requirements for a valid 振替休日: (1) provisions for holiday transfer must exist in the work rules (就業規則) or similar; (2) the substitute holiday date must be specified in advance; (3) the statutory holiday of once per week (or 4 days in 4 weeks) must still be secured.

After a holiday transfer, the annual calendar must be rechecked to confirm that one statutory holiday per week remains. To keep one statutory holiday per week, consecutive work is allowed for at most 12 days.

If the original statutory holiday becomes a work day through a valid 振替休日, that day is no longer a statutory holiday, so there is no obligation to pay the premium wage for statutory holiday work. However, if the transfer causes weekly hours to exceed 40, the overtime (法定時間外労働) premium is still owed.

Example: if an employee already worked 40 hours Monday–Friday and Saturday is changed from a holiday to a working day by 振替休日, Saturday’s hours are statutory overtime and require the overtime premium. Payroll errors on the over-40-hours portion are common in practice.

代休 is rest given after holiday work has already occurred: a later specific working day is given off as compensation. It is not an advance transfer of the holiday, so the fact of having worked on a holiday does not disappear.

Unlike 振替休日, 代休 after work on a statutory holiday requires a 36 Agreement (三六協定) and payment of the statutory holiday-work premium. The Labor Standards Act does not itself obligate employers to grant 代休; that is left to work rules or similar internal rules.

In Japanese labor practice, cases are observed where work that is actually 代休 (daikyū / compensatory leave taken after holiday work) is processed as 振替休日 (furikae kyūjitsu / pre-arranged holiday substitution) in order to avoid paying 割増賃金 (premium wages). This is a violation of the 労働基準法 (Labor Standards Act) and must be avoided.
When operating 振替休日, employers should prepare application forms and other documentation, and must always retain a historical record proving that the substitution was arranged in advance.
It is recommended to adopt a rule that the substitute holiday (振替先) is permitted only within the same attendance aggregation period (勤怠の集計期間), for example within the same month.
The subsequent topic (ツボ 029) covers operation of 年次有給休暇 (annual paid leave).

In Japanese labor law, 振替休日 (furikae kyujitsu, substituted/swapped holiday) and 代休 (daikyu, compensatory leave) are legally distinct; treating actual 代休 as 振替休日 is a Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) violation.

振替休日 prerequisites: the substitution system must be stipulated in the 就業規則 (work rules/employment regulations); a scheduled holiday and a scheduled work day are swapped in advance by application so the original holiday is treated as an ordinary work day.

On a properly substituted 振替休日 day, 休日割増賃金 (holiday premium wages) do not arise because the day is treated the same as a regular work day; however, if weekly hours exceed 40, 時間外労働賃金 (overtime pay) still applies, and one statutory holiday per week must still be secured.

代休 is leave given later as compensation after holiday work has already been performed; 休日割増賃金 arises for the holiday work itself, and whether the later 代休 day is paid or unpaid is determined by the 就業規則.
Making employees work on a 法定休日 (statutory holiday) requires conclusion of a 36協定 (Article 36 labor-management agreement).

To lawfully use 振替休日, the fact that the swap was made in advance must be recorded (e.g., via application forms) so there is a documentary history that substitution occurred before the original holiday.
休日の振替 (holiday substitution / furikae kyujitsu) should be performed as much as possible within the wage calculation period (e.g., within the same month).
Key statement: 「休日の振替はできる限り賃金計算期間内（同月内など）で行うようにしましょう」
Annual paid leave (年次有給休暇) is a system established by Japan's Labor Standards Act for the purpose of refreshing workers' mind and body.

It must be granted, regardless of employment type (including managerial supervisors and fixed-term workers), when two conditions are met: continuous employment for 6 months from the hiring date, and attendance of 80% or more of all working days.

The employer must grant leave on the date the worker wishes to take it, except when it would interfere with the normal operation of the business. Interference is quite limited and the hurdle is high (e.g., a large number of employees requesting leave in the same period).
Employers are obligated to create an annual leave management book (年休管理簿) for each worker and retain it for 3 years; it must record the timing (season), number of days, and base date (基準日).

When the number of employees is large, managing different base dates per person becomes cumbersome. Unifying the base date (e.g., granting annual leave to all employees on April 1 each year) is one practical approach.

To unify the base date, first identify each worker's statutory grant timing and number of days, then grant leave in advance on the unified date so that it is never less favorable than the statutory requirement.

Because take-up rates remain low (due to busy workplaces, consideration for others, hesitation, etc.), employers have a legal duty (時季指定義務) to specify the timing for 5 days of annual paid leave for any worker granted 10 or more days (including managers).

The 5-day specification obligation applies even if the employer repeatedly urged the worker to take leave but the worker still did not take it. The employer must first hear the worker's opinion, but ultimately the company must complete the specification. Specification cannot be done for a worker who has already requested or taken 5 or more days.
The employer's intention to specify timing must be stated in the employment rules (就業規則).
Violations of the relevant labor rules carry a penalty of a fine of 300,000 yen or less.
If an employer fails to have workers take 5 days of annual paid leave (年次有給休暇) per year, the penalty is a fine of 300,000 yen or less per person.
The next key point (ツボ 030) addresses the future of working hours (労働時間).

Japanese labor law requires employers to grant annual paid leave (年次有給休暇 / 年休) after 6 months of continuous service if the worker has attended at least 80% of all working days. Days granted increase with tenure: 10 days (6 months), 11 days (1 year 6 months), 12 days (2 years 6 months), 14 days (3 years 6 months), 16 days (4 years 6 months), 18 days (5 years 6 months), and 20 days (6 years 6 months or more).
Part-time and similar workers receive annual paid leave on a proportional basis according to their prescribed number of working days, not the full statutory amounts.
Workers may take annual leave on dates they request, except when doing so would interfere with the normal operation of the business (事業の正常な運営を妨げる場合).

Employers have a legal duty to ensure every covered worker takes at least 5 days of annual paid leave each year by specifying the timing themselves (時季指定義務). This applies to managerial supervisors (管理監督者) and fixed-term employees (有期雇用労働者) as well as regular staff.
Employers must create and maintain an annual leave management ledger (年休管理簿) and thoroughly implement the 5-day timing-specification requirement.
Failure to have a worker take the mandatory 5 days of annual paid leave can result in a fine of up to 300,000 yen per person.
In Japan, cases of guidance (指導事例) issued by the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署) concerning annual paid leave (年次有給休暇) have been increasing.
Hybrid Career (WorkStyle 3.0), proposed by Yusuke Iwata, describes an integrated evolution of work that combines flexibility in time, place, and affiliation rather than treating them separately.
Workstyle 1.0 refers to the traditional Japanese company model: exclusive full-time employees of a single firm who commute to an office and work together in person.

Workstyle 2.0 emerged from declining labor population and changing worker needs; companies made gradual, partial innovations such as flextime (time), telework and workcation (place), and side jobs or parallel careers (affiliation).

Workstyle 3.0 was driven by the 2018 trend of lifting bans on side/concurrent jobs and the COVID-19 pandemic from 2020 onward; companies were forced to combine and integrate changes across time, place, and affiliation rather than addressing them in isolation.
Under Workstyle 3.0, labor/HR functions must not merely adapt to external pressure; they need consistency grounded in the company’s own philosophy and personnel strategy.

Administrative bodies publish model regulations and guidelines to help companies introduce new work styles (telework, workcation, side/concurrent jobs), including the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare’s “Guidelines for Promoting Side Jobs and Concurrent Jobs” and the Japan Business Federation’s “Workcation Model Regulations.”
The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare website also hosts Q&A covering finer points of practical operation of these new work arrangements.
Work-style topics continually generate new trends and issues; organizations should independently research them and verify whether each practice actually fits their own company.

Workstyle 3.0 is a framework that aims for the company-optimal 'way of working' in the current era by combining not only time-based measures but also affiliation (employment relationship) and place/location policies.
Workstyle 3.0 is grounded in the company's own philosophy and human resources (HR) strategy rather than adopting generic flexibility practices in isolation.
Workstyle 1.0 represents the traditional model of full-time regular employees working at the office.
Workstyle 2.0 expands freedom of place and time and includes telework, workation (work + vacation), side jobs, concurrent employment (兼業), and parallel careers.

Key external drivers pushing companies from Workstyle 1.0/2.0 toward 3.0 include a declining labor force/population, diversifying employee needs regarding the work environment, the trend of lifting bans on side jobs, and the COVID-19 pandemic.
The diagram positions Workstyle 3.0 as an integration layer above 1.0 and 2.0 practices so that time, affiliation, and location policies are designed together rather than as separate add-ons.
Companies should continuously update and refine the working style that is optimal for their own organization.
Key statement: 自社に最適な働き方のアップデートを常に行い続けましょう (Let's always keep updating the way of working that is optimal for our company.)

Chapter 3 covers 労働時間 (working hours). Its summary presents key points (ツボ) 021–030 as a Q&A list and gives role-specific messages for 労務担当者 (labor/HR staff), 経営者 (executives), マネージャー/管理職 (managers), and all workers.
Labor/HR staff should first correctly grasp working hours and properly distinguish 所定労働日 (prescribed working days), 休日 (holidays), and 休暇 (leave/vacation) (ツボ 023, 027, 028).
Attendance-management software is becoming more feature-rich; as a result, some organizations take incorrect actions without understanding the fundamental principles of working hours.
Staff should re-learn from the basics the definition of 労働時間 (ツボ 021) and the working-hour system the company actually uses.
Executives should verbalize a philosophy of 働き方 (work styles) after comprehensively considering employee needs, future management strategy, and management philosophy (ツボ 030).
Working hours and holiday/leave systems are extremely important elements that define a company’s 働き方.
Depending on organizational culture and business model, highly flexible work is not necessarily always best; the working-hour system should fit the company’s philosophy and HR strategy.
Managers should start by reading the 厚生労働省 (Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare) guidelines (ツボ 023).
Success or failure of working-hour management depends extremely heavily on managers’ management.

Whether time counts as 労働時間 is interpreted according to the presence or absence of a manager’s instructions/commands (明示又は黙示の指示・指揮命令) and whether 恒常的な時間外労働 (constant overtime) exists in the workplace (ツボ 021).
Employees must first thoroughly and correctly record their own work/attendance status as a fundamental practice.
Ambiguous cases of whether an activity counts as working hours (労働時間) must not be self-judged; they should be confirmed with a manager or labor affairs staff (referenced as ツボ 021).

Flexible working styles unconstrained by time or place are becoming more widespread, but realizing them requires every individual to correctly understand the work rules (ワークルール) stipulated in Japan's Labor Standards Act (労働基準法).
Correct understanding of legally defined work rules is a necessary condition (必要条件) for implementing flexible work arrangements.
The subsequent chapter (Chapter 4) addresses compensation for labor (労働の対価).
Working hours (労働時間) are defined as time during which the worker is placed under the employer's command and order (使用者の指揮命令下に置かれている時間).
A 36 Agreement (36協定 / サブロク協定) is the required legal procedure under Japan's Labor Standards Act when an employer wishes to have employees perform overtime work or holiday work (時間外労働・休日出勤).
Working hours should be managed in accordance with the guidelines issued by Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省のガイドライン).
Even under a discretionary labor system (裁量労働制), the employer is still required to grasp and record actual working hours.
Introduction of a flextime system (フレックスタイム制) is presented as a powerful/practical measure for working-hour management.
Holidays must be determined by always creating an annual calendar (年間カレンダー) at the beginning of the year.
Substitute holidays (振替休日) and compensatory leave (代休) must be strictly distinguished; treating compensatory leave as if it were a substitute holiday is illegal.
For operation of annual paid leave (年次有給休暇): create a paid-leave management ledger (年休管理簿) and thoroughly implement the mandatory seasonal designation of at least 5 days per year (年間5日の時季指定).
Future working-hour policy should combine not only time-based rules but also affiliation and location measures in order to pursue the company's own optimal 'way of working' (働き方) for the current era.

The author (古茶) started their career in recruitment HR, later worked as an HR consultant, and then oversaw all HR functions including labor affairs (労務) at a social welfare corporation; the book is written based on this real experience.
Someone deeply immersed in the worldview of talent management (人材マネジメント) may understand labor affairs (労務) intellectually but not truly grasp its importance in the heart.

Handling labor affairs forced a change in values after a period when mental-health issues (メンタル不調) and resignations surged, including mid-level employees who had supported the company, people the author had wanted to hire, and even new graduates who had chosen the firm as their first career (some of whom took leave of absence / 休職).
A core realization from that period: merely coming to work healthy is something to be truly grateful for; simply being alive and present in good health is itself precious.
In the series 「理論と実践100のツボ」, HR (人事) is defined as 「人を生かして事をなす」 (making things happen by giving life to people). The verb is written 生かして rather than 活かして.
The reason for 生かして: a person must first be 生きている (alive) in order to be 活かされる (utilized). Talent management alone cannot truly make people happy.
Labor affairs (労務) form the foundation; talent management is stacked on top of it. When the two interact, companies that can truly make people happy are created.
HR professionals whose livelihood has been talent management therefore especially need to study labor affairs thoroughly. This insight was the starting point for writing the book.

The Five Principles of Wage Payment (賃金支払の五原則) under Japan's Labor Standards Act Article 24 require that wages be paid: (1) in currency, (2) directly to the worker, (3) in full, (4) at least once a month, and (5) on a fixed date.

When introducing new wage-payment methods such as digital payroll (デジタル給与払い / so-called ○○ペイ) or peer-bonus systems (employees sending small incentives to each other), always verify that the method still satisfies all five principles.

The currency-payment principle prohibits in-kind wages. Providing a commuter pass in kind therefore violates the principle, although an exception is possible if a labor-union collective agreement is concluded.

Bank transfer of wages requires the individual worker's consent. The account must be in the worker's own name at a financial institution the worker designates; the employer may not designate a bank merely to save fees.

Statutory deductions (income-tax withholding and social-insurance premiums) do not violate the full-payment principle. Other deductions (company-housing rent, training costs, union dues, etc.) require a labor-management agreement known as a 24 Agreement.
Many companies fail to conclude the necessary 24 Agreement for wage deductions; a model form is available on the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare website.

Minimum wage (最低賃金) is the legally mandated lowest amount an employer must pay. It consists of a prefecture-specific regional minimum wage plus industry-specific minimum wages; both should be checked every year.

Japan has two types of statutory minimum wages: the regional minimum wage (地域別最低賃金) that applies to all workers, and the specific (industry-specific) minimum wage (特定(産業別)最低賃金) that is set for workers in particular industries.

Minimum wage amounts may be reviewed every year, with revisions typically taking effect around October 1 or later; employers should regularly check news reports and the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) dedicated Minimum Wage System website.
Wages subject to the minimum wage are the basic wages paid monthly. Overtime pay (残業代) and bonuses are excluded from the comparison.
When a company uses a fixed overtime pay system (固定残業代), the fixed overtime portion must be excluded from the wage amount used to check compliance with the minimum wage.
The next section (ツボ 032) covers the overall flow of payroll (salary) calculation.

The five principles of wage payment (賃金支払の五原則) under Japanese labor standards: payment in currency (通貨払い), direct payment to the worker (直接払い), payment in full (全額払い), payment at least once a month (毎月1回以上払い), and payment on a regularly scheduled date (一定期日払い).
Payment in kind (現物支給) of commuter passes (通勤定期券) requires conclusion of a labor-management agreement (労使協定).
Bank transfer of wages (銀行口座への給与振込) requires the individual worker's consent (労働者本人の同意).
Deductions from wages (賃金からの控除) for items such as company housing rent (社宅家賃), training costs (研修費用), or labor union dues (労働組合の組合費) require a labor-management agreement (労使協定).

Exceptions to the currency, full-amount, and related principles are tightly constrained: in-kind commuting benefits and certain deductions cannot be made unilaterally and need either worker consent or a formal 労使協定.
Monthly salary systems (月給制) are prone to overlooking or missing minimum wage (最低賃金) compliance checks, so extra caution is required.
To verify minimum-wage compliance for monthly-salaried workers, convert the monthly pay into an equivalent hourly wage (時給換算) and compare that figure against the applicable minimum wage.
Monthly payroll calculation consists of three sequential processes: attendance aggregation (勤怠集計), payment amount calculation (支給額計算), and deduction amount calculation (控除額計算).
Attendance aggregation calculates and verifies each employee's working hours and leave/holidays (as covered in Chapter 3). The critical point is the attendance system's initial settings.

Common attendance-system setting errors include: improper rounding of working hours under labor law; mis-aggregation of actual working hours under flextime; and failure to count statutory overtime beyond 40 hours per week.
Even when initial settings are wrong, attendance systems still produce seemingly correct automatic totals, which frequently causes long-term unpaid wages.

Payment-amount calculation uses attendance results to compute basic salary, allowances, and premium wages (overtime, holiday, late-night) in accordance with the Labor Standards Act and the work rules (Chapter 2).
The key to premium-wage calculation is correctly deriving the hourly rate that serves as the statutory basis (see ツボ 033).
For monthly-salary employees, confirm that the 'average prescribed working hours per month' (ツボ 027) is correctly reflected in the payroll software.
Lateness, early leaving, and absence are generally deducted from pay under the no-work-no-pay principle.
Deduction-amount calculation computes insurance premiums and taxes and subtracts them from the gross payment.
Employment insurance: each payday, deduct the insured person's share by multiplying total wages by the employment-insurance premium rate.

Social insurance (health insurance, long-term care insurance, employees' pension): premiums are calculated from the employee's standard monthly remuneration. Kyokai Kenpo uses prefecture-specific premium tables.
Income tax: after checking the 'Salary Earner's Dependent Deduction (Change) Declaration,' apply the Withholding Tax Amount Table. Monthly withholding uses approximate rates.

Year-end adjustment (年末調整) is the procedure that settles the difference between the annual total of amounts withheld and the final annual tax liability; it is performed when the last salary of the year is paid.
After year-end adjustment (年末調整), the company issues a withholding tax slip (源泉徴収票) to employees.
Resident tax (住民税) is deducted according to the amount stated on the special collection tax amount notification (特別徴収税額通知書).
After year-end adjustment, the company must submit a salary payment report (給与支払報告書) by January 31 to the municipality where each employee resides.
Municipalities calculate resident tax amounts based on the salary payment report and send the special collection tax amount notification to the company around May each year.
The resident tax year runs from June of each year through the end of May of the following year.
The next section (ツボ 033) covers calculation of extra wages (割増賃金).
Monthly payroll calculation (給与計算) follows a three-step flow: (1) attendance aggregation (勤怠集計), (2) payment-amount calculation (支給額計算), and (3) deduction-amount calculation (控除額計算).
Attendance aggregation extracts correct attendance data for each employee, including attendance days (出勤日数), paid-leave days (有休日数), and tardiness/early leave (遅刻早退).
Payment-amount calculation uses the aggregated attendance data to compute gross pay, including various allowances (各種手当) and overtime/premium pay (割増).

Deduction-amount calculation computes social insurance and taxes and subtracts them from the payment amount; items include employment insurance (雇用保険), social insurance covering health insurance, nursing-care insurance, and employees’ pension (健康保険・介護保険・厚生年金), and resident tax (住民税).
The overall process produces net pay by first determining correct attendance, then calculating gross payment, then applying statutory and other deductions.
Correctly aggregating attendance (勤怠) is the starting point of all payroll calculations (給与計算).
Key statement: 勤怠を正しく集計することが給与計算のすべての起点です

In Japanese payroll calculation, a key issue for premium wages (割増賃金) is whether various allowances besides basic salary are included in the hourly rate (時間単価, the wage amount per hour) used as the calculation base.

The Labor Standards Act specifies an exhaustive (not illustrative) list of items that may be excluded from the hourly-rate calculation for premium wages. Any wages or allowances not on this list must all be included.

Items that can be excluded from the premium-wage hourly-rate base: (1) family allowance (家族手当), (2) commuting allowance (通勤手当), (3) separation/living-apart allowance (別居手当), (4) children's education allowance (子女教育手当), (5) housing allowance (住宅手当), (6) temporarily paid wages, and (7) wages paid for periods exceeding one month.
Matching the name of an allowance (e.g., family or housing allowance) is not sufficient for exclusion; the actual substance of the payment is examined.
Example of non-excludable family allowance: payment made uniformly regardless of whether the employee has dependents or how many family members there are cannot be excluded from the hourly-rate base.
Example of non-excludable housing allowance: a fixed amount paid uniformly according to housing type cannot be excluded from the hourly-rate base.

Strict rules on the premium-wage calculation base exist to prevent employers from suppressing overtime pay by paying allowances separately from basic salary in order to improperly lower the hourly rate.

Statutory premium wage rates (割増賃金率) under the Labor Standards Act: overtime premium of 25% or more for work exceeding 8 hours per day or 40 hours per week (50% or more for the portion of monthly statutory overtime exceeding 60 hours); holiday premium of 35% or more for work on statutory holidays; night premium of 25% or more for work between 22:00 and 5:00.
The night premium rate is added (combined) with the overtime or holiday premium rate when night work overlaps with statutory overtime or statutory holiday work.
When overtime work is performed during late-night hours, the late-night premium wage rate of 25% is added to the overtime premium wage rate of 50%, for a combined premium of 75%.
In calculating monthly overtime hours against the 60-hour threshold, hours worked on statutory holidays (法定休日) are excluded, but hours worked on other prescribed holidays (所定休日) are included.
Managerial supervisors (管理監督者) are not subject to overtime premium wages or holiday premium wages, but late-night premium wages still apply to them.
Fixed overtime pay (固定残業代) is covered in the following section (ツボ 034).
For monthly-salary workers, premium wages (割増賃金) are calculated from an hourly unit price (時間単価) that serves as the statutory calculation base (算定基礎).

Wages used to derive that hourly rate exclude: family allowance (家族手当), commute allowance (通勤手当), separate-living allowance (別居手当), children’s education allowance (子女教育手当), housing allowance (住宅手当), wages paid on a temporary basis (臨時に支払われた賃金), and wages paid for periods longer than one month (1か月を超える期間ごとに支払われる賃金).
The hourly rate is obtained by dividing the remaining monthly wages by the average prescribed working hours in a month (1か月の平均所定労働時間).
Statutory premium rates applied to that hourly rate are: overtime work (時間外労働) 25% (rising to 50% for hours beyond 60 in a month), holiday work 35%, and late-night work (深夜労働) 25%.
When studying premium wage rates (割増賃金率), distinguish statutory overtime (法定時間外) from company-prescribed overtime (所定時間外), and statutory holidays (法定休日) from company-prescribed holidays (所定休日).
This distinction is required because legal premium percentages and whether a premium is mandatory at all differ between the statutory categories and the merely contractual/prescribed categories.
固定残業代 (fixed overtime pay / fixed overtime allowance) is premium wages (割増賃金) paid in a predetermined fixed amount in advance for a certain number of hours of overtime work (時間外労働).
Companies often introduce 固定残業代 to simplify payroll calculation and to make the apparent offered annual salary look higher, but it is a theme that easily leads to labor-management disputes (労使トラブル).

Even when a 固定残業代 system is in place, actual overtime must still be calculated. If actual overtime pay exceeds the fixed overtime amount, the difference must be additionally settled. Therefore employee attendance/time management (勤怠管理) remains necessary.
If a 固定残業代 system is denied in court, the company cannot claim that overtime has already been paid, and must pay overtime wages again. The impact of such denial is enormous.

Items that can be excluded from the calculation base of premium wages (割増賃金の算定基礎) are limited. If previously paid 固定残業代 is judged not to have been overtime pay, that paid amount is included in the premium-wage calculation base. As a result the overtime hourly rate rises, and unpaid wages often become a substantially large amount.

For 固定残業代 to be recognized as valid official overtime pay, past court precedents require mainly two conditions: (1) 対価性 (consideration / quid-pro-quo nature) — whether it is paid as consideration for overtime work (e.g., clearly stating in work rules, wage regulations, or individual employment contracts that the allowance is paid as overtime pay); (2) 明確区分性 (clear distinguishability) — whether prescribed inner wages (所定内賃金) and the premium-wage portion can be clearly distinguished (e.g., amounts of base salary and 固定残業代 are separately stated on the labor-condition notice and pay slip).

Besides other legal requirements for fixed overtime pay (固定残業代), there are court cases in which companies that introduced a fixed overtime allowance exceeding 80 hours were ruled illegal as a violation of public order and morals (公序良俗違反).
Regarding the number of hours covered by fixed overtime pay, it is desirable to set the amount at 45 hours or less, also taking into account consistency with the 36 Agreement (36協定) on overtime.

Introduction of a fixed overtime pay system should be decided with caution. Once introduced, abolishing the system later constitutes a disadvantageous change (不利益変更) to working conditions, making it difficult to reverse.
If the amount of overtime work varies among employees, a fixed overtime pay system may create a sense of unfairness.
The next section (ツボ 035) covers methods for calculating insurance premiums (保険料).

The fixed overtime pay system (固定残業代制度) is valid only if it satisfies 対価性 (being genuine compensation for overtime labor), 明確区分性 (clear distinguishability of wage components), and proper attendance management (勤怠管理).

対価性 requires that the payment actually constitutes consideration for overtime work (時間外労働の対価) and must be expressly stated in the work rules (就業規則), wage regulations (賃金規程), and individual employment contracts (個別の雇用契約書).

明確区分性 requires that the regular (in-hours) wage (所定内賃金) and the premium/overtime portion (割増賃金部分) can be clearly separated; a typical method is to itemize the respective amounts of basic salary (基本給) and fixed overtime pay (固定残業代) on the labor-conditions notice (労働条件通知書) and pay slips (給与明細).
Attendance management is mandatory because any overtime actually worked that exceeds the hours covered by the fixed overtime amount must be paid as a difference (差額分を追加精算する).
These three requirements were established by Japanese court precedents (過去の判例・裁判例) as necessary conditions for a lawful fixed-overtime-pay arrangement.

固定残業代 (fixed/deemed overtime allowance) is prone to recognition gaps or misunderstandings (認識違い) during hiring/recruitment (採用), because candidates may not clearly grasp how the fixed amount relates to actual overtime hours or statutory overtime pay.

When issuing the labor-conditions notification (労働条件通知), employers should therefore give a careful, thorough explanation (丁寧な説明) of how the 固定残業代 is calculated, what hours it covers, and how additional overtime beyond that amount will be paid.
Social insurance premiums in Japan (健康保険料 health insurance and 厚生年金保険料 welfare pension insurance) are shared by both the company and the worker; the worker's share is deducted from monthly salary.
Calculating social insurance premiums requires determining the 標準報酬月額 (standard monthly remuneration / hyōjun hōshū getsugaku).
報酬月額 (monthly remuneration) is the total monthly cash payment of basic salary plus various allowances, excluding bonuses and similar payments.
Standard monthly remuneration and 等級 (grade / tōkyū) are obtained by mapping monthly remuneration onto the official insurance premium amount table.

定時決定 (regular determination): standard monthly remuneration and grade are normally fixed from the April–May–June monthly remunerations and then applied from September through August of the following year.

資格取得時決定 (determination at qualification acquisition): at hiring, because there is no payment history, the company reports the expected monthly amount based on work rules or the labor contract; estimated commuting allowance and overtime pay must be included in that amount.
Social insurance premiums for the previous month are deducted from the current month’s payroll, so a timing lag exists between a change in standard monthly remuneration and the actual deduction.
現物給与 (in-kind benefits / genbutsu kyūyo) count as remuneration: meals, company housing, dormitories, etc., provided by the employer are included, not only cash.
In-kind meals and housing are converted to yen using the 全国現物給与価額一覧表 (National In-kind Benefit Value List) prescribed by the Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare.
雇用保険料 (employment insurance premiums) are likewise deducted from monthly salary for the worker’s share.
Employment insurance is calculated by multiplying the total wages subject to labor insurance by the employment-insurance premium rate that applies to that type of business.
Unlike social insurance, employment-insurance amounts change every month whenever the wage total changes.
Premium rates are reviewed every year, so the latest information should be confirmed on the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare website and similar sources.
Labor insurance premiums (労働保険料) combine employment insurance premiums (雇用保険料) and workers' accident compensation insurance premiums (労災保険料).
Labor insurance premiums are calculated using an insurance year of one year from April 1 to March 31 of the following year.
Declaration and payment of estimated premiums for the next fiscal year and confirmed premiums for the previous fiscal year are implemented at the same time; this is called annual update (年度更新).
Annual update is implemented every year during the period from June 1 to July 10.

Japanese social insurance (健康保険・厚生年金保険) premiums are calculated by multiplying the insured person's 標準報酬月額 (standard monthly remuneration) by the applicable premium rate; employment insurance (雇用保険) instead multiplies 賃金総額 (total wages) by its premium rate.

標準報酬月額 is assigned in discrete grades corresponding to ranges of actual pay; example grades for Tokyo as of March Reiwa 6 (2024) include 83,000, 101,000, 130,000, 165,000, 250,000, 290,000 and 370,000 yen.

Health-insurance premium rate in Tokyo (Reiwa 6, from March) is 9.98% when the person is not a 介護保険第2号被保険者 (Category-2 long-term-care insured) and 11.58% when they are; the resulting amount is split equally (折半) between employer and employee.
Employees' pension insurance premium rate (excluding certain members) is 18.300% of 標準報酬月額 and is likewise split equally between employer and employee.
Official source of the tabulated amounts is the Japan Health Insurance Association (全国健康保険協会) 令和6年度保険料額表 effective from March 2024.
Social insurance premiums (社会保険料) are paid monthly (毎月納付).
Employment insurance premiums (雇用保険料) are paid once a year in a lump sum (年に1回まとめて納付).

Common mistakes in Japanese payroll calculation (給与計算) often occur when deducting social insurance premiums (社会保険料) and employment insurance premiums (雇用保険料). Four key points requiring caution are covered.

Point 1: Failure to reflect ad-hoc revisions (随時改定) of social insurance premiums. Regular determination (定時決定) of health insurance premiums (健康保険料) and employee pension insurance premiums (厚生年金保険料) is normally based on April, May, and June, applying from September through the following August.

Ad-hoc revision (随時改定) occurs when a raise or reduction in fixed wages causes a large change in remuneration, updating the standard monthly remuneration (標準報酬月額) and grade without waiting for regular determination.

Both conditions must be met for 随時改定: (1) a difference of 2 grades or more between the standard remuneration monthly amount from the 3 months of paid remuneration and the previous amount; (2) payment foundation days (支払基礎日数) of 17 days in all three months. The revision then applies from the 4th month counted from the month the changed remuneration was first received (example: variation in April-paid salary revises from July).
To prevent missed 随時改定 reflections, create a management table. When introducing a payroll system, choose one with automatic detection and alert functions for 随時改定.

Point 2: Failure to reflect health insurance premium rate (健康保険料率) revisions. Rates are reviewed annually and typically revised from March each year (for Association Kenpo / 協会けんぽ). Rates differ by prefecture. Obtain the latest premium amount table from the Association Kenpo website.

Point 3: Missing the start timing of nursing care insurance premiums (介護保険料). Health insurance enrollees aged 40–64 pay nursing care insurance added onto health insurance premiums. Collection starts upon reaching full age 40. A frequent payroll error is missing the age-based premium rate switch procedure.
Legally, age is incremented on the day before the birthday. Example: a person with a December 1 birthday reaches age 40 on November 30, so nursing care premiums apply from November.
Point 4 (text truncated): Missing notification/filing of lump-sum payments (一時金の届出漏れ).

In Japanese social insurance (社会保険), when paying a bonus (賞与) fewer than 4 times per year, submit the required notification to the pension office (年金事務所) and deduct social insurance contributions from the payment. If paid 4 or more times a year, the amount is treated as ordinary remuneration (通常の報酬) and the bonus-specific filing is unnecessary.

One-time payments that do not look like typical bonuses can still be classified as 賞与 under social insurance rules. Examples include inflation allowance (インフレ手当) and employee referral/referral bonus (社員紹介手当 / リファラル手当).
Whenever a new one-time payment is made separately from regular monthly salary, it is advisable to inquire in advance with the competent pension office (所轄の年金事務所) to confirm how it will be treated.
The subsequent topic (ツボ 037) covers the establishment of new allowances (手当新設).

Four common mistakes in Japanese social insurance premium deductions (社会保険料控除ミス4選) are: failure to reflect ad-hoc revisions (随時改定), failure to reflect health insurance premium rate revisions, omission of nursing-care insurance premiums starting, and omission of lump-sum payment reports.

随時改定 (ad-hoc revision): When remuneration changes significantly, the standard monthly remuneration grade (標準報酬月額等級) is updated without waiting for the regular determination (定時決定); a management table is required to track this.
Health insurance premium rates (健康保険料率) are reviewed every March; always confirm the latest premium amount table (保険料額表) to avoid using outdated rates.
Nursing-care insurance premiums (介護保険料) begin collection from the time a person reaches age 40 (満40歳に達したとき); the start date is the day before the birthday (誕生日の前日).

Lump-sum payments (一時金) paid three times or fewer per year require submission of a bonus payment report (賞与支払届) so that social insurance premiums can be deducted from the payment; extra caution is needed for lump sums that are not ordinary bonuses.
Payroll calculation mistakes (給与計算ミス) rank among the top causes of 随時改定 (timely/ad-hoc revision of standard remuneration in Japanese social insurance).
Always perform a double-check (ダブルチェック) on payroll calculations to prevent such errors.

Allowances (手当) are wages paid by a company besides basic salary, such as overtime allowance (時間外手当), commuting allowance (通勤手当), and housing allowance (住宅手当). They have high design freedom and readily reflect company intent within the wage system.
When newly introducing an allowance, first grasp its effects on premium (overtime) wages (割増賃金), income tax (所得税), and social insurance premiums (社会保険料).

Premium wages: Determine whether the allowance counts as 'wages forming the basis of premium wages' (割増賃金の基礎となる賃金). A common practical error is excluding housing allowances that cannot legally be excluded.

Income tax: Always consult a tax accountant (税理士) on the income-tax treatment of the allowance. Certain commuting allowances and business-trip allowances that meet statutory criteria are treated as non-taxable. Incorrect handling can distort employees' income-tax calculations and necessitate redoing year-end adjustments or additional collections.

Social insurance premiums: These are calculated from the standard monthly remuneration (標準報酬月額). Consult a social-insurance labor consultant (社会保険労務士) or pension office on whether the allowance must be included in 'remuneration' (報酬).

Remuneration for standard monthly remuneration comprises 'all things received regularly and substantially as compensation for labor that are applied to the insured person's usual living expenses.' It is not limited to cash; in-kind benefits such as commuting passes, meals, and housing are also included.
If an amount is paid three times or fewer per year, even if labeled an 'allowance,' it is treated as a bonus (賞与) for social-insurance purposes.

Allowances fall into two types: one-time (lump-sum) payments made once when conditions are met, and continuous monthly payments made while conditions continue to be met. Examples of one-time payments include relocation or overseas-assignment preparation money; examples of continuous payments include housing allowance and single-assignment allowance.

Once an allowance is established, abolishing it later (even if it becomes unnecessary) requires addressing the issue of disadvantageous change of working conditions (労働条件の不利益変更). Continuous-payment-type allowances in particular demand extra caution.
When abolishing an allowance, the degree of disadvantage (不利益) for employees currently receiving it becomes large.
Wage systems that include allowances (手当) affect a company's personnel-cost structure decades into the future and are therefore a medium- to long-term theme, not a short-term decision.

Continuing-payment type allowances (継続支給タイプの手当) should not be newly created without treating abolition-time risk (廃止時のリスク) as a judgment factor, because future impact on employees and labor costs is hard to reverse.
The next topic (ツボ 038) addresses equal pay for equal work (同一労働同一賃金).
When newly establishing employee allowances (手当), consider impacts on premium/overtime wages (割増賃金), income tax (所得税), and social insurance premiums (社会保険料).
Also evaluate risks that arise if the allowance is later abolished (廃止時のリスク).
Chart 03Z covers the consideration points (検討ポイント) for creating a new allowance.
Labor/HR staff (労務担当者) initiate and carry out this review before introducing a new allowance.
When newly designing an allowance (手当), always consult both a tax accountant (税理士) and a labor and social security attorney (社会保険労務士).
This dual consultation is required because allowances affect both tax treatment and social insurance/labor regulations.

同一労働同一賃金 (equal pay for equal work) under Japan's Part-time and Fixed-term Employment Labor Act (パートタイム・有期労働法) prohibits unreasonable differences in any treatment—including basic pay (基本給), bonuses (賞与), and allowances (手当)—between regular employees (正社員) and part-time/fixed-term workers (パートタイム・有期労働者) working at the same company.
Being a part-time or fixed-term worker is not, by itself, a lawful reason to withhold allowances or systems that apply to regular employees.

Whether a difference in treatment is reasonable is judged comprehensively, for each item of pay or treatment, using three factors: (1) 職務内容 — the content of the work and the degree of responsibility that accompanies it; (2) 職務内容・配置の変更の範囲 — the scope of possible changes in job content and assignment, including future prospects such as transfers, promotions, and role changes; (3) その他の事情 — other circumstances such as performance, ability, experience, reasonable labor-management practices, and the history of labor-management negotiations.

The law addresses only differences between regular employees and part-time/fixed-term workers; it does not regulate differences among regular employees themselves or among part-time/fixed-term workers themselves.

Practical compliance step: list every pay item or system that differs between regular and non-regular staff and write an explanation of why the treatment differs; use the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's 「パートタイム・有期雇用労働法対応のための取組手順書」 as a guide. If the only explanation is “because they are part-time,” the difference is likely to violate the principle.

Court cases frequently turn on the “支給目的” (purpose of payment) of an allowance. Example: a year-end/New Year work allowance paid as compensation for working holiday-period shifts. The burden of working those shifts does not differ by employment status, so paying it only to regular employees may constitute an unreasonable difference in treatment.

When studying court precedents on allowances (手当), do not look only at the conclusion portion and interpret based on the allowance name (e.g., concluding that a given allowance 'does not become unreasonable'). Many people misunderstand cases this way.
Even allowances with the same name can be judged differently as to whether they are unreasonable (不合理), depending on the purpose of the allowance.
Always return to the 'purpose of paying the allowance' (手当の支給目的) as the starting point for analysis.

After identifying the payment purpose, analyze differences in three elements: (1) job content / duties (職務内容); (2) the range/scope of possible changes in job content and assignment/placement (職務内容・配置の変更の範囲); (3) other circumstances (その他の事情).
Based on that three-element analysis of differences, draw a conclusion appropriate to one's own company rather than mechanically applying a case-law label attached to an allowance name.

This framework is used in the context of determining unreasonableness of treatment differences (related to equal-pay / part-time and fixed-term worker rules). Next topic in the series is the retirement-benefit (退職金) system.

When confirming the rationality of differences in treatment (待遇の違いの合理性) under Japan's Part-Time and Fixed-Term Employment Labor Act, commuting allowance (通勤手当) must be checked to see whether it is paid to regular employees (正社員), part-time workers (短時間労働者), and fixed-term workers (有期雇用労働者) under the same criteria.

If commuting allowance is paid to regular employees but not to part-time or fixed-term workers, or if it is paid to all groups but under different payment criteria, the employer should write down the purpose of the allowance.
A typical purpose of commuting allowance is to compensate for transportation costs required for commuting (通勤に要する交通費を補填する目的で支給).
If differences in treatment exist, the employer must document what the differences are and the reasons for establishing those differences.
An example of equal payment practice is granting a commuting allowance equivalent to the full actual transportation expenses (交通費実費の全額に相当する通勤手当を支給).

This worksheet approach comes from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare guidebook for compliance with the Part-Time and Fixed-Term Employment Labor Act, used to verify that any disparity in allowances is rationally justified.
Merely tracing or copying the conclusions of judicial precedents (判例) is very dangerous as a method of legal analysis.
The purpose of payment for every type of allowance (手当) must be thoroughly examined and scrutinized rather than relying only on case-law outcomes.
Retirement benefit systems (退職金制度) are widely adopted in Japan; the introduction rate among companies with 50 or more employees is about 90%.
A retirement benefit system is defined by three elements: purpose (what it is for), payment criteria (on what basis it is paid), and amount (how much is paid).

Funding and accumulation methods include schemes such as 中退共 (Chutaikyo / Smaller Enterprise Retirement Allowance Mutual Aid), 厚生年金基金 (Employees' Pension Fund), 確定給付企業年金 (Defined Benefit Corporate Pension), and 確定拠出年金 (企業型) (corporate-type Defined Contribution Pension).
Employees' primary concern is typically 'how much will I receive at retirement?' Labor/HR staff should understand the calculation methods and be able to explain them.

Three main types of amount calculation methods exist: (1) Final-salary proportional (最終給与比例): retirement-month salary multiplied by a payment rate that varies by years of service and reason for leaving; (2) Fixed amount by years of service (勤続年数定額): predetermined amounts set in advance according to length of service; (3) Point system (ポイント制): points are accumulated according to chosen factors such as grade, position, and evaluation, then multiplied by a point unit price.
The point system is increasingly adopted because of its flexibility in system design.
A characteristic of retirement benefit systems is the risk of negative surprise at the time of leaving (e.g., receiving only a small sum after more than ten years of service).

When explaining the company's system, many HR staff discuss only the funding/accumulation method; what must actually be communicated is the internal consistency of purpose, payment criteria, and amount.

Employees need to understand the purpose for which the company's retirement system was designed, which payment criteria (years of service, grade, etc.) are therefore emphasized, and how those choices determine the amount that will actually be paid.
Consistently explaining a company's own retirement benefit system (退職金制度) prevents negative surprises (ネガティブサプライズ) for employees.

Retirement-system explanations should not be limited to recruitment interviews and onboarding; they should also be given at later opportunities such as career-design and life-plan training (キャリアデザイン・ライフプラン研修).
Repeated, coherent communication of the retirement system at multiple career stages is recommended so employees understand how the system will apply to them.
The next key point (ツボ 040) covers welfare/benefit systems (福利厚生制度).

A company's retirement benefit (退職金) system should consistently communicate three aligned elements: the purpose (何のために / 目的), the payment criteria (どのような基準で / 支給基準), and the amount paid (いくら支給するか / 金額).
Example purposes of a retirement benefit system include guaranteeing post-retirement living after long service (長く勤めて定年後の生活を保障したい) and rewarding employees for their role contributions (役割貢献に報いたい).

Example payment criteria (支給基準) include years of service (勤続年数), whether the employee has reached retirement age (定年を迎えたか否か), and the employee's role or grade, especially when they have undertaken important roles (役割・等級).
Example methods for determining the amount (金額) include a formula proportional to final salary (最終給与比例), a fixed amount based on years of service (勤続年数定額), and a point-based system (ポイント制).
The design principle illustrated is internal consistency: purpose, eligibility/criteria, and payout method should form one coherent story that the company can explain uniformly to employees.
A system or institution fails when the purpose for which it is carried out is not communicated: 「何のために」行うのかが伝わっていない制度は失敗です.
Core principle: Merely having a procedure or institution is insufficient; people must understand why they are doing it, otherwise the system cannot succeed.
Welfare benefits (福利厚生) are compensation and services other than salary and bonuses that a company provides to employees or their families.
Statutory welfare benefits (法定福利厚生) consist mainly of social insurance such as health insurance and employee pension insurance.

Non-statutory welfare benefits (法定外福利厚生) include health and medical services (e.g., subsidies for comprehensive health checkups/人間ドック), congratulations and condolence subsidies, self-development support, leave systems, recreation (subsidies for resort facilities or sports gyms), and asset formation (retirement benefit systems, employee stock ownership plans/持株会).
Do not copy-paste welfare systems from other companies even in the same industry, because employee needs differ and the copied system may not be effective.
Before introducing any welfare system, first define its purpose: why it is being introduced and what effects are intended.

Welfare systems require funding (原資) drawn from the company's total allowable personnel costs, which must be allocated among wages, bonuses, and welfare; this typically creates a trade-off with other compensation systems.
Although utilization rate is often used as a KPI for welfare systems, proper allocation of total personnel costs remains essential.
Welfare can be used not only to meet current employee needs but also as a symbolic measure that conveys the company's message and helps create a desired organizational culture (組織風土).

Examples of culture-shaping welfare: book-purchase subsidies to foster a self-learning culture; volunteer programs to raise social-contribution awareness; smoking-cessation subsidies to promote health management.
Original, company-specific measures aligned with the company's own purpose convey the intended message more clearly than copied examples from other firms.
Welfare benefits should be considered from both the perspectives of extrinsic rewards (外的報酬) and intrinsic rewards (内的報酬).

Compensation for labor includes both extrinsic rewards (外的報酬) such as salary (給与), allowances (手当), and bonuses (賞与), and intrinsic rewards (内的報酬) such as fulfillment (やりがい) and a sense of achievement (達成感) from the work itself.

Extrinsic rewards are important, but overemphasizing them can make obtaining those rewards the goal, causing originally present intrinsic motivation to be lost. This drawback is called the undermining effect (アンダーマイニング効果).
Effective compensation should be considered from both extrinsic and intrinsic perspectives together, known as total reward (トータルリワード).
Do not copy-and-paste other companies’ case examples; instead define your own company’s purpose and intended effects.
Herzberg’s two-factor theory distinguishes hygiene factors (extrinsic rewards given from outside) from motivation factors (rewards that arise from the work itself).
