Hygiene factors include salary, allowances, bonuses, job titles/positions, physical work environment (PCs, chairs, etc.), and holidays/rest.
Motivation factors include a sense of fulfillment from the work itself, the joy of career advancement, and rich human relationships.
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but do not by themselves create lasting motivation; motivation factors are what generate genuine engagement and satisfaction.
A labor/HR system that is different from other companies but well-suited to one's own company constitutes differentiation and competitive advantage in labor affairs (労務上の差別化・競争優位).
Key statement: 「他社とは違うけれど自社にあっている制度」こそが労務上の差別化・競争優位です

Payroll calculation (給与計算) is not merely clerical or administrative work; it is a highly creative and specialized professional job. Labor/HR staff should take pride in it, maintain an expert mindset, continuously input knowledge of labor laws, social-insurance-related laws, and tax laws, and strengthen communication with both management and employees.

Executives should humanely design “compensation for labor” (労働の対価) from both extrinsic-reward (外的報酬: salary, incentives, etc.) and intrinsic-reward (内的報酬: fulfillment, meaning, motivation) perspectives rather than treating compensation as a purely financial matter.

Over-reliance on intrinsic rewards can become “やりがい搾取” (yarigai sakushu)—exploitation of workers’ sense of purpose or fulfillment. Conversely, attempting to compensate everything solely through extrinsic rewards also has significant drawbacks.
Companies should not be swayed by other firms’ compensation examples. Instead they should conceive an optimal, company-specific overall picture of labor compensation that balances both reward types.

Managers are in the best position to surface employees’ real needs regarding reward-system design—what would raise motivation and enable people to work with a sense of purpose—and to feed those insights back to the company.

A core managerial role is to accurately communicate the intent and rationale of the company’s reward system to team members and to act as a middle-up-down conduit between the organization and employees.
As a working member/employee, the first priority is to understand how to read a pay slip (給与明細).
A typical Japanese pay slip (給与明細) is composed of three blocks: 勤怠 (attendance/work-hour records), 支給 (payments/earnings), and 控除 (deductions). This structure is referenced as ツボ 032.
Form the monthly habit of reviewing every line item on the pay slip and checking that it does not differ significantly from your own records or understanding.
As a working adult (社会人), it is important to acquire at least the minimum practical knowledge of social insurance (社会保険) and taxes (税金).
The following chapter (Chapter 5) addresses 「生活と健康」 (life and health).
Payroll (wage) processing should be performed in this order: attendance aggregation (勤怠集計), payment amount calculation (支給額計算), then deduction amount calculation (控除額計算).
A key point in wage calculation is the hourly unit price (時間単価) that serves as the calculation basis (算定基礎).

When introducing a fixed overtime pay system (固定残業代), the pay must have consideration/quid pro quo (対価性) and clear distinction (明確区分性) from other pay, and attendance management must still be performed.

Social insurance premiums are calculated by multiplying the standard monthly remuneration (標準報酬月額) by the premium rate; employment insurance premiums are calculated by multiplying total wages (賃金総額) by the premium rate.
When considering employee welfare benefits (福利厚生), do not copy-paste other companies’ examples; instead define your own company’s purpose and intended effects.

Related payroll/HR considerations include impacts on income tax and social insurance premiums, and risks that arise if a system (e.g. an allowance) is later abolished, as well as following established rules/provisions and communicating consistently.

The Japanese proverb 「時は金なり」 (time is money) is questioned: the author 坪谷邦生 argues that time has overwhelmingly higher value than money because the total sum of time constitutes one's life itself; without life nothing can be felt and money becomes unnecessary.

Money is required for basic living necessities such as housing, water, gas, electricity and food; in modern Japan living without money is almost impossible. In contrast, without time nothing at all can be done, making time the scarcest resource.
Social ecologist P.F. Drucker stated that 「時間こそ普遍的な制約条件であり必要不可欠な資源」 (time is the universal constraint condition and an indispensable resource).

Michael Ende's children's novel 『モモ』 (Momo) features 'gray men' who steal time. Townspeople persuaded to save 'wasted time' and live efficiently lose their rich, abundant time and their hearts become barren.

In Momo, the time-governing character Meister Hora tells the protagonist: “人間はじぶんの時間をどうするかは、じぶんできめなくてはならないからだよ。だから時間をぬすまれないように守ることだって、じぶんでやらなくてはいけない。” (Humans must decide for themselves what to do with their own time; therefore they themselves must also protect it from being stolen.)
Labor has an aspect of unavoidable hardship performed in order to live. Converting labor time into wages is an exchange of one's most valuable resource—one's own time—for the money needed to survive.

How a person uses their time should be decided by the worker themselves. Therefore labor management (労務) ought to function like Meister Hora: using law to protect the conditions under which people can decide their own use of time.
Labor affairs are closely related to employees' lives and health. During long corporate careers, many employees experience life events such as pregnancy, childbirth, childcare, and caregiving.

Companies are required to provide an environment in which employees can continue working with peace of mind. Corporate duties regarding support for balancing occupational life and family life are stipulated in the Child Care and Family Care Leave Act.

Under the Act on Employment Promotion of Persons with Disabilities, companies have an obligation to employ persons with disabilities at or above the statutory employment rate. The purpose is equal opportunities between persons with and without disabilities and enabling persons with disabilities to demonstrate their abilities.

Regardless of personal life considerations or the presence or absence of disabilities, creating an internal environment in which anyone can realize the way of working they desire is the first step toward better organizational culture.

Work involves potential risks that place a burden on employees' mind and body. Depending on occupation there are risks of occupational accidents, and physical and mental fatigue from long working hours and stress is also a frequent problem.

To mitigate these risks, companies must engage in occupational safety and health management. They need to actively promote measures to protect employee health, such as improving the workplace environment and advancing mental healthcare.

Employees' lives and health cover a very wide range of topics. It is difficult for labor personnel to possess all specialized knowledge, so they first need to grasp the overall picture of external support resources.
External support resources for pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare include municipalities, Hello Work (public employment security offices), health insurance associations, and daycare centers.
External support resources for caregiving include community comprehensive support centers and care managers.

Support for balancing medical treatment and work (治療と就労の両立支援) involves the Industrial Health Comprehensive Support Center (産業保健総合支援センター), medical institutions including the attending physician (主治医), and work-life balance support coordinators (両立支援コーディネーター).
Safety and health management (安全衛生管理) involves the Industrial Health Comprehensive Support Center, medical institutions (attending physician), and the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署).

For consultations on pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare, labor staff provide support regarding assistance programs from local governments (自治体) and health insurance associations (健保組合), as well as procedural support for childcare leave (育児休業).

For caregiving, internal arrangements such as remote work (在宅勤務) or reduced working hours (時短勤務) are proposed based on care plans (ケアプラン) prepared by community comprehensive support centers (地域包括支援センター) and care managers (ケアマネージャー).
The role of labor affairs personnel (労務担当者) is that of a coordinator who organically links internal and external support resources and delivers support tailored to each individual employee.
The following section (ツボ 042) covers support for balancing work during pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare.
Labor/HR (労務) functions as a coordinator of external support resources for employees, connecting the company and workers to the right public agencies, institutions, and specialists.
The core practice is to connect with appropriate stakeholders (適切なステークホルダーと接続する) rather than handling all employee life-event support internally.

Relevant Japanese external resources include: local governments (自治体), Hello Work public employment offices (ハローワーク), health insurance associations (健保組合), nurseries/daycare (保育園), community comprehensive support centers (地域包括支援センター), Labor Standards Inspection Offices (労働基準監督署), medical institutions and attending physicians (医療機関・主治医), care managers (ケアマネージャー), industrial health comprehensive support centers (産業保健総合支援センター), and work–treatment balance support coordinators (両立支援コーディネーター).
Typical employee situations that require this coordination include childbirth (出産), childcare, caregiving (介護), and balancing medical treatment with continued employment (治療と就労の両立支援).
The coordinator role links the firm and its employees on one side with external organizations and experts (団体・専門家) on the other.
Supporting employees' life and health (生活と健康) is itself a source of competitive advantage and differentiation in talent/HR strategy (人材戦略上の競争優位・差別化).
Key statement: 従業員の「生活と健康」の支え方こそが、人材戦略上の競争優位・差別化になります
Under Japan's Labor Standards Act, an employer must not have a woman work for 6 weeks before childbirth (14 weeks in the case of multiple pregnancy) or for 8 weeks after childbirth.

Prenatal leave (産前休業) is a period during which a female employee must not be made to work if she requests it. Because the prenatal period is physically and mentally demanding, employers should create an environment in which employees can take prenatal leave without hesitation.

Postnatal leave (産後休業): the first 6 weeks after childbirth are mandatory leave. After those 6 weeks have passed, the employee may return to work if she requests it and a physician certifies that there is no impediment to the duties she would perform.

Childcare leave (育児休業): both male and female employees may take leave until the child reaches 1 year of age upon request. If the child cannot enter a daycare or similar circumstances apply, leave may be extended until the child reaches 1 year 6 months or 2 years. Childcare leave may be split into up to two periods.

Birth-time childcare leave / postnatal papa leave (出生時育児休業 / 産後パパ育休) is separate from ordinary childcare leave. It may be taken for up to 4 weeks within 8 weeks after the child's birth, including at the same time as the spouse's 8-week postnatal leave. It is also called 'male maternity leave' (男性版産休).

Employers have a legal duty to improve the employment environment so that childcare leave is easy to take. They must implement at least one of: (1) training on childcare leave and postnatal papa leave; (2) a consultation system such as a consultation desk; (3) collecting and providing in-house examples of employees who took these leaves; (4) informing workers of the leave systems and of the company's policy to promote taking leave.

When a worker notifies the employer of pregnancy or childbirth (their own or their spouse's), the employer must individually inform them about childcare leave and confirm their intention to take it, by interview, written notice, or similar method.

Employers are encouraged to formulate a 'childcare-leave return support plan' (育休復帰支援プラン) so that employees can take leave and return to work with peace of mind, and so that the workplace can send the employee off on leave willingly.
When formulating a parental leave (育休) plan, hold a three-party meeting (三者面談) among the employee taking leave, their supervisor, and the HR representative.
After the three-party meeting, conduct a work inventory (業務の棚卸) and then formulate a handover plan (引継ぎの計画).
Required forms and manuals for parental-leave planning are available on the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) website.
Employees—especially male employees—often do not know when or for how long they should take parental leave; the HR department should therefore proactively propose timing and duration.
The next topic (ツボ 043) addresses support for balancing caregiving and work (介護と仕事の両立支援).
A three-party interview (三者面談) should be conducted to formulate a Childcare Leave Return Support Plan (育休復帰支援プラン).

The 育休復帰支援プラン is a structured HR document used to support an employee's smooth return from parental/childcare leave, including fields for the target employee's name, maternity leave start date (産休開始日), expected delivery date (出産予定日), planned leave start date (休業開始予定日), and actual childcare leave start date.

Individual notification and explanation of childcare leave systems (育児休業等の制度) to the employee is an obligation (義務); the plan records the date the systems were explained and the date of individual notification.
The plan records the date of intention confirmation regarding whether the employee will take childcare leave, along with the employee's situation and workplace situation.
An action/initiative plan (取組計画) section lists necessary workplace measures, their contents, and the dates when each initiative was completed.
The template is based on (and adapted from) the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) manual for SMEs: 「円滑な育休取得から職場復帰に向けて 中小企業のための『育休復帰支援プラン』策定マニュアル」.

When communicating a workplace system or policy (制度) to employees, explaining the content itself is necessary but secondary; the highest priority is to empathize with and address employees' anxieties and worries.
Key statement: 内容の説明もさることながら、従業員の不安や悩みに寄り添うことが一番重要です (While explaining the content is a given, the most important thing is to stand by employees' anxieties and concerns.)
Caregiving leave (介護休業) differs from childcare leave because the triggering event occurs suddenly, so companies must respond with no preparation period.
要介護状態 (condition requiring care) is defined as injury, disease, or physical or mental disability that requires constant caregiving for a period of two weeks or more.
An employee may take caregiving leave to care for a target family member in 要介護状態: up to three times per family member, for a cumulative total of 93 days.

A common employee misconception is that 93 days is too short for the family member to recover, so resignation is the only option. The true purpose of the leave is not for the employee to be the primary caregiver during that period, but to use the 93 days to put in place a sustainable system for balancing work and caregiving.
Companies should use internal training so employees correctly understand the purpose of caregiving leave.
When an employee consults about caregiving, first hold a three-party meeting (employee, supervisor, HR) to hear the current situation, consider immediate responses, and explain the leave system.
If the employee lacks basic knowledge of caregiving, advise them to consult their municipal office or a 地域包括支援センター (Community Comprehensive Support Center).

A 地域包括支援センター is established by the municipality and staffed with public health nurses, social workers, and chief care-support specialists; it is a comprehensive consultation window for older people's health and daily living.

Once caregiving methods and services are decided, hold another three-party meeting and, taking into account the care-insurance services the person needing care will use, formulate a company 両立支援プラン (work–care balance support plan).
The overall aim of these measures is to reduce サイレント離職 (silent resignation) caused by caregiving.

Unlike childcare (育児), caregiving (介護) frequently leads to 'silent resignation' (サイレント離職), in which employees quit without telling the company about their caregiving situation because they do not want to cause trouble for the employer.

Companies should communicate and embed their policies for supporting the coexistence of caregiving and work through training and messages from top management so that employees become aware of available support.

A fundamental countermeasure is for the enterprise to build a system that can continue operations even if anyone suddenly takes leave; this is achieved through work efficiency improvements, documentation/manualization, multi-skilling (多能工化), automation, and similar measures.
The next section (ツボ 044) addresses support for balancing medical treatment and work.
Japanese companies are expected to use the 93-day family-care leave period (介護休業) to put in place a work–care compatibility system so employees can continue working while providing care.

A Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) “Work and Caregiving Balance Support Response Model” (仕事と介護の両立支援対応モデル) organizes company actions around training, surveys, consultation, system design, and work-style adjustments.

MHLW supplies ready-made tools for this model, including: an internal “Work and Caregiving Balance Seminar” text for HR; a post-training follow-up survey for employees; an actual-situation (実態把握) survey form; a “Work and Caregiving Balance Preparation Guide” leaflet for employees; a checklist of things employees should find out while parents are still healthy; a checklist of what HR should do when an employee consults about caregiving; guidance on HR–caregiving system design; a checklist of points to confirm when consulting a care manager (ケアマネージャー); an employee caregiving-support plan; and a managers’ checklist for considering work-style adjustments (“働き方の工夫を考えよう”).
All of the listed checklists, leaflets, and survey forms are published on the MHLW website and can be used as-is by companies implementing the model.
The source of the model and tools is the MHLW “Manual for Practical Support of Work and Caregiving Balance in Companies” (企業における仕事と介護の両立支援実践マニュアル).
Support for balancing caregiving (介護) and work should begin with grasping the current situation through methods such as questionnaires (アンケート) and with training (研修).
A practical starting approach for work-caregiving compatibility support is: first conduct status assessment (e.g., surveys) then implement training.
Medical advances have transformed formerly incurable diseases such as cancer into chronic conditions that people live with while continuing treatment over a long period.
As the working-age population grows older due to delayed retirement, companies urgently need to establish systems that support the balance between medical treatment and employment (治療と就労の両立).
The first step in supporting treatment-work balance is to accurately grasp each individual employee's health condition and treatment status.
Close collaboration between occupational health staff (industrial physicians and public health nurses) and the employee's attending physician is indispensable.

According to Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare 'Guidelines for Supporting Balancing Treatment and Work in the Workplace', companies should obtain from the employee: (1) current symptoms, need for and duration of hospitalization or outpatient care, treatment content and schedule, and any symptoms or side effects that could affect commuting or job performance; (2) the physician's opinion on whether work can continue after discharge or during outpatient treatment; (3) recommended work accommodations such as tasks to avoid, overtime restrictions, and business-trip restrictions; (4) other practical needs such as time for hospital visits and a rest area.

Disease-related information is highly sensitive personal data; companies must handle it appropriately. Managers and labor-affairs staff who receive consultations must be trained in information handling. Disclosing personal medical information without the person's consent constitutes power harassment (パワーハラスメント).

Employees who cannot consult their employer about their illness often resign, resulting in financial hardship; this is especially common at the moment a disease is first discovered. Creating an environment in which it is easy to consult and offering flexible working arrangements are therefore essential.

Employees undergoing medical treatment (such as for cancer) may feel confused and be unable to make sound judgments about continuing work; companies should therefore communicate and instill their official stance on treatment–work balance support in advance.
Important supporting measures include setting up an internal consultation desk and creating an always-available consultation environment through regular 1-on-1 meetings with managers.

Cross-company communities for treatment–work compatibility support now exist; a well-known example is がんアライ部 (Gan Ally Bu, https://www.gan-ally-bu.com/), which publishes handbooks and case-study collections.

Practical, highly effective policies include remote-work / telework systems to ease commuting, flextime, accumulated annual-leave banks, and “comeback” (re-employment) schemes that allow former employees to return after recovery even if they previously resigned.
The next learning point (ツボ 045) covers employment of persons with disabilities.

Three key points for supporting employees in balancing medical treatment and work (治療と就労の両立): (1) grasping needs, (2) creating an environment that is easy to consult in, and (3) establishing flexible ways of working.
Needs assessment: Accurately grasp each employee's health condition and treatment status. Cooperate closely with the occupational physician (産業医) and the employee's attending physician as needed.
Consultable environment: Make the company's stance on work-treatment balance support known and permeated in advance. Set up consultation windows/desks so employees can seek advice easily.
Flexible working arrangements: Prepare measures that make it easier to combine treatment and work, such as work-from-home (在宅勤務) systems and flextime (フレックスタイム) systems.

In 1-on-1 meetings between supervisors (上司) and subordinates (部下), it is important to build a relationship of trust (信頼関係づくり) such that the subordinate can also consult about lifestyle and health aspects (生活・健康面).
1on1 (one-on-one) meetings should not be limited to work topics; psychological safety that extends to personal life and health consultation is a key management practice.

Under Japan's Act on Employment Promotion of Persons with Disabilities, private employers are legally obligated to employ persons with disabilities at or above the statutory employment rate, which as of April 1, 2024 (Reiwa 6) is 2.5%.

Employers with 40 or more employees must hire at least one person with a disability; those who fail to meet the obligation may receive administrative guidance from Hello Work (public employment security offices).
Employers with 40 or more employees must report their disability employment status as of June 1 each year to Hello Work.

The disability employment levy system requires companies with more than 100 regular workers that fail to meet the employment rate to pay a levy of 50,000 yen per month for each person short of the quota; collected funds are used to pay adjustment subsidies and rewards to companies that achieve the rate.

Employers must provide reasonable accommodation (gōriteki hairyo) by taking necessary measures that consider the characteristics of a person's disability when requested during recruitment and hiring, unless doing so would impose an undue burden on the employer.
Example of reasonable accommodation at recruitment/hiring: conducting interviews via written communication for a person with hearing or speech disabilities.
Example of reasonable accommodation after hiring: creating work manuals that use diagrams for a person with an intellectual disability.
Regional Disability Vocational Centers employ job coaches (jobu kōchi), specialists in disability employment who support workplace adaptation.
Job coaches advise persons with disabilities on how to interact with coworkers and on efficient ways to perform tasks.
Job coaches advise employers on job designs that allow the person to demonstrate their abilities and on teaching methods that take disability characteristics into account.
The underlying philosophy of employing persons with disabilities is the realization of a 共生社会 (kyōsei shakai / inclusive coexistence society).
共生社会 means a society in which all people, regardless of disability, can participate in society through work according to their own hopes and abilities.
A reluctant or cold stance of hiring persons with disabilities only because the law requires it contradicts this philosophy.
Organizations should mutually recognize each other's circumstances, backgrounds, and diversity—including disability, illness, childcare, caregiving, nationality, and gender.
They should creatively devise assignments and management that utilize people's talents, accept them, and support one another.
Organizations that practice such mutual recognition, creative talent utilization, acceptance, and support are the ones that attract excellent human resources.
Reasonable accommodation (合理的配慮) in the workplace should be provided by discussing with the person themselves and consulting with a job coach (ジョブコーチ).

The provision process for reasonable accommodation consists of four steps: (1) consultation and confirmation, (2) agreement and implementation of accommodations, (3) provision of the accommodations, and (4) review and improvement.

STEP 1 — Consultation/confirmation: Receive an expression of intent requesting accommodation from the person, their family, or supporters. If the company already employs people with disabilities, the company should confirm with the person what circumstances are causing difficulties at work (e.g., by setting up a consultation desk).
STEP 2 — Consultation and consideration: When recruiting or hiring, the person and the company consult and consider together what accommodations are possible.
STEP 3 — Agreement and implementation: The person and the company agree on which accommodations will be implemented, and then carry them out.
STEP 4 — Review and improvement: After accommodations have been implemented, they should be periodically reviewed and improved.
The process is iterative: accommodations are not one-time measures but should be revisited regularly based on the person’s situation and workplace conditions.
Source framework: LITALICO Partners workplace reasonable-accommodation guidebook, emphasizing individualized ways of working (一人ひとりに合った働き方).
Under Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act (労働安全衛生法), companies are legally obligated to ensure workers' safety and health.

Required company measures include: (1) establishing a safety and health management system; (2) measures to prevent worker danger or health impairment; (3) permission procedures for machinery, dangerous substances, and harmful substances; (4) safety and health education; (5) health examinations, interview guidance, and related actions.
The required safety and health management structure varies by workplace industry type and employee headcount.
Basic formation: a General Safety and Health Manager (統括安全衛生管理者) oversees a Safety Manager (安全管理者) and a Health Manager (衛生管理者), with an Occupational Physician (産業医) appointed for medical expertise.
Workplaces with 50 or more regular employees, regardless of industry, must appoint a health manager and occupational physician and hold health committee meetings.

Safety Committees (安全委員会) and Health Committees (衛生委員会) must be established and convened under specified conditions so that workers, including those on site, can discuss and investigate prevention of dangers and health hazards.

Companies must conduct health checkups to grasp workers' health status: a hiring-time health examination (雇い入れ時の健康診断) when regularly employing workers, plus a periodic health examination (定期健康診断) at least once a year thereafter.
Many companies fail to conduct the hiring-time health examination; this is a common compliance gap to watch.
When checkup results show abnormal findings, the company must obtain a physician's opinion.

Company health examinations (健康診断) frequently enable early detection and treatment of life-threatening serious diseases; workplaces should thoroughly aim for a 100% examination participation rate to protect employees' lives.

Interview guidance (面接指導) by a physician must be provided, upon the worker's request, to long-hours workers whose overtime and holiday work exceeds 80 hours per month and who show accumulated fatigue; this obligation includes managerial supervisors (管理監督者).
Workplaces that regularly employ 50 or more workers must conduct a stress check (ストレスチェック) once a year to grasp the degree of workers' psychological burden.
If a high-stress person requests it, physician interview guidance must be implemented.
The next section (ツボ 047) covers mental health measures that should be carried out in the workplace.

Under Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act (労働安全衛生法), workplaces must establish a safety and health management system (安全衛生管理体制), implement health checkups (健康診断), and conduct interview guidance (面談指導) and stress checks (ストレスチェック).

Safety and health management organizations are structured by workplace scale (number of workers) and industry type, with industries classified under Ordinance Article 2 into three categories (令2条1号, 2号, and 3号の業種).
Type 3 industries (令2条3号) include sectors such as transportation (運送), furniture/fittings/household goods retail (家具・建具・じゅう器小売業), and automobile maintenance (自動車整備業).
Workplaces with 1,000 or more workers must appoint a General Safety and Health Manager (総括安全衛生管理者) in applicable industries.
Workplaces with 50 or more workers generally require appointment of an industrial physician (産業医).
Workplaces with 100 or more workers require appointment of Safety Managers (安全管理者) and/or Health Managers (衛生管理者) depending on industry type.
Workplaces with 10–49 workers must appoint a Safety and Health Promoter (安全衛生推進者).
Even in smaller workplaces or certain industries, guidelines recommend appointment of a Safety Promoter (安全推進者).
The organizational chart distinguishes appointment duties across scales including 1,000+, 100+, 50–999, 50–99, 10–49, and 1–9 workers, with variations by the three industry categories.
Workplace safety and health management should be undertaken with a sense of mission to protect the safety and health of workers (労働者の安全と健康を守るという使命感を持って、安全衛生管理に取り組みましょう).
Approximately 1 in 15 Japanese people will experience depression at least once in their lifetime; depression is described as a representative mental disorder.
Workers' compensation applications related to mental disorders have nearly doubled over the past 10 years, making workplace mental health measures a high-priority theme in employee health management.
The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's 'Guidelines for Maintaining and Promoting Workers' Mental Health' states that workplace mental health measures require three types of prevention.
Primary prevention: prevent employees' mental health issues in advance by using the stress check system and improving the workplace environment.
Secondary prevention: early detection of mental health issues and taking appropriate measures.
Tertiary prevention: support for the return to work of workers who have developed mental health issues, among other measures.

Primary prevention is especially important; when stress checks are conducted, group analysis results should be used to identify departments with many high-stress workers, assign priorities, and efficiently implement workplace environment improvements.
The same MHLW guidelines present four types of care as the implementing entities of mental health care; the three preventions proceed smoothly when these four cares are promoted in a balanced way.
Self-care: correct understanding of stress and mental health, grasping one's own stress, and dealing with it appropriately.
Line care: managers grasping and improving the workplace environment, responding to consultations from workers, and supporting the return to work of those with mental health issues.

Care by occupational health staff within the workplace: occupational physicians, hygiene managers, and others supporting self-care and line care, plus planning and implementing mental health measures.
Care by external resources: advice and consultation windows provided by external institutions and experts.
The continuous and planned implementation status of the four types of care should be regularly monitored as an agenda item of the hygiene committee (衛生委員会).
Details on the hygiene committee are covered in Tsubo 046.
The next section (Tsubo 048) explains workers' compensation (労災) certification for mental disorders (精神障害).
Japanese workplace mental health measures (職場のメンタルヘルス対策) are structured around four types of care (4つのケア) as the main approach, through which three types of prevention (3つの予防) are implemented.

The three preventions follow a public-health-style staged model applied to occupational mental health: primary prevention (一次予防) aims to stop mental health problems before they occur by using the stress-check system (ストレスチェック制度) and improving the workplace environment so that employees’ mental-health issues are prevented in advance.
Secondary prevention (二次予防) consists of early detection of mental-health disorders (メンタルヘルス不調) and the taking of appropriate measures.
Tertiary prevention (三次予防) consists of support for return to work (職場復帰の支援) and related measures for workers who have already developed mental-health problems.

The four cares that form the operational core are: (1) self-care (セルフケア) by the worker, (2) line care (ラインケア) by supervisors/managers, (3) care provided by in-house occupational-health staff and related personnel (事業場内産業保健スタッフ等によるケア), and (4) care provided by external resources (事業場外資源によるケア).
These concepts are drawn from the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare guideline “職場における心の健康づくり～労働者の心の健康の保持増進のための指針” (Guidelines for maintaining and promoting workers’ mental health).
For mental health measures (メンタルヘルス対策), using an external consultation window/service (社外の相談窓口) such as an EAP (Employee Assistance Program) is also effective.

Japanese workers' compensation (労災) is divided into two categories: work-related disasters (業務上災害) and commuting disasters (通勤災害). Work-related disasters require two certification criteria: 業務遂行性 (the injury or illness occurred while performing work duties) and 業務起因性 (a causal relationship exists between the work and the injury or illness).

Commuting disasters cover injuries or illnesses suffered while commuting, but only if they meet the statutory definition of 'commute' under the Workers' Accident Compensation Insurance Act. Workers' accident insurance compensates these work and commuting disasters, whereas health insurance covers non-work private injuries and illnesses.
When a labor accident occurs, a Worker Death/Injury/Illness Report (労働者死傷病報告) must be submitted to the Labor Standards Inspection Office.

Mental disorders are harder to certify as work-related than physical accident injuries because the cause of onset is often difficult to pinpoint, making 業務起因性 hard to establish. Certification therefore follows the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's 'Certification Criteria for Mental Disorders Due to Psychological Load.'

A mental disorder is treated as a work-related disease if three requirements are all met: (1) the person has developed a mental disorder that falls within the scope of the certification criteria; (2) strong psychological load due to work is recognized in approximately the six months before onset; and (3) the disorder is not attributable to non-work psychological load or individual (personal) factors.

The presence of 'strong psychological load due to work' is evaluated using the appendix 'Psychological Load Evaluation Table Due to Work' (業務による心理的負荷評価表). If a 'special event' exists—such as extreme long working hours exceeding roughly 160 hours in the month immediately before onset—the load is judged 'strong' at that point without further analysis.

When no special events are present, actual work-related incidents are matched against the 29 types of 'specific events' listed in the evaluation table. Each event type includes concrete examples classified as weak (弱), medium (中), or strong (強) psychological load, and the overall strength is assessed accordingly.
In cases of mental disorders (精神障害), labor and management frequently have differing views on whether the condition qualifies as a work-related accident (労災), so particular caution is required.

When an employee wishes to apply for workers' compensation (労災申請), providing them with the same evaluation form used internally and explaining the B determination criteria helps align perspectives between the parties.
The company should not discourage or restrain an employee from filing a 労災 application; the employee's own wishes must be respected.
However, due to differences of opinion, the employer is not required to enter on the application form any matters that the business owner cannot certify.
The final determination of whether the case constitutes 労災 is made through investigation by the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督) and related processes.
The subsequent section (ツボ 049) covers the private injury/illness leave system (私傷病休職制度).
精神障害の労災認定は、厚生労働省の「心理的負荷による精神障害の認定基準」に基づいて判断される。
精神障害の労災認定の3要件：(1) 認定基準の対象となる精神障害を発病していること。(2) 認定基準の対象となる精神障害の発病前おおむね6か月の間に、業務による強い心理的負荷が認められること。(3) 業務以外の心理的負荷や個体側要因により発病したとは認められないこと。
「業務による強い心理的負荷」は、特別な出来事、または特別な出来事以外（心理的負荷が極度のもの、極度の長時間労働など）に該当する場合に認定される。
業務による心理的負荷の判定は、厚生労働省「精神障害の労災認定」資料中の「業務による心理的負荷評価表」をもとに行われる。
私傷病休職制度 (personal injury/illness leave) has no statutory legal rules in Japan; companies must define it in their own 就業規則 (work rules).
The system provides a grace period instead of immediately dismissing a worker whose ability to work is impaired by non-work-related injury or illness.
Leave duration is commonly set at 6 months to 2 years depending on years of service.

Issuance requirements for a leave order must be clearly specified in the work rules, typically including continued absence due to personal injury/illness for a set period or other work-related obstacles.
A leave order must be issued in writing after confirming the attending physician’s diagnosis and the industrial physician’s opinion.
Because the leave is based on the worker’s own circumstances, unpaid leave (ノーワーク・ノーペイ / no work, no pay) is acceptable.
Health-insurance insured persons who meet the requirements can receive 傷病手当金 (sickness allowance) of about two-thirds of standard monthly remuneration for up to 1 year and 6 months (協会けんぽ).
Companies should institutionalize monthly written progress reports and industrial-physician interviews during leave so that the employee’s medical condition can be monitored.
Attending-physician certificates should not be allowed to expire; they typically state a treatment-needed-until date.

If the employee recovers during the leave period and the company judges return possible, a workplace-return support program should be prepared jointly by the supervisor, HR/labor staff, and industrial physician (MHLW “Guidelines for supporting return to work of workers who took leave due to mental health problems” is a useful reference).
Work rules often provide that failure to recover by the end of the leave period results in 自然退職 (natural retirement), but this is not automatic.
If recovery is reasonably expected within a further 2–3 months, the employee should be assigned light duties until recovery rather than being treated as retired immediately.

For unrestricted 総合職 (general-career) employees, the company must also consider whether other actually available jobs exist and whether transfer/reassignment is possible before deciding that return is impossible.

When the industrial physician and attending physician disagree on fitness to return, the company (via the industrial physician) should, with the employee’s consent, request information from the attending physician.
After sending documents and grasping more detailed information about the medical condition, a return-to-work (復職) judgment is performed.

To carry out an appropriate return-to-work judgment, it is effective to hear the opinion of an occupational physician (産業医) and others, and then implement “trial attendance” (試し出勤) before the leave period expires.
The next topic (ツボ 050) covers health and productivity management (健康経営).

Companies should stipulate leave-of-absence (休職) periods in employment rules (就業規則) and design return-to-work judgment (復職判定) plus a support process (支援プロセス), especially for mental-health-related leave.
When conditions are in place, present a workplace return support program (職場復帰支援プログラム).
Typical process stages: leave interview (休職面談) → progress observation (経過観察) → trial attendance (試し出勤) → return to work (復職).
Leave interview: meeting between the employee and labor-affairs staff; explanation of injury/sickness allowance (傷病手当金); guidance on how to spend the leave period.

Progress observation: monthly written (or equivalent) reports from the employee to labor-affairs staff; regular medical-visit guidance; occupational-physician interviews; collection of the attending physician’s diagnosis.
Trial attendance (試し出勤): experimentally attending the original workplace for a set period, occupying a seat, etc., before full return.
After return: continue observation with regular interviews for at least the first six months.
If the employee has not recovered by the end of the stipulated leave period, natural retirement (自然退職) may occur under the employment rules when return within the period is judged difficult.

The process is based on Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare / Japan Organization of Occupational Health and Safety guidelines for workplace return support of workers who took leave due to mental health problems.
To prevent trouble when a leave-of-absence period expires (休職期間満了時), communication should be in writing (書面) rather than oral (口頭).

健康経営 (Kenko Keiei / Health and Productivity Management) is a series of strategic initiatives that treat employee health maintenance and promotion as an 'investment' expected to raise future profitability and other business outcomes, approaching health management from a managerial rather than purely welfare perspective.

WHO-proposed concepts essential to health management: Absenteeism is absence from work due to health problems (sick leave); Presenteeism is reduced productivity while still attending work, which does not appear in attendance records.
Traditional labor management focused mainly on Absenteeism (leave, long-term absence). Health management additionally requires preventing performance losses caused by Presenteeism.
Health-management scope includes lifestyle support such as exercise, sleep, diet, and smoking-cessation measures.

Japanese government visualization/award systems (led by METI) include 健康経営銘柄 (Health and Productivity Stock Selection, for listed companies) and 健康経営優良法人認定制度 (Certified Health & Productivity Management Outstanding Organizations Recognition Program). Applying for these programs can serve as a company-wide trigger.

Practice process step 1: Position health management in corporate philosophy and strategy. Top-management commitment is indispensable; formulate an explicit 健康経営方針 (Health Management Policy) and communicate it to employees, investors, and other stakeholders.

Practice process step 2: Build a dedicated promotion/execution organization (new specialist unit or assigned existing department such as HR). Avoid simply dumping the work. Example: DeNA established a CHO (Chief Health Officer) office to signal that employee health is a core management issue.
When executing health-management systems and evaluating initiatives, use existing data such as health-checkup information and attendance records to plan concrete measures.
If employees in poor health are concentrated in a particular department, improve the workplace environment of that department.
Use company-wide age composition and smoking rates to design and implement programs targeting lifestyle-related diseases and smoking cessation.
Set KPIs that match the stated objectives so that post-implementation evaluation and improvement can be carried out.
Promoting health management (kenko keiei) directly raises corporate value in the eyes of investors and job seekers.
Health management should not be treated as a narrow HR activity; it must be positioned as a core theme of management strategy.
Presenteeism (プレゼンティーイズム) should be treated as an important theme in management strategy, with commitment from top management (経営トップのコミットメント).
Absenteeism (アブセンティーイズム) cost is given as 4.4% of health-related total costs in the referenced data.
Workers' compensation benefits (労災給付金) account for 0.9% and sickness allowance (傷病手当金) for 1.0% of the health-related total costs.
The cost data come from 3 companies/organizations and 3,429 cases.

Absenteeism is defined as a state in which work itself cannot be performed, including lateness or early leaving due to physical or mental health problems, as well as absences and leaves of absence that make work difficult.
Presenteeism is defined as a state in which, despite attending work, physical or mental health problems prevent performance from rising.
Presenteeism is measured as relative presenteeism using the WHO HPQ: the ratio of one's own performance over the past 4 weeks compared with people doing similar work.
Absenteeism is measured by sick-day counts obtained from a questionnaire.

The material is based on Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) Insurance Bureau guidelines on data health and collaborative health for promoting health and productivity management (健康経営).
In the era of human capital management (人的資本経営), the importance of health management (健康経営) becomes even greater.
Chapter 5 (生活と健康 / Life and Health) summary directs readers to Q&A points 041–050 and gives role-specific messages for HR/labor staff, executives, managers, and all workers.
HR/labor staff should grasp the full picture of employees’ life and health that the company must support, plus external support resources (ツボ 041), and know where to consult for each company theme.
The life-and-health field has frequent legal amendments and easily generates new themes in line with social trends (e.g. ツボ 050); HR must continually catch up on the latest information.
Executives should first understand the concept of health management / 健康経営 (ツボ 050): investing in employee health is important for creating sustainable corporate value.
Promoting health management presupposes top-management commitment; companies should start by verbalizing their philosophy and policies on how they will support employees’ life and health.
Managers need basic knowledge of childcare leave (育児休業) and nursing-care leave (介護休業) (ツボ 042, 043).
Managers should routinely advance internal assignment design, multi-skilling (多能工化), and work-style reform so operations do not stall whenever anyone takes leave or absence.
Managers also play a key line-care (ラインケア) role in workplace mental-health measures (ツボ 047) and should acquire the related basic knowledge.
A career is not a sprint (short-distance race) but a marathon; over a long working life, people will inevitably face life events and health challenges.
When facing such challenges, employees should not hesitate and should first consult the company.
Mental health measures include self-care as an important element (referenced as ツボ047).
Maintaining one's own health so that high work performance can always be delivered is directly linked to contributing to 健康経営 (kenkō keiei / health and productivity management) (referenced as ツボ050).
The following Chapter 6 addresses 社内秩序 (internal company order/discipline).
The framework 「人・本・旅」(hito-hon-tabi: people, books, travel) is presented as a way to polish creativity, in contrast to the basic living pattern 「メシ・風呂・寝る」(meshi-furo-neru: meals, bath, sleep).

Haruaki Deguchi argues that the basics of life should be switched from 「メシ・風呂・寝る」 to 「人・本・旅」. Finishing work early, meeting people, reading books, and sometimes traveling are needed to stimulate the brain; otherwise groundbreaking ideas will not emerge. This appears in his book 『知的生産術』 (Intellectual Production Techniques).

Personal case: Yusuke Iwata joined LifeNet Life Insurance mid-career in HR with no practical experience and initially intended to cover gaps by working more overtime than anyone else. That approach was quickly overturned by Deguchi’s 「人・本・旅」 teaching while Iwata ran the internal study group 「出口塾」(Deguchi Juku).
Iwata later uses workation (ワーケーション) to travel and work across Japan. Active discussion with local people during workation produces new ideas and perspectives that feed back into his job.

Labor/HR work (労務) can be understood as polishing employee and organizational creativity through work-style reform (働き方改革) and thereby promoting innovation; its possibilities are described as unlimited.
秩序 (order) is defined as the sequence and rules by which a society or group maintains a desirable state; it is the situation in which rules have been decided and are being followed.
Even as work-style freedom increases and words like 'order' or 'rules' may feel old-fashioned or rigid, companies still require 社内秩序 (internal company order).

Society-wide analogy: without the order of 'obeying the law,' people who harm or damage others would face no punishment, and a safe living environment would disappear. Laws and penalties exist so that many people can live safely and with peace of mind.

The same logic applies inside companies. Employment rules (就業規則), beginning with 服務規律 (service/work discipline), impose various rules on employees. When an employee violates them, some measure must be taken to maintain internal order; leaving violations unaddressed lowers compliance awareness and morale.

No organization, however free, can do without internal order—just as society cannot say 'if morals and ethics are solid, we do not need laws.' A free organizational climate is built on top of internal order: 'Do it freely—after these points are secured.'
Employment rules can be established unilaterally by the employer after hearing the opinion of the majority representative (see ツボ 017). That does not mean any rule may be imposed.
The judgment criterion is 'maintenance of internal order.' Rules such as service discipline must be clearly explainable as necessary for that purpose.
Example: a rule prohibiting beards or a particular hairstyle may be imposed only when it actually disrupts internal order (郵政事業 (身だしなみ基準) 事件 / Japan Post Service grooming-standards case).
Even a rule that is necessary for internal order is invalid if it excessively infringes workers' rights and freedoms. A company version of overly strict 'black school rules' is not permitted.
Unreasonable or clearly inappropriate school rules are called 'black school rules' (ブラック校則) and have become a target of criticism.
Black school rules are also not permitted in companies (企業においてもブラック校則は認められません).
Recent points of contention in companies include whether side jobs (副業) or RE are allowed (see Tsubo 059) and the obligation for sexual minorities to wear uniforms.
The next section (Tsubo 052) covers disciplinary actions (懲戒処分).
Freedom can only be established on the foundation of order (秩序の上にこそ、自由が成り立つ).
Figure 051 illustrates 'freedom upon order' (秩序の上の自由), contrasting it with 'freedom without order' (秩序なき自由).
Soccer example: except for the goalkeeper and throw-ins, using the hands is prohibited (handling).

Throwing the ball with the hands to score a goal because it is 'effective' is not free play; it is a rule violation that results in a free kick or penalty kick for the opponent and may lead to being sent off.
Praised, expansive 'free play' consists of playing freely while strictly observing the rules and thereby maintaining the order of the game.
Once you create a rule, you must monitor it.

Disciplinary action (懲戒処分) is a disadvantageous sanction imposed when an employee commits an act that violates internal company order. It is indispensable for maintaining workplace order, but because it inflicts significant harm on the employee, it must be applied with great caution.

The principle of legality (罪刑法定主義) from criminal law applies to company disciplinary actions: the content of punishable acts and the corresponding punishments must be stipulated in advance. Punishments not written in the rules cannot be imposed (no after-the-fact penalties).
Grounds for discipline and the types/degrees of disciplinary measures must be clearly specified in the work rules (就業規則) and made known to employees.

Japanese Constitution Article 39 principles apply analogously to disciplinary actions: the non-retroactivity principle (不遡及の原則) means an act that was lawful at the time cannot later be punished by going back in time; the double-jeopardy principle (一事不再理の原則) means the same disciplinary ground cannot be punished more than once.

Disciplinary measures cannot be applied retroactively to conduct that occurred before the relevant disciplinary grounds were established in the work rules, and the same ground cannot be used for two or more separate punishments.

Common types of disciplinary action include: (1) Reprimand/warning (譴責・戒告) — requiring the employee to submit a written apology (始末書) and to reform future behavior; (3) Pay reduction (減給) — deducting a certain amount from wages, subject to legal limits: a single deduction may not exceed 50% of one day's average wage, and the total deductions in one wage-payment period may not exceed 10% of the total wages for that period.
Disciplinary demotion (降格): placing an employee in a lower-ranking position for the purpose of sanctions.
Work suspension (出勤停止): prohibiting the employee from working for a fixed period and not paying wages during that period.

Disciplinary dismissal (懲戒解雇): the most severe disciplinary penalty; immediate dismissal without a notice period. A slightly lighter related measure is 諭旨解雇 (yushi kaiko), in which the worker is first made to submit a resignation and is then dismissed.

Demotion comes in two legally distinct forms: (1) as a disciplinary sanction (懲戒処分) and (2) as an ordinary exercise of the employer’s personnel authority (人事権). Which of the two is being used must be made explicit.

一事不再理 (ne bis in idem / no double punishment) principle: an employee already given a disciplinary pay cut (減給) for power harassment cannot then be demoted as a second disciplinary sanction for the same conduct.

Even after a prior disciplinary pay cut, demotion may still be lawful if it is framed as an exercise of personnel rights based on a judgment that the person lacks the ability or suitability required of a managerial post.

Practical rule: always distinguish clearly whether a given demotion is a disciplinary measure or a personnel-management decision, because the two rest on different legal bases and cannot be stacked as double discipline.
Disciplinary actions (懲戒処分) in a company exist to maintain internal order (社内秩序) and must follow principles analogous to criminal and constitutional law.

Principle of legality (罪刑法定主義): An employer cannot impose discipline unless the 'offense' (罪) and the 'punishment' (罰) have been clearly stipulated in the employment rules (就業規則) in advance. After-the-fact (後出し) rules or punishments are not permitted.

Principle of non-retroactivity (不遡及の原則): Newly established disciplinary rules cannot be applied retroactively to facts that occurred before the rules were enacted. Past conduct is not subject to later-created sanctions.

One-punishment / ne bis in idem principle: For the same matter, disciplinary action may be imposed only once. An employer cannot impose two or more disciplinary sanctions for the same incident, analogous to not stacking overlapping criminal liability for the same criminal act.

These constraints (legality, non-retroactivity, and prohibition of double punishment) are applications of legal and constitutional principles to workplace disciplinary procedures, as summarized in Figure 052 (懲戒処分に適用される原則).
A key distinction to clarify in employment/HR contexts is whether demotion (降格) constitutes a disciplinary action/punishment (懲戒処分) or an exercise of personnel/management rights (人事権の行使).
This classification matters because the legal standards, procedures, justifications, and employee protections differ depending on which category the demotion falls under.

When a scandal or misconduct occurs that may constitute a disciplinary ground, first investigate the facts: conduct interviews (事情聴取) with the parties and related persons, and collect objective evidence such as emails.
Base fact-finding on 5W1H (いつ、誰が、どこで、何を、どうした — when, who, where, what, how) to establish the facts of the conduct in question. The fact-finding process is often neglected.
Until proficiency in fact-finding is achieved, it is desirable to have a lawyer or other expert accompany the investigation of the facts.
Once facts are established, individually match each act against the specific disciplinary grounds (懲戒事由) listed in the employment rules (就業規則) and make a judgment.
Disciplinary action (懲戒処分) is a penalty to maintain internal company order. Because it imposes a disadvantageous measure on the worker, the procedures require considerable strictness.

Procedures stipulated in the employment rules must be followed exactly. Example: if the rules state that disciplinary decisions must be made via resolution of the rewards-and-punishments committee (賞罰委員会), that resolution step is mandatory.
If the employment rules require that an opportunity to explain (弁明の機会) be given before a disciplinary decision, that opportunity must not be omitted.

Labor Contract Act (労働契約法) Article 15 provides that a disciplinary action lacking objectively reasonable grounds and not recognized as socially appropriate constitutes an abuse of rights (権利濫用) and is invalid.

Disciplinary actions are frequently litigated. If a court finds the company’s action to be an abuse of rights, the discipline itself is invalid and the company may also face liability for damages to the worker.
A common issue in determining abuse of disciplinary authority is the balance between the content and maliciousness of the worker’s conduct and the severity of the punishment imposed.
When imposing disciplinary action, being carried away by the sentiment that a heavy punishment should be given makes it difficult to guarantee objectivity.
Have the investigation report also reviewed by external experts and make a calm judgment on the severity of the punishment (see tip 084).
If disciplinary action has been taken in similar cases in the past, also consider whether the current disposition lacks balance compared with the content of those earlier punishments.
The next tip (054) explains the types of harassment.
Disciplinary action (懲戒処分) follows a four-step process: fact investigation (事実の調査), fact determination (事実認定), decision of the sanction (処分の決定), and written notification to the employee (本人への通達).
Core principles throughout the process are strict adherence to procedure (手続きの厳守), guaranteeing objectivity (客観性の担保), and accompaniment by specialists (専門家の伴走).

Fact investigation must establish 5W1H (いつ、誰が、どこで、何を、どうした) by interviewing the employee and related parties and recording every statement in writing, while collecting objective evidence such as e-mails.
Facts the employee admits are certified as established; facts the employee denies may still be certified if supported by objective evidence.
The sanction decision requires mapping each certified act individually onto the disciplinary grounds listed in the work rules (就業規則).
Notification of the sanction must always be given in writing.
When conducting an investigation (調査), one must take care that subjectivity (主観) and imagination (想像) do not become mixed in.
This is a methodological caution to preserve objectivity and factual accuracy during research or inquiry.

In Japanese law, legally defined workplace harassment consists of three types: power harassment (パワーハラスメント / パワハラ), sexual harassment (セクシュアルハラスメント / セクハラ), and pregnancy/childbirth/childcare-leave etc. harassment (マタハラ / パタハラ / ケアハラ).

Customer harassment (カスタマーハラスメント / カスハラ)—severe nuisance conduct from customers, business partners, facility users, etc.—has been added to the workers’ compensation certification criteria for mental disorders.
Guidelines also require prevention measures against sexual harassment and power harassment directed at students during job hunting or internships.

Power harassment is defined as workplace conduct that satisfies all three elements: (1) words or actions based on a superior relationship, (2) that exceed what is necessary and reasonable for the performance of work, and (3) that harm the worker’s employment environment.

Whether the employment environment is harmed is judged by the perception of an average (socially typical) worker, not solely by the individual’s subjective feeling. Proper, necessary, and reasonable work instructions or guidance do not constitute power harassment.

Sexual harassment is unwanted sexual remarks or behavior in the workplace that either inflicts a disadvantage on the worker’s working conditions or harms the employment environment. It is classified into quid-pro-quo type (対価型) and hostile-environment type (環境型).
Quid-pro-quo example: an employer in the office demands a sexual relationship from a worker and, after refusal, dismisses the worker.
Hostile-environment example: obscene posters displayed in the office cause a worker distress and prevent concentration on work.

Maternity/paternity/care harassment (マタハラ/パタハラ/ケアハラ) is defined as harm to the employment environment of workers who have requested or taken pregnancy, childbirth, childcare leave, nursing-care leave, or similar, caused by words or actions of superiors or colleagues.
These forms of harassment are classified into two main types: harassment targeting use of the relevant systems (制度等の利用への嫌がらせ型) and harassment targeting the worker’s condition or state (状態への嫌がらせ型).
Example of system-use harassment: after a worker consults a supervisor about taking childcare leave, the supervisor says ‘It’s unthinkable for a man to take childcare leave.’
Example of condition-based harassment: colleagues repeatedly tell a pregnant worker ‘I can’t believe you’d get pregnant at such a busy time.’
Under Japanese labor law, workplace harassment is classified into three types: power harassment (パワハラ), sexual harassment (セクハラ), and maternity/paternity/care harassment (マタハラ・パタハラ・ケアハラ).

Power harassment (パワハラ) requires three elements: (1) speech or conduct against a background of a superior relationship; (2) that exceeds what is necessary and appropriate for work; and (3) that harms the worker's employment environment.

Typical categories of power harassment include physical attacks, mental attacks, excessive work demands, insufficient work demands, isolation from human relationships, and intrusion into personal affairs.
Sexual harassment (セクハラ) consists of sexual speech or conduct contrary to the worker's will that harms the worker's employment environment; one recognized form is the hostile-environment (嫌がらせ) type.

Maternity/paternity/care harassment occurs when speech or conduct by a supervisor or colleague harms the employment environment of a worker who has applied for or taken leave related to pregnancy, childbirth, childcare, or family caregiving.
Study tip for law: first firmly grasp the legal definition (法律上の定義をまずはしっかりと押さえましょう).

Proper work instructions and guidance are indispensable to getting work done, so judging the boundary between them and power harassment (パワハラ) is a difficult point; by contrast, sexual remarks and remarks that obstruct use of childcare/caregiving systems have no necessity for performing work, so whether they constitute sexual harassment or maternity/paternity/care harassment is rarely debated.

Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Power Harassment Prevention Guidelines classify パワハラ into six types: (1) physical attacks, (2) mental attacks, (3) isolation from human relationships, (4) excessive demands, (5) insufficient demands, and (6) invasion of individuality (excessively interfering in private matters). These should be communicated in harassment training.

The most common actual パワハラ cases are type 2, mental attacks. Examples include: speech that denies a person’s personality; repeatedly giving unnecessarily long, harsh reprimands related to work performance; repeatedly giving loud, intimidating reprimands in front of other workers; and sending emails (including to the person and other workers) that deny the person’s ability and make them feel hopeless.

Type 6, invasion of individuality, also requires caution. An example is exposing sensitive personal information—sexual orientation, gender identity, medical history, infertility treatment, etc.—to other workers without the worker’s consent.

Managers often accidentally leak sensitive personal information while intending to be considerate; this is a common real パワハラ case. When disclosure is necessary for job performance, always obtain the person’s clear consent on what may be communicated and to what extent before proceeding.
Discussion of gray-zone cases is fruitless (グレーゾーンの議論は不毛).

Power harassment (パワハラ) determination should start from understanding the three elements of its definition as a foundation, rather than drawing a simple line of 'how far is OK versus where it becomes パワハラ'.
Judging each individual remark or action (言動) in black-and-white terms as harassment or not is fruitless.
If the purpose or motive of an action is to vent one's own emotions (especially anger) onto the other person, any type of remark or action tends to easily develop into trouble.
Even identical remarks or actions are perceived differently depending on the quality of everyday communication and the trust relationship with members or subordinates.

The fundamental solution is not the surface remarks/actions themselves, but (1) becoming aware of the purpose (motive) behind one's words and actions and (2) raising the quality of the relationship (関係性の質).
Subsequent material covers concrete measures to prevent harassment (ハラスメントの防止措置).
Power harassment (パワーハラスメント / パワハラ) is defined as conduct that satisfies all three elements of the official definition.

Element 1: Conduct against the background of a superior relationship (優越的な関係を背景とした言動). This means actions performed against a relationship in which, in the course of work duties, there is a high probability that the person cannot resist or refuse.

Element 2: Exceeding what is necessary and appropriate for work (業務上必要かつ相当な範囲を超えたもの). In light of social conventions (社会通念), the conduct clearly lacks necessity for the employer's business, or its manner is not appropriate.

Element 3: Harming the worker's employment environment (労働者の就業環境が害されるもの). Physical or mental pain is inflicted, causing a significant adverse effect on the ability to demonstrate capabilities; this is judged based on the feelings of an average worker.

These three elements come from Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) guidance on workplace power harassment, sexual harassment, and pregnancy/childbirth/childcare-leave harassment; prevention measures are an employer's legal obligation.
Managers and supervisors (管理職・マネージャー) should acquire anger-management (アンガーマネジメント) skills.
Japanese MHLW (厚生労働省) guidelines legally obligate employers to take specified workplace harassment prevention measures.
Required measure ①: Clarify the employer’s anti-harassment policy and disseminate/raise awareness of it (周知・啓発), e.g., via top-management messages and training.
Required measure ②: Build a system that can receive consultations (including complaints) and respond appropriately.
Required measure ③: After a power-harassment (パワーハラスメント) incident occurs, respond promptly and appropriately.

Additional required measures: protect privacy of consultants and alleged perpetrators and inform workers of those protections; stipulate that consulting (or related actions) will not lead to dismissal or other disadvantageous treatment, and inform/enlighten workers of that guarantee.
Further required action: take steps to remove causes and background factors of harassment related to pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare leave.
Ready-to-use policy-message drafts, training materials, and videos are provided by MHLW’s “あかるい職場応援団” site (https://www.no-harassment.mhlw.go.jp/); using them allows training to start immediately.
A consultation window must be designated in advance and announced to all workers; it is desirable to staff it with multiple people of both genders.

Consultation-window staff need listening (傾聴) skills; counseling-method training should be provided because even a seemingly minor complaint may conceal a serious problem, and poor handling can create distrust toward the company.

Staff must stay neutral: statements such as “this much is normal / you’re overthinking it” or “you also had some fault” reflect personal values or prejudice and are inappropriate; equally inappropriate is over-empathizing by declaring “that is definitely terrible harassment.”
In organizations of a certain size or larger, it is healthier for the harassment consultation desk (ハラスメントの相談窓口) to receive consultations on a constant basis rather than none at all.

「相談件数ゼロ」(zero consultation cases) may look preferable on the surface but actually requires caution (要注意); it can indicate that the consultation channel is not functioning or that employees do not feel safe using it.

Organizations should continuously check two things: (1) whether the consultation window is operating properly, and (2) whether an environment has been built in which employees find it easy to seek advice.
Zero reported cases is therefore not a success metric by itself; the absence of reports can mask unreported harassment rather than prove a healthy workplace.

Workplace harassment prevention measures in Japan include establishing consultation windows (相談窓口) both internally (社内) and externally (社外) so employees can consult as easily as possible, preferably at an early stage.
All employees should receive harassment-related training every year.

The Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) “Akarui Shokuba Oendan” (明るい職場応援団) provides ready-to-use points for setting up and operating consultation windows, lists of usable consultation destinations, and specific tools at https://www.no-harassment.mhlw.go.jp/jinji/measures/inquiry_counter.
Training should deepen knowledge and understanding of harassment prevention measures, effective and efficient consultation responses, and methods of fact confirmation (事実確認).

Ready-made training videos and materials targeted separately at business operators, consultation-window staff, managers, and employees are available from MHLW “Akarui Shokuba Oendan” under “ハラスメント対策研修動画” and “動画で学ぶハラスメント” (https://www.no-harassment.mhlw.go.jp/events and https://www.no-harassment.mhlw.go.jp/movie/index).
These measures form part of Chart 056 on harassment prevention (ハラスメントの防止措置).
Consultation desk staff (相談窓口担当者) must take care not to cause secondary harassment (セカンドハラスメント) when handling reports or consultations.
When a company receives a harassment consultation, it should start the fact-finding (事実認定) process.
First confirm the complainant's (相談者) intentions: present the investigation process and always confirm whether they will cooperate with the investigation.
Complainants often fear retaliation from the other party, so carefully explain privacy handling of the complainant's information and consultation content, as well as measures prohibiting retaliation.

Emergency measures (緊急措置) may be needed to separate the complainant from the accused, such as prohibiting contact, routing necessary work communication through a third party, changing work location, or work suspension (出勤停止).
Work suspension during the investigation stage is not a disciplinary action (懲戒処分), so as a general rule the company cannot avoid its obligation to pay wages.

If unpaid work suspension is imposed as a disciplinary action at the investigation stage, later disciplinary action after investigation may become invalid due to the principle of ne bis in idem (一事不再理の原則).
Hearings should be conducted first with the complainant, then with the accused party.

In the complainant's hearing, gather details of the alleged harassment: when, from whom, and what kind of words or actions were received; also confirm existence of witnesses and objective evidence (e.g. emails) and the complainant's desired outcome (e.g. disciplinary action, apology).
After organizing the alleged harassment acts in chronological order, conduct a hearing with the accused.
If the accused admits the facts, recognize the reported acts as facts.
Even if the accused does not admit the facts, recognize them as facts if there is objective evidence or strong eyewitness testimony (conduct third-party hearings if necessary).
If there is neither admission, objective evidence, nor strong testimony, fact-finding cannot be made. The governing principle is 「疑わしきは罰せず」 (when in doubt, do not punish).
After fact-finding, the process proceeds to harassment recognition, disciplinary action, and recurrence-prevention measures.
After facts have been established regarding an act, determine whether it constitutes harassment according to the legal definition (Tsubo 054).
For the perpetrator, consider disciplinary action based on the provisions of the employment rules (Tsubo 053).
For the victim, communicate a summary of the investigation results and the disciplinary outcome.
Implement recurrence-prevention measures such as harassment training and awareness-raising activities.
The next section (Tsubo 058) covers customer harassment (カスタマーハラスメント) and job-hunting harassment (就活ハラスメント).
Figure 057 (図表057) presents a fact-finding process (事実認定のプロセス) used after a consultation is received.
The process must start only after confirming the consultee’s (相談者) intentions: 相談者の意向を確認してから、事実認定のプロセスを開始する.
The flow begins with receiving a consultation (相談を受ける).
A branch then checks whether investigation cooperation can be obtained (調査協力を得られる) or cannot be obtained (調査協力を得られない).
The process includes judging whether emergency measures are needed (緊急措置の要否判断), with outcomes of not needed (不要) or needed (必要).
Hearings/interviews of the consultee (相談者への事情聴取) and of the other party (相手方への事情聴取) are part of fact-finding.
A decision point asks whether the other party admitted the relevant facts (相手方が当該事実を認めたか), with outcomes admitted (認めた) or did not admit (認めない).
Another decision point asks whether objective evidence exists (客観的証拠があるか), with outcomes yes (ある) or no (ない).
Hearing results (ヒアリング結果) and witnesses/objective evidence (目撃者/客観的証拠) are used as inputs to the fact-finding determination.
Harassment (ハラスメント) is not solely the fault of the perpetrator (加害者).
The company also bears legal responsibility (法的責任) as the employer under employer liability (使用者責任).
Key principle: ハラスメントは加害者だけでなく、会社も使用者責任としての法的責任を負います.
Besides legally defined harassment types, modern HR/labor themes to address include customer harassment (カスハラ) and job-hunting harassment (就活ハラスメント).

Customer complaints fall into two categories: legitimate ones seeking improvement within a reasonable range, and malicious ones involving excessive demands or unjust accusations; カスハラ refers to the latter.

Whether something constitutes カスハラ is judged on two points: (1) whether the customer's demand content is reasonable (e.g., stemming from company fault such as a product defect), and (2) whether the means and manner of pursuing the demand stay within socially acceptable bounds (e.g., not prolonged complaints or violent/intimidating speech and behavior).
Leaving カスハラ unaddressed imposes a large mental and physical burden on customer-facing employees, raises turnover, harms future staffing, and negatively affects the whole workplace.

If countermeasures are insufficient, employees may pursue legal liability against the company. カスハラ has been added to workers' compensation (労災) certification criteria, increasing the importance of taking action.
Prevention measures for カスハラ, similar to other harassment, include clarifying a basic policy, informing employees, establishing a consultation desk, and creating post-incident response procedures.
就活ハラスメント is sexual harassment or power harassment directed at students during job hunting or internships.

Representative examples of 就活ハラスメント include asking in a hiring interview whether the candidate has a romantic partner, and intimidatingly pressuring a job seeker to decline other companies' offers as a condition of receiving one's own company's offer.
Countermeasures for 就活ハラスメント include establishing and publicizing a consultation window for students regarding job-hunting harassment.
When interacting with students in a recruitment context, respond with two or more people whenever possible.
Formulate behavioral guidelines (行動指針) and manuals for employees involved in recruitment activities.
Make some of an applicant's personal information on the entry sheet (エントリーシート) non-public in order to prevent use of personal information for purposes other than those intended.
Job-hunting harassment (就活ハラスメント) countermeasures should be combined with awareness-raising on employment discrimination (就職差別).

Asking about matters for which the person is not responsible (本人に責任のない事項), such as registered domicile/hometown (本籍) or family-related matters, or about thought and creed (思想信条), during recruitment activities may lead to employment discrimination.
Fair recruitment and selection guidance is provided by Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) on its dedicated site for impartial hiring.
カスタマーハラスメント (customer harassment) is defined as malicious complaints involving excessive demands or unreasonable accusations that harm employees' working environment.
Prevention measures required for customer harassment include clarifying basic policy, notifying employees, establishing consultation windows, and creating post-incident response procedures.

Specific tools and consultation resources for customer harassment are provided by Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) site 明るい職場応援団 at https://www.no-harassment.mhlw.go.jp/customer_hara_index
就活ハラスメント (job-hunting harassment) refers to sexual harassment or power harassment directed at students during job-hunting activities or internships.

Because victims of job-hunting harassment exist outside the company, a different response from other harassment types is required; companies should establish and publicize student-oriented consultation windows.
