Specific tools and consultation resources for job-hunting harassment are provided by Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare 明るい職場応援団 at https://www.no-harassment.mhlw.go.jp/syukatsu_hara_index
In conducting business activities, always maintain the perspective of asking whether anyone is in trouble or being harmed as a result of those activities.
A core mindset for responsible business: continually check '困っている人がいないか?' (are there people who are struggling/in difficulty?) due to the company's operations.
Uniform prohibition of side jobs/dual employment (副業・兼業) is not desirable. Court precedents hold that how workers use time outside working hours is basically the worker's freedom.

Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Model Employment Rules illustrate cases where side jobs can be prohibited or restricted: (1) interference with provision of labor; (2) leakage of company secrets; (3) acts that damage company honor/credit or destroy the trust relationship; (4) harming company interests through competition.

The restriction criteria are somewhat abstract. When an employee files a prior notification of a side job, companies should interview the employee in advance to confirm the specific work they plan to perform.
Even if the destination is not a competitor, if the side-job work is a new business it may still fall under grounds for non-permission.
Depending on hours spent on the side job, long working hours can harm health and constitute 'interference with provision of labor.' Confirm estimated working hours in the interview.
Employees trying a side job for the first time may be in high spirits. Conducting anti-social-force (反社) checks on the destination helps protect employees from inappropriate transactions.

A Cabinet Office survey found that over 60% of workers are either already doing side jobs or interested in them. Refusing to allow side jobs is therefore also undesirable from a recruitment-strategy standpoint.
Companies should also consider accepting excellent talent who remain employed at other firms as side-job/dual-employment workers.
Labor management (労務) must be conducted on the premise that personnel with side jobs (副業) or concurrent employment (兼業) exist.
When a worker is employed (雇用) at a side job or concurrent job, working hours must be aggregated (労働時間を通算しなければならない).
Many companies restrict side jobs/concurrent employment under employment contracts in order to avoid the working-hours aggregation obligation.
The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) Q&A X7 states that such contractual restrictions are 'not very desirable' (あまり望ましくない).
When allowing side jobs/concurrent employment, it is acceptable to principally adopt the management model (管理モデル; see ツボ026).
The following section (ツボ060) addresses the stance of rule-making (ルールづくりのスタンス).

Uniform prohibition of side jobs and concurrent employment (副業・兼業) is not desirable; employers should define the scope of prohibition or restriction by referring to the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Model Employment Rules (モデル就業規則).
How workers use time outside working hours is basically the worker’s freedom.

Prohibition or restriction of side jobs is possible only when one of four grounds applies: (1) interference with the provision of labor (労務提供上の支障がある場合); (2) leakage of company secrets (企業秘密が漏洩する場合); (3) acts that damage the company’s honor or credit (会社の名誉や信用を損なう行為); (4) acts that destroy the relationship of trust or harm the company’s interests (信頼関係を破壊する行為や利益を害する場合).
Side jobs are a matter of strong interest to many workers, so a blanket ban is also unwise as a recruitment strategy.
Source framework: Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Model Employment Rules (厚労省「モデル就業規則」).
Companies should accept (受け止めましょう) the will/intention (Will / 意志) of employees who want to engage in side jobs (副業) or concurrent/dual employment (兼業).
Key statement: 副業・兼業をしたいという従業員の Will (意志) を企業として受け止めましょう

When creating and monitoring rules to maintain internal company order, a common debate is whether to assume 性悪説 (theory of innate evil/human nature as bad) or 性善説 (theory of innate good/human nature as good).
Under 性悪説, rules are designed in as much detail as possible in advance and monitoring is thorough. Under 性善説, both rules and monitoring are kept to a minimum.
A frequent pattern is that executives who start with a 性善説 stance toward employees become distrustful after a single labor-related trouble and abruptly switch to a 性悪説 approach.

性弱説 (theory of human weakness) is an alternative to the 性悪説/性善説 dichotomy: even normally rational and reasonable people may commit fraud or take irrational actions when mentally or economically cornered, because everyone has weaknesses.
Personnel management based on 性弱説 means creating rules that preserve important internal order even when a person's weakness surfaces, while also protecting that person themselves.
Corporate scandals and fraud all originate from people.
The Fraud Triangle (不正のトライアングル), proposed by organizational crime researcher Donald Cressey and modeled by accounting scholar Steve Albrecht, holds that fraud occurs when three conditions coincide.
One element of the Fraud Triangle is Opportunity: deficiencies in check/control functions.
Another element of the Fraud Triangle is Rationalization, for example believing that others are doing the same thing or that the impact of the fraud is minor.
Based on the 'weak human nature theory' (性弱説), even people who are normally good can easily develop motivation for misconduct when they are mentally or economically cornered.
Creating a workplace environment in which such motivations for misconduct do not arise is an important role of labor management (労務).

If even minor misconduct is openly left unaddressed without the company warning employees, justification pressure rises among others ('it was allowed for others'), and this can escalate into serious fraud.
Appropriate application of disciplinary action is important for preventing internal fraud (see ツボ052).
The fraud-prevention framing uses three elements: ① opportunity (機会), ②③ motivation (動機), and ③ justification/rationalization (正当化).
Even if motivation and justification are both present, fraud will not occur if there is no opportunity.
Building an organizational structure that is conscious of governance is therefore also essential.
The next chapter covers worker employment: joining the company, transfers, and resignation/retirement.
The Fraud Triangle (不正のトライアングル) states that fraud occurs when three elements are present together: opportunity, pressure/incentive, and rationalization.

Opportunity (機会) arises from deficiencies in check/control functions (チェック機能の不備). Preventive measures include organizing internal business processes, incorporating double-check functions, and creating regular opportunities for external oversight/review.

Pressure/incentive factors include economic hardship (経済的な困窮) and overly strict quotas or norms (厳しいノルマ). Organizations should periodically check, via surveys and interviews, whether unreasonable or impossible demands are rampant in the workplace.

Rationalization factors include beliefs such as 'everyone else is doing it' (周りもやっている) and 'the impact of the fraud is minor' (不正の影響は軽微). Maintaining internal order requires consistent operationalization of disciplinary actions and related activities.
The framework is based on W.S. Albrecht, M.B. Romney, C.J. Cherrington, I.R. Payne, and A.V. Roe, How To Detect and Prevent Business Fraud (1982).
An important role of labor management (労務) is facing and dealing with 「人の届さ」 (human reach/weakness/frailty as rendered).
労務は個別の従業員の就業環境を整備するだけでなく、社内全体の秩序・規律を維持していく役割も担っている（ツボ051）。
ハラスメント事案への対応では、法令や就業規則に則った法的な対応のかたわらで、ハラスメントの相談者に対する親身な対応も求められる（ツボ057）。
労務担当者は、リーガル（法的対応）とヒューマン（人情・共感）のバランス感覚を養う必要がある。
経営者に知ってもらいたい人間観は「性弱説」である（ツボ060）。どんな人間にも弱い部分はあるという前提で、組織のルールや規律を定めるべきである。大切な仲間である従業員を信じられないのは悲しいことである。
社内秩序は経営者を映す鏡である。経営者自身のコンプライアンス意識や道徳的な価値観がそのまま組織に反映される。まずは自らを律し、率先垂範することが求められる。
マネージャーが特に意識すべきは職場のハラスメント対策である。パワハラについては業務上の指導との境界線が曖昧になりがちである（ツボ055）。
過度に敏感になりすぎて部下を指導できなくなってしまっては組織運営は成り立たない。マネージャーは自らの感情を適切にコントロールできるようになる必要がある。
本章（社内秩序）では、労務担当者・経営者・マネージャー（管理職）・メンバー（すべての働く人）それぞれに向けたメッセージが示されている。
Key principle members should know: 「秩序の上にこそ、自由が成り立つ」 (freedom can only be established on a foundation of order); see ツボ051.
Work cannot be accomplished by one person alone.
Workplace relationships with superiors and colleagues are raised through the accumulated efforts of both parties involved, not by one side only.

A common organizational gap exists between 労務担当者 (labor-affairs staff) and 人事担当者 responsible for 人材マネジメント (talent management): the latter often label the former as conservative, while the former criticize the latter as selfish and as treating employees unequally.
The divide is caused by differences in role, not by differences in personality. Realizing this distinction enables smoother communication and collaboration.
Definition of 労務: treat every employee equally in order to care for working people and protect their livelihoods (「働く人をいたわり生活を守るために全員を平等に扱う」).
Definition of 人材マネジメント: invest preferentially/biasedly in particular talent so that the enterprise can win (「企業が勝つために特定の人材に偏りを持たせて投資する」).
Because one function starts from ‘investment’ while the other starts from ‘equal treatment,’ it is natural that their opinions do not immediately coincide.

Practical communication method: when an HR team discusses an issue, always preface remarks with the pillow phrases 「これは労務的に捉えると」 or 「人材マネジメントの視点で考えると」. This framing made previously stalled collaboration flow and raised the productivity of the HR team.
People who simultaneously hold both 労務 and 人材マネジメント responsibilities should first clarify internally: 「今、自分はどの立場で課題に向き合っているのか？」 (From which standpoint am I currently facing this issue?).

Despite different roles, both functions share the same ultimate goal: 「人を生かして事をなす」 (to accomplish work by bringing people to life / utilizing people). Mutual, accurate understanding and respect for each other’s roles is the starting point for bridging the gap.
Upon hiring, the first thing labor/HR must do is notify the worker of labor conditions (労働条件の通知).
Under Japan's Civil Code (民法), an employment contract can be formed orally, so there is no legal obligation to exchange a written employment contract.

Oral-only agreements risk 'he said / she said' disputes and workers being forced into disadvantageous conditions, so the Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) imposes an obligation to explicitly state labor conditions (労働条件の明示義務).
Items 1–6 of the required labor conditions (as listed in the accompanying chart) must be explicitly stated by delivering a written document.
Labor condition notices may be sent by email or via electronic contract services, but only if the worker has requested a non-written method AND the notice can be output to create a paper document.

For part-time and fixed-term workers, additional items must also be stated in writing: (7) whether there are salary increases, (8) whether there is a retirement allowance, (9) whether there are bonuses, and information about the consultation window (相談窓口).

Companies have been referred for prosecution (書類送検) by Labor Standards Inspection Offices for failing this obligation; missing required items is common regardless of company size, so firms should recheck their labor condition notice forms.
A legal amendment effective April of Reiwa 6 (2024) made it mandatory to explicitly state the 'scope of changes in work location and duties' (就業場所・業務の変更の範囲).
Japan has traditionally used membership-type employment (メンバーシップ型雇用) with non-limited comprehensive jobs (総合職) and often left labor conditions vague rather than defining them in detail in advance.

Job-type (ジョブ型) employment contracts are becoming more important for attracting highly specialized talent and foreign workers with strong contract awareness; the recent amendment is seen as the government promoting job-type employment.

Additional explicit-statement duties for fixed-term contract workers now include: whether there is a renewal limit and its content, and—if unlimited conversion rights have arisen—the opportunity to apply for unlimited conversion plus the labor conditions after conversion.
Many companies use their own proprietary templates for labor condition notification documents (労働条件通知書) and employment contracts (雇用契約書).

Considering the costs of responding to legal amendments and similar changes, it is recommended to use the official Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) Labor Conditions Notification Document (労働条件通知書) instead of custom templates.
The official MHLW form is available at https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11200000/001156118.pdf.
The subsequent section (ツボ 062) covers social insurance procedures at the time of joining and leaving a company (入退社時の社会保険手続).

Under Japan's Labor Standards Act (Labor Standards Act of 1947, Act No. 49), Article 15 requires that an employer, at the time of concluding a labor contract, must explicitly notify the worker of wages, working hours, and other working conditions.

Matters relating to wages and working hours, as well as other items specified by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, must be disclosed using the method prescribed by that ordinance (typically in writing).
If the working conditions that were explicitly stated differ from the actual facts, the worker has the right to immediately cancel (terminate) the labor contract.

When a worker who changed residence in order to take the job cancels the contract under the above rule and returns home within 14 days of the cancellation date, the employer must bear the necessary travel expenses.
Mandatory disclosure of working conditions is intended to prevent labor-management disputes and to protect employees.

Items that must always be explicitly stated include (among others) whether the contract has a fixed term, the worker's share of costs such as meals and work supplies, disaster compensation, pay raises, commendations and sanctions, and leave of absence (休職).
Certain of these items must be delivered in writing rather than only stated orally.
労働条件は一つの契約であるという意識を持ち、入社前にすり合わせましょう (Have the awareness that working conditions constitute a single contract, and align/discuss them with the employer before joining the company).
Social insurance in Japan consists of Health Insurance (健康保険) and Employees' Pension Insurance (厚生年金保険).

Corporations such as stock companies (株式会社) are in principle required to enroll in social insurance as mandatory application workplaces (強制適用事業所). The insured persons (被保険者) are regularly employed employees.
Enrollment requirements are independent of job titles such as 'full-time employee' (正社員) or 'part-timer' (パートタイマー).

Requirement A: Weekly prescribed working hours AND monthly prescribed working days must be 3/4 or more of those of regular full-time employees. Example: If full-time staff work 8 hours/day, 5 days/week (40 hours), and 20 days/month, then part-timers with 30+ hours/week AND 15+ days/month also qualify.

Requirement B applies even if Requirement A is not met, at specific applicable workplaces (特定適用事業所) with a certain number of insured persons: 101 or more before October 2024 (Reiwa 6), and 51 or more from October 2024 onward. Short-time workers become covered if they meet ALL four conditions: (1) prescribed weekly hours of 20 or more; (2) prescribed monthly wage of 88,000 yen or more; (3) not a student; (4) expected employment exceeding 2 months.

Upon hiring, submit the Insured Person Qualification Acquisition Notification (被保険者資格取得届) to the jurisdictional pension office (and also to the health insurance association if the company belongs to one). The 'remuneration monthly amount' (報酬月額) must include not only basic salary but also regular allowances such as commuting allowance and housing allowance.

If the employee has dependents, also submit the Health Insurance Dependent (Change) Notification (健康保険被扶養者(異動)届) at the same time. The company must verify both cohabitation requirements and annual income requirements for claimed dependents.

Upon resignation, submit the Health Insurance and Employees' Pension Insurance Insured Person Qualification Loss Notification (健康保険・厚生年金保険被保険者資格喪失届) to the jurisdictional pension office (and health insurance association if applicable).

If prescribed requirements are met, the Voluntary Continued Insured Person System (任意継続被保険者制度) allows a former employee to remain covered under the previous health insurance for up to 2 years after leaving the company.
任意継続被保険者 (voluntary continued insured person) under Japanese health insurance: after losing employee status, a person may continue coverage if two requirements are met.
Requirement (1): There must be a continuous insured period of 2 months or more up to the day before the qualification-loss date (資格喪失日).
Requirement (2): The application must be filed within 20 days from the qualification-loss date.
The application itself is a procedure the employee performs, but the company should still inform and guide the departing employee about the option.
This material is part of social-insurance (健康保険) exit procedures; the following section (ツボ 063) covers labor-insurance procedures.
Health insurance (健康保険) and employees' pension insurance (厚生年金保険) enrollment in Japan depends on the worker's own requirements (本人の要件) relative to the workplace's regular employees.
If the worker's prescribed weekly working hours (週の所定労働時間) are three-quarters (4分の3) or more of those of regular employees at the employer, the worker is enrolled as an insured person (被保険者).

Part-time or shorter-hour workers who do not meet the three-quarters threshold may still be enrolled if they work at a company meeting a size threshold and they satisfy all four of the following conditions: (1) prescribed weekly working hours of 20 hours or more; (2) prescribed monthly wage (所定内賃金) of 88,000 yen or more; (3) the person is not a student; (4) there is an expectation of employment lasting more than two months.

The company-size threshold for the four-condition part-time rule was 101 or more insured persons until October of Reiwa 6 (2024); from October of that year onward the threshold became 51 or more insured persons.
Health-insurance dependents (被扶養者) are determined by two independent tests: the scope of who may qualify as a dependent, and the livelihood-maintenance (生計維持) income conditions.

The scope of dependents is one of two groups: (1) the insured person's direct lineal ascendants (直系尊属), spouse (including a person in a de-facto marital relationship), children, grandchildren, and siblings (these relatives need not live with the insured); or (2) relatives within the third degree of kinship who live with the insured (excluding those already in group 1), plus the parents and children of a de-facto spouse (including after the spouse's death).

Livelihood-maintenance conditions are one of two: (1) if cohabiting, the dependent's annual income must be less than 1.3 million yen and also less than half of the insured person's annual income; (2) if living separately, the dependent's annual income must be less than 1.3 million yen and less than the amount of remittances/aid received from the insured person.
For dependents aged 60 or older, or who have a certain disability, the annual-income ceiling used in the livelihood-maintenance test is raised from 1.3 million yen to 1.8 million yen.
When confirming the requirements for dependents (被扶養者の要件確認), the resident register (住民票) and income verification documents (収入確認の証明書類) must always be checked.
This verification step is mandatory in the dependent eligibility confirmation process.
労働保険 is the collective term for 労災保険 (労働者災害補償保険 / workers' accident compensation insurance) and 雇用保険 (employment insurance).
労災保険 covers work-related injury, illness, or death of a worker, as well as commuting accidents. 雇用保険 covers unemployment and cases where continuing to work becomes difficult.

労災保険 applies to every business that employs even one worker, regardless of industry or size. Employment type (including part-time and arubaito) does not matter. In principle there are therefore no individual join/leave procedures per worker for 労災保険.
雇用保険 has enrollment requirements. Both of the following must be met: (1) expected continuous employment of 31 days or more; (2) prescribed weekly working hours of 20 hours or more.

Example: a part-timer working 3 days a week, 5 hours a day, does not meet the 20-hours-per-week requirement and is not enrolled in 雇用保険. Students (except night school or those on leave of absence) are not enrolled even if the hours requirement is met.

On joining: submit 雇用保険被保険者資格取得届 to the jurisdictional Hello Work by the 10th of the month following the join date. If the employment insurance number is unknown, bring a résumé showing the previous employer; Hello Work can look it up.
On leaving: submit 雇用保険被保険者資格喪失届 to Hello Work within 10 days from the day after the person ceases to be an insured person.

離職票 (needed for unemployment benefits) is issued at the employee's request. For employees aged 59 or older it must be issued regardless of request. It is prepared together with the loss-of-qualification notification and submitted to Hello Work.

If the company and employee disagree on whether separation was voluntary (自己都合) or company-initiated (会社都合), the company records the facts as it recognizes them on the 離職票. Hello Work makes the final determination and investigates if the claims conflict. Facts must not be distorted even if the employee requests it.
When an employee joins a company (入社時), pay careful attention to the enrollment requirements for employment insurance (雇用保険).
When an employee resigns (退職時), promptly issue the separation notice (離職票).

離職票 issuance procedure flow (図表 063): (1) The employer/labor affairs staff confirms employment insurance enrollment; (2) issuance of the 離職票 is requested; (3) the qualification-loss notification (資格喪失届) and separation certificate (離職証明書) are submitted; (5) the 離職票 is sent to the retiree; (6) the retiree submits the 離職票 to Hello Work (ハローワーク).
The 離職票 is the document a former employee needs in order to claim unemployment benefits at Hello Work.
離職票 (rishoku-hyo, employment separation/leaving certificate) is required in order to receive 失業手当 (unemployment benefits/allowance).
Issuance procedures for the 離職票 should be carried out promptly/early so that unemployment benefits can be claimed without delay.
A probationary period (試用期間) is defined as a period for judging an employee's ability and aptitude and deciding whether to convert them to full (regular) employment.

Refusal of full employment during probation (本採用拒否) is considered allowable in a somewhat broader range than ordinary dismissal under an employment contract, but it is permitted only when there is an objectively reasonable reason, judged in light of the purpose of the probationary period, and the refusal is socially appropriate (社会通念上相当).

Common misconceptions—that companies can refuse full employment merely because 'ability was not as expected' or 'the person does not fit the company atmosphere'—are often insufficient; such reasons are frequently not judged to meet the 'objectively reasonable and socially appropriate' standard.
In practice, refusal of full employment during probation should be treated as not substantially easier than ordinary dismissal.

No statute specifies the length of a probationary period; companies set the rules in work regulations (就業規則) or similar. Excessively long probationary periods can be invalid as contrary to public order and morals (公序良俗).

A typical, appropriate length is a 3-month principal probationary period, with a possible 3-month extension (about 6 months total) when there is doubt about whether the employee should complete probation.
Companies should formalize who makes the final full-employment decision at the end of probation and on what evaluation materials; many firms lack a proper evaluation system during probation.

Sudden refusal of full employment only at the original end of the probationary period is undesirable. Once grounds that could lead to refusal are identified, the employee should be given prompt feedback.
If no improvement is shown on items that were fed back during probation, the first step should usually be to extend the probationary period rather than immediately refuse full employment.
Extensions and performance issues should be documented in writing (e.g., evaluation sheets, improvement-goal sheets), not only orally.

Even if no improvement is observed during an extended probationary period (延長後の試用期間), do not suddenly refuse conversion to regular employment (本採用拒否). Instead, hold discussions aimed at mutually agreed resignation (合意退職) and strive for a conclusion that both parties can accept as far as possible.
Even when conversion to regular employment proceeds without problems, it is recommended to conduct an HR interview (人事面談) before the probationary period expires.
After about three months from joining, gaps between pre-joining expectations of the company and actual reality tend to become apparent to a greater or lesser degree.
Identifying and resolving these expectation-reality gaps early is important from the standpoint of medium- to long-term talent retention (人材定着).
The subsequent key point (ツボ 065) addresses job transfers (転勤).
Trial-period (試用期間) operations are used to prevent mismatches between a company and its employees by clarifying expectations, giving structured feedback, and documenting decisions.
At the start of employment, explain the positioning and duration of the trial period as written in the Labor Conditions Notification (労働条件通知書) and obtain the employee’s understanding.
When facts that could justify refusing regular employment arise during the trial period, give the employee rapid, specific feedback on ability and aptitude.
Use mutual feedback from the time of joining to close gaps between the company’s expectations and the employee’s performance or understanding of the role.
If improvement in ability or aptitude is observed, the trial period may be extended (an example of three months is shown) rather than immediately refusing regular employment.
If no improvement occurs, hold discussions aimed at mutually agreed resignation (合意退職) or proceed to refusal of regular employment (本採用拒否).
Because later disputes are possible, every feedback session, improvement plan, extension, and termination-related discussion must be recorded in writing.

The operational flow is: start → explain trial period in the labor-conditions notice → ongoing feedback on ability/aptitude → if improvable, extend or continue; if not, discuss agreed resignation or refuse regular hiring, always documenting in writing.
The trial/probation period (試用期間) is a major dividing line or milestone in employment.
Allowing a trial period to expire in a piecemeal, half-hearted, or gradual manner (なし崩し的に満了させる) constitutes a risk.
Key statement: 試用期間は大きな一つの区切り。なし崩し的に満了させることはリスクとなります

In Japan's membership-type employment (メンバーシップ型雇用), employment contracts often leave work location and duties unlimited, so transfers (転勤) and reassignments (配置転換) are typically ordered at the company's convenience without individual worker consent.

If work rules (就業規則) state that transfers or reassignments may be ordered for business reasons, and such orders are actually issued frequently in practice, the company may legally order them without each worker's consent.
Companies should still correctly grasp an employee's family situation and take the person's wishes into account when deciding transfer orders.

Personnel authority (人事権) is abused when there is no business necessity, when the motive is improper (e.g., forcing resignation or discrimination), or when the order imposes a disadvantage that significantly exceeds the degree a worker should normally endure (通常甘受すべき程度).

Case law treats being forced into single-person assignment (単身赴任) as generally within the range workers should endure, but an extremely serious family situation (e.g., a dependent family member requiring care) can render the transfer order invalid.
The Childcare and Family Care Leave Act (育児・介護休業法) imposes a duty of consideration toward workers for whom a transfer would make childcare or family caregiving difficult.

Worker attitudes are shifting: the popular term '配属ガチャ' (assignment lottery) reflects growing aversion to opaque post-hire placement and a desire for personal career autonomy rather than leaving career formation entirely to the company.
In response, large firms have begun introducing job-type hiring (職種別採用) even for inexperienced new graduates, specifying the assigned job in advance.

The spread of telework after COVID-19 has led companies to revise transfer policies, including abolishing single-person assignments via remote work (examples: NTT Group, Calbee, Fujitsu), introducing remote-location work systems (examples: JTB, LINE Yahoo), and allowing temporary exemptions from transfers.
Some Japanese companies (e.g. Mitsubishi Chemical) have introduced 勤務地継続制度 (work-location continuation systems) that allow employees to remain at the same workplace rather than being transferred.
Traditional ジョブローテーション (job rotation) for 総合職 (comprehensive career-track) employees has been built on the premise that nationwide 転勤 (relocation) is mandatory.
That premise itself should be re-examined from the root: why are 人事異動 (personnel transfers) and 転勤 necessary in the first place?
The following unit (ツボ 066) addresses caution points specific to 出向 (secondment/temporary assignment to another company).
転勤命令は就業規則に定められていれば可能だが、労働者の家族状況に配慮すべきである。
会社は家族状況を把握して配慮する必要がある。育児・介護の状況によっては、転勤命令が「通常甘受すべき程度」を著しく超え、人事権の濫用となるため状況把握が重要。
育児・介護休業法では転勤命令への配慮義務がある。
就業規則への記載がない場合、転勤命令自体が無効になる可能性がある。
会社都合で転勤を命じることは可能だが、業務上の必要性がない場合、または通常甘受すべき程度を著しく超えている場合は人事権の濫用と見なされる。
配置転換について自社なりのポリシー（持論）がなければ、変化する働き手のニーズに応えられない。
Do not halt critical thinking with the conventional justification that 'because it is a sogo-shoku (総合職, comprehensive/generalist career track) there will be transfers and relocations (異動・転勤)'.
Instead, return to and re-examine the WHY (目的, the underlying purpose) of the practice.

This is a methodology for avoiding 'thinking stoppage' (思考停止) on accepted organizational norms such as mandatory job rotation in Japanese companies, by always circling back to purpose rather than accepting surface-level labels.

出向 (secondment/transfer of workers) was traditionally mainly personnel exchange between parent companies and affiliated (group) companies, but recently large enterprises increasingly second their own employees to venture companies they have invested in or formed capital partnerships with. During the COVID-19 pandemic, subsidies were paid for secondments aimed at maintaining employment, attracting significant attention.

The four requirements that 出向 must satisfy: (1) not terminating the worker’s employment but securing employment opportunities at related companies; (2) implementation of management guidance and technical guidance; (3) conducted as part of vocational ability development; (4) conducted as part of personnel exchange within the corporate group.

A secondment order is an exercise of personnel rights (人事権). Therefore it must be stipulated in the work rules (就業規則) or labor agreement (労働協約), or individual consent must be obtained from the worker concerned.
If the selection criteria for seconded workers lack rationality, or if working conditions at the destination significantly deteriorate, it may be regarded as abuse of secondment rights (出向権の濫用).
Prescribed working hours and annual holidays often differ between the original company (出向元) and the destination (出向先). When such disadvantages arise, compensatory measures should be considered.
There are two types of secondment: 在籍型出向 (employment contract with the original company is maintained) and 移籍型出向 (employment contract with the original company is terminated).

In 在籍型出向 a new employment contract also arises with the destination company while the original contract continues. To prevent ambiguity in labor-management responsibility, the division of roles between 出向元 and 出向先 must be clarified in a 出向契約 (secondment contract) or 出向協定 (secondment agreement).

A secondment contract typically stipulates: (1) secondment period; (2) job content at the destination; (3) working hours; (4) break times; (5) secondment cost burden (出向負担金); (6) social insurance and labor insurance; (7) welfare benefits; (8) which company’s work rules apply (出向元 vs. 出向先).

When an employee is seconded (出向), a new employment contract also arises with the destination company (出向先), so labor conditions must be explicitly stated (労働条件の明示; see ツボ 061). Proxy disclosure by the original company (出向元) is also permitted.
Secondment contract templates and examples of labor-condition disclosure appear in the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare handbook 「在籍型出向「基本がわかる」ハンドブック (第2版)」.
During secondment, workers’ accident compensation insurance (労災保険) is in principle applied at the destination company (出向先).
At the time of the annual update (年度更新; see ツボ 035), wages paid by the original company (出向元) must also be included in the calculation.
Items typically addressed in secondment arrangements include whether company rules apply, personnel evaluation (人事考課・人事評価), confidentiality obligations (守秘義務), and mid-term cancellation (途中解約).
The following section (ツボ 067) explains fixed-term employment contracts (有期雇用契約).

在籍型出向 (zaiseki-gata shukko) is a form of employee secondment in which, through a secondment contract (出向契約) between the original company (出向元企業) and the destination company (出向先企業), the worker enters employment contracts with both companies and works continuously at the destination company for a certain period.

To qualify as legitimate 在籍型出向 and not constitute abuse of secondment rights (出向権の濫用), three conditions apply: it must not amount to abuse of the right to second employees; management responsibilities must be clearly defined in the secondment contract; and labor conditions at the destination must be explicitly stated to the worker.
Management responsibilities between 出向元 and 出向先 must be clearly delineated (who performs which functions) so that they do not become ambiguous.
Labor conditions at the destination workplace must be explicitly notified; this notification may be performed by the original company acting as a proxy.

The legal/contractual structure consists of: (1) a 出向契約 between the two companies, (2) an employment contract (雇用契約) between the worker and the original company, and (3) an employment contract between the worker and the destination company.
In Japanese labor law, 出向 (shukko / secondment or temporary transfer of an employee to another company) raises a core issue of which party's labor conditions apply.

A major point of contention (大きな論点) is whether the working conditions of the 出向先 (shukko-saki, the destination/receiving company) or the 出向元 (shukko-moto, the original/sending employer) should be applied.
Key statement: 「出向先と出向元、どちらの労働条件を適用するのかが大きな論点です」 (Whether to apply the labor conditions of the secondment destination or the origin is a major point of contention.)
Many companies mistakenly believe that fixed-term contract employees (契約社員) can have their employment terminated without any restrictions once the contract period ends.
Under Japan's Labor Contract Act (労働契約法), there are strict rules governing 雇止め (non-renewal / refusal to renew a fixed-term labor contract at expiration).

雇止め is not permitted in two main cases: (1) when a fixed-term labor contract has been repeatedly renewed in the past and the non-renewal can be regarded as equivalent, in social common sense, to dismissal of an indefinite-term labor contract; or (2) when there is a reasonable reason for the worker to expect that the fixed-term contract will be renewed at expiration.
If renewal procedures have become a mere formality (形骸化), the legal risk that 雇止め due to contract expiration will not be recognized increases.
For fixed-term employment, the labor conditions notice (労働条件通知書) must clearly state 'whether there will be renewal' (更新の有無) and the 'criteria for renewal' (更新の基準).
Employers should conduct interviews with the employee at each contract-renewal timing in accordance with the stated renewal criteria and implement renewal procedures as defined.

Advance notice of 雇止め is required: if a fixed-term labor contract has been renewed 3 or more times, or if the worker has been continuously employed for more than 1 year, the employer must give 雇止め notice at least 30 days before the contract period expires when it will not be renewed.

After giving 雇止め notice, if the worker requests a certificate stating the reasons for 雇止め, the employer must issue it without delay; the same obligation applies if the request is made after the 雇止め has occurred.

The content of the 雇止め-reason certificate is highly important if a labor dispute later arises; employers should consult experts such as lawyers or social insurance labor consultants (社会保険労務士) before implementing 雇止め.

Reasonable expectation (合理的期待) of contract renewal increases—and therefore 雇止め risk rises—when the work performed is of a permanent/ongoing nature, or when other contract employees engaged in the same type of work have almost without exception had their contracts renewed.

Managerial comments that raise expectations (e.g., 'I definitely want you to become a regular employee of our company in the near future' or 'In a growing company like ours, your work will only increase') also heighten the worker's reasonable expectation of renewal and increase 雇止め risk.
Statements or actions implying continued employment can raise workers' reasonable expectations (合理的な期待) of contract renewal under Japanese labor practice.
If contract renewal (契約更新) can actually be guaranteed, promising it is acceptable; otherwise it should be avoided.
Business environments now change rapidly and organizational policies shift flexibly, creating uncertainty.
In such opaque conditions, managers (管理職) should refrain from casually or independently promising future contract renewals to employees on fixed-term employment contracts (有期雇用契約).
The next key point (ツボ 068) covers retirement age (定年).
Labor Contract Act (労働契約法) Article 19 restricts 雇止め (non-renewal / termination at expiry of a fixed-term employment contract) when either of two situations applies.

Target type ①: a fixed-term labor contract that has been repeatedly renewed in the past, and whose 雇止め is recognized as socially equivalent (社会通念上同視できる) to dismissal of an indefinite-term (無期) labor contract.
Target type ②: a case in which the worker has a reasonable ground (合理的な理由) to expect that the fixed-term contract will be renewed at expiry of the contract period.
If either ① or ② applies, and the employer’s 雇止め lacks an objectively reasonable reason (客観的に合理的な理由を欠き) and is not recognized as socially appropriate (社会通念上相当であると認められない), the 雇止め is not permitted.
When 雇止め is thus invalid, the fixed-term labor contract is renewed on the same working conditions as before (従前と同一の労働条件で、有期労働契約が更新されます).
These rules come from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare explanation of the Labor Contract Act amendment (労働契約法改正のポイント).
It is desirable to establish and operate a personnel evaluation (performance appraisal) system for fixed-term contract employees (有期雇用の契約社員) as well, not only for regular employees.
定年とは、労働者が一定の年齢に達したことを退職の理由とする制度である。
定年を定めるか否かは企業の自由だが、定める場合は定年年齢を60歳未満にすることはできない。
定年を65歳未満に設定している場合、65歳までの雇用確保措置を講じる義務がある。
高齢者の雇用確保措置は次の3つ：①定年の引き上げ、②希望者全員を対象とする継続雇用制度の導入、③定年の定めの廃止。
実際の導入状況では、約7割程度の企業が継続雇用制度を採用している。
70歳までの就業確保は努力義務となっている。
継続雇用制度では、正社員としての雇用は終了し、嘱託社員等として再雇用する形が一般的である。
会社側が再雇用するかどうかを自由に決められるというのは誤解であり、希望者全員を65歳まで働き続けられる制度にしなければ法律違反となる。
継続雇用をしなくてよいのは、就業規則に定める解雇・退職事由（年齢に係るものを除く）に該当する場合に限られ、かなり限定的である。
継続雇用制度は65歳までの雇用機会が確保されていれば足り、定年前の労働条件の維持や希望に合致した労働条件での雇用を義務付けるものではない。
ただし、定年前と全く職務が変わらないのに賃金等の処遇が大きく切り下げられる場合は、同一労働同一賃金の観点から問題となりうる。

The indefinite-term conversion rule for fixed-term (有期雇用) contract employees also applies in principle after retirement when a person is repeatedly rehired as a contract (嘱託) employee and the cumulative term exceeds 5 years.
To exclude application of the indefinite conversion rule for post-retirement rehires, the employer must obtain Type 2 Plan Certification (第二種計画認定) from the Prefectural Labor Bureau Director.
Companies should clearly define the expected roles of senior/re-hired employees rather than assigning them only to auxiliary tasks, which commonly lowers motivation.
In Japan’s shrinking working-age population and labor shortage, experienced senior employees constitute important human capital (人的資本).
Post-retirement evaluation systems and wage systems will become increasingly important to utilize seniors effectively.
The next topic (ツボ 069) covers retirement recommendation (退職勧奨).

Japan's Elderly Employment Stabilization Act (高年齢者雇用安定法) requires employers to implement employment security measures so that all workers who wish to continue working can do so until age 65; failure to do so is a legal violation.

Mandatory employment security measures until age 65 consist of one of: (1) raising the retirement age (定年の引き上げ), (2) introducing a continued-employment system covering all who wish to remain (希望者全員を対象とする継続雇用制度の導入), or (3) abolishing a fixed retirement age (定年の定め廃止). These form a statutory floor that cannot be undercut.

There is a separate effort obligation (努力義務) to secure employment opportunities until age 70. In addition to measures similar to the 65-year requirement, this includes introducing a system of continuous business-consignment contracts until age 70, and introducing systems enabling engagement until 70 in social-contribution projects run by the employer or by organizations the employer commissions or funds.
For senior personnel, organizations are expected to assign activities suited to older workers, clarify roles, and consider continued employment, raising the retirement age, or abolishing retirement.

The 70-year employment-opportunity measures are not as strictly mandatory as the 65-year employment-security measures; the former is an effort obligation while the latter is a legal requirement for all who wish to continue working.
An increasing number of companies are considering extending the retirement age (定年延長) or abolishing the retirement age (定年廃止) in order to make use of senior employees (シニア社員).
Managers often want to dismiss mismatched personnel too quickly; both the worker and the hiring company share responsibility for the mismatch and should address it accordingly.
First step for mismatch: communicate with the worker to identify the cause—the gap between the company’s required standards/roles and the worker’s current situation—and mutually recognize that gap.

Next, jointly discuss with the worker how to close the gap and create a 業務改善計画 (performance/business improvement plan). Setting unrealistically difficult goals can be treated as an improper means to force resignation.
Goals in an improvement plan must be based on the worker’s current abilities; supervisors should provide continuous, ongoing improvement coaching.

Even when both sides work on improvement, mismatch may remain unresolved. From the worker’s perspective, they may be happier at another company; in that case consider 退職勧奨 (retirement recommendation).

退職勧奨 means presenting resignation as an option to an underperforming worker so the worker themselves decides to leave. Legally it is 合意退職 (agreed resignation), not dismissal, though the two are often confused.

退職強要 (forced resignation) is illegal. It is defined as the company applying undue pressure or persistent recommendation to compel a resignation decision. Retirement recommendation itself is not illegal, but coercion is.

Acts that are likely to be certified as illegal 退職強要 include: semi-forced retirement recommendations; and disadvantageous measures against those who refuse (withholding preferential treatment, reassignment, disciplinary action, or denial of pay raises).
When conducting 退職勧奨, first clearly communicate that whether to resign is solely the worker’s final decision, and keep each interview to about 30 minutes.

When conducting 退職勧奨 (encouragement/recommendation to resign), fine-grained considerations (細かな配慮) are required, such as setting a limit (e.g., on number of times) and the rule that if the employee has once decided not to resign, no further recommendations should be made thereafter.
Prepare a script (台本) and Q&A in advance before approaching 退職勧奨.
It is recommended to proceed in collaboration with external experts (外部の専門家), referring to ツボ 084.
The next section (ツボ 070) covers 解雇規制 (dismissal/termination regulations).

Response to mismatched personnel (ミスマッチ人材への対応): Identify the cause of the mismatch, create a work improvement plan (業務改善計画), provide improvement coaching; if still too difficult, use resignation recommendation (退職勧奨).

STEP 1 — Cause identification: Through communication with the worker, identify the mismatch cause; both sides mutually recognize the gap between the company’s required standards/roles and the worker’s current situation.
STEP 2 — Improvement plan and coaching: Jointly examine ways to close the gap and create a work improvement plan; the supervisor then provides continuous improvement guidance.
Caution on goal-setting: Setting unrealistically difficult targets can be treated as an improper means of forcing the worker to resign; goals must be set based on the worker’s current abilities.
STEP 3 — Resignation as last option: If performance still does not improve, present resignation as one option so the worker can decide to resign of their own volition.
Caution on legality: Applying undue pressure that forces an employee to decide to resign constitutes forced resignation (退職強要) and is illegal.
Advice on persistence: Do not immediately decide something is a mismatch; instead, face it patiently and persistently (すぐに ミス マッチ だ と 決め つけ ず に 、 根 気 強く 向き 合い まし ょ う).

Dismissal (解雇) is the unilateral termination of a labor contract at the employer's initiative. It is invalid if it lacks objectively reasonable grounds and is not recognized as socially appropriate under prevailing social norms.
Dismissal is prohibited under certain conditions, including during leave for work-related injury or illness, during prenatal and postnatal leave, and for 30 days thereafter.

Japanese law classifies dismissal into three types based on reason: (1) ordinary dismissal (普通解雇) due to the worker's lack of ability or similar personal factors; (2) disciplinary dismissal (懲戒解雇) for conduct constituting a disciplinary offense; (3) economic/restructuring dismissal (整理解雇) for personnel reductions based on business necessity.

Ordinary and disciplinary dismissals are attributable to the individual worker, whereas restructuring dismissal is not the worker's fault; therefore the latter is subject to especially strict legal requirements.

The four requirements for a valid restructuring dismissal (整理解雇の四要件) are: (a) necessity of personnel reduction; (b) efforts to avoid dismissal; (c) rationality of the selection criteria for those dismissed; (d) procedural fairness of the dismissal process.
If a company implements restructuring dismissals while simultaneously conducting new hiring, the necessity of personnel reduction (requirement a) becomes questionable.
Selection of employees for restructuring dismissal must exclude employer arbitrariness and rest on objective criteria such as work performance and length of service (requirement c).

Failure to first solicit voluntary resignations (希望退職) before implementing restructuring dismissals often leads to a finding that the employer did not make sufficient efforts to avoid dismissal (requirement b).

One frequently cited reason dismissal is difficult in Japan is the underlying membership-type employment system (メンバーシップ型雇用), in which employees are hired as organization members rather than for specific jobs.

Japanese companies under membership-type employment (メンバーシップ型雇用) hold broad personnel authority over transfers (配転), including the power to order personnel moves (人事異動) without the employee's consent when job duties are not specified, provided the order has a basis in work rules (就業規則) and does not constitute an abuse of rights (権利濫用).
Companies in Japan also possess authority to issue transfer orders such as job relocations (転勤) that substantially affect employees' lives.
By contrast, job-type employment (ジョブ型雇用) systems typical of Western countries generally require the employee's consent for personnel transfers.

Because Japanese employers can reassign workers across occupations and workplaces inside the firm, courts have applied strict scrutiny to dismissals: if an employee fails to perform in one department, the company can move them to another rather than terminate them.
This strict dismissal regime is therefore not a one-sided disadvantage to employers; it reflects courts' attempt to balance interests within Japan's membership-type employment practices.
If Japan's employment practices change substantially in the future, judicial judgments on dismissal and transfer authority may also change.
In Japanese employment practice, membership-type employment (メンバーシップ型雇用) is associated with recognition of extensive personnel rights (広範な人事権) over transfers and reassignments (配転).

Dismissals (解雇) are classified by type/cause: (1) dismissal due to the worker’s lack of ability or similar reasons (労働者の能力不足等による解雇); (2) dismissal for conduct that constitutes a disciplinary ground (懲戒事由に該当したことによる解雇); (3) dismissal based on business/management necessity (経営上の必要性に基づく解雇).

For ability-based and disciplinary dismissals, the cause of dismissal is attributed to the individual worker (本人). For dismissals based on business necessity, the cause is attributed to the company (会社).

Economic/restructuring dismissal (整理解雇) based on business necessity is subject to four legal requirements (整理解雇の四要件): (a) necessity of personnel reduction (人員削減の必要性); (b) efforts to avoid dismissal (解雇回避努力); (c) reasonableness of the selection of those to be dismissed (人選の合理性); (d) appropriateness of the dismissal procedures (解雇手続きの妥当性).
Japanese employment case law and judicial precedents (裁判例・判例) have accumulated in accordance with the actual conditions and practices of Japanese employment customs (日本の雇用慣行の実態).

Chapter 7 summary on joining a company (入社), personnel moves/transfers (異動), and resignation/retirement (退職) compiles Q&A from ツボ 061–070 and addresses role-specific messages to labor/HR staff, executives, managers, and all workers.

Labor/HR staff must know the laws and procedures for joining and leaving (ツボ 061–063). Transfers (転勤, ツボ 065), secondment (出向, ツボ 066), non-renewal/雇止め (ツボ 067), and resignation (ツボ 069–070) readily escalate into labor-management disputes; grasp the legal issues and cautions for each and, when a concrete case arises, respond carefully while coordinating with specialists.

Some executives abandon underperforming employees too quickly by treating the situation as a mismatch (ツボ 068). Although executives are pressed for rapid decisions, they must sit down and persistently engage with employees. Causes of mismatch typically exist on both the employer and employee sides rather than only one.

Managers should pay special attention to the probationary/trial period (試用期間, ツボ 064). The beginning of the employment relationship is decisive for preventing mismatch. If performance or mindset concerns appear during probation, hold real-time dialogue with the employee and give the necessary feedback.
As a team member, cultivate sunao-sa (素直さ): the humility and openness to accept feedback without defensiveness.
Feedback arrives through multiple channels: the probationary period, annual personnel evaluations (人事評価), and ongoing 1-on-1s with one's supervisor (see related tips 064 and 069).
Some feedback will be unpleasant or 'painful to the ear' (耳の痛い); accepting it honestly and acting on it is what produces personal growth.
Managers are expected to provide improvement guidance (改善指導) to members.
The following chapter addresses labor-management relations (労使関係).
When hiring, clearly specify working conditions (労働条件) first in order to prevent labor-management disputes (労使トラブル) and protect employees.
Correctly understand enrollment requirements (加入要件) for relevant insurance and related systems.
At joining, pay close attention to employment insurance (雇用保険) enrollment requirements; at resignation, promptly issue the unemployment/separation certificate (離職票).
A trial/probation period (試用期間) is set to prevent mismatch between company and employee; it is possible if stipulated in the work rules (就業規則).
Company-initiated transfers (転勤) are possible, but the worker’s family circumstances should be taken into consideration.

When seconding (出向) a worker: it must not constitute abuse of secondment rights; management responsibility must be clarified in the secondment contract; working conditions at the destination must be explicitly stated.
For ending special treatment or fixed-term arrangements, extra caution is required with non-renewal (雇止め) when the worker has a reasonable expectation of renewal.

Retirement age (定年) should be set by expecting suitable roles for senior talent, clarifying those roles, and considering continued employment, retirement-age extension, or abolition of a fixed retirement age.
For mismatched personnel: identify the cause of the mismatch, create a work-improvement plan, and provide improvement guidance; only if that still fails, consider recommending resignation (退職勧奨).
Dismissal is difficult in Japan because membership-type employment (メンバーシップ型雇用) grants employers broad personnel authority over transfers (配転).
In organizational development (組織開発), what matters is not “やり方” (methods / how-to) but “あり方” (way of being / attitude / presence).
The essence of organizational development is 関係性の向上 (improvement of relationships), not the specific interventions used.
Common OD interventions—taking an organization survey and feeding it back, gathering everyone for an offsite meeting—are only methodologies (“やり方”), not the essence.

A concrete illustration of “あり方”: a colleague who had not yet been able to contribute much to the department decided to contribute at least through energy, greeting everyone loudly and brightly every morning; that greeting was his full contribution, improved workplace atmosphere, and was received as real value.

The same relational, “あり方”-based approach is possible in labor affairs (労務): even a single greeting or a single document exchange can improve relationships when done from the stance of “I want to contribute.”
The colleague in the story (Yoshida Yosuke) later founded 人事図書館 (an HR library/facility); his “あり方” of wanting to contribute eventually helped many HR practitioners.
労使関係 (labor-management relations) refers to the relationship between workers (労働者) and employers/users (使用者, the company).
A good labor-management relationship is grounded in the rights and obligations of the labor contract (労働契約).
Labor Contract Act provision: workers and employers must comply with the labor contract and, in accordance with good faith (信義), sincerely exercise rights and fulfill obligations.

A relationship is not 'good' if workers neglect duties to the company while only asserting rights, or if employers fail to secure workers' rights (leave, wages, etc.) while strongly demanding results.
From the employer's side, properly fulfilling labor-contract obligations toward workers is a core role of 労務 (labor affairs / HR labor management).

Impressive purpose (パーパス), attractive HR systems, and org-development for motivation are insufficient if labor-contract obligations are unmet; workers then lose trust and enter a cynical/apathetic state (しらけた状態).
Relationships have both a contractual aspect and a communication aspect.

Three relationship types: (1) 生ぬるい関係性 (lukewarm) — typical of traditional Japanese firms under lifetime employment (終身雇用) and seniority (年功序列); mutual dependence in which employees surrender career to the company in exchange for life security.

(2) 熱すぎる関係性 (too hot) — common in founding-stage ventures/startups; based on fervor for founder, philosophy, and organization; offers passion and purpose but risks burnout and physical/mental exhaustion.

(3) あたたかい関係性 (warm) — ideal for modern firms emphasizing psychological safety (心理的安全性) and Diversity & Inclusion (ダイバーシティ&インクルージョン); covers relations among management and workers, bosses and subordinates, and colleagues.

A good labor-management relationship (よい労使関係) is a relationship in which companies, business partners, and all people understand each other's positions and values, empathize with one another, and are bound by bonds of gratitude and trust.
The mission of people engaged in labor affairs (労務) is to design the ideal good labor-management relationship.
The next section (ツボ 072) explains the interests/stakeholder relations (利害関係) in labor-management relations.
Good labor-management relations (よい労使関係) are built by first fulfilling each party's mutual obligations (義務) and then aiming for a warm relationship (あたたかい関係性).
Comprehensive communication underpins good labor-management relations.

Relationship types include a lukewarm relationship (生ぬるい関係性), an overly intense/hot relationship (熱すぎる関係性) premised on mutual dependence and enthusiasm, and a warm relationship (あたたかい関係性) bound by gratitude and trust (感謝と信頼の絆).
The labor contract (労働契約) is the foundation of the labor-management relationship.
Workers and employers must comply with the labor contract and, in accordance with good faith, exercise rights and fulfill obligations: 「労働者及び使用者は、労働契約を遵守するとともに、信義に従い誠実に、権利を行使し、及び義務を履行しなければならない。」
Good labor-management relations (よい労使関係) are an extremely important factor that enhances a company's competitive advantage (競争優位性).
Key statement: よい労使関係は、企業としての競争優位性を高める極めて重要な要素です

In pursuing good labor-management relations, conflicts of interest inevitably arise between workers and employers. A representative example is that workers want higher wages while employers (companies) want to keep personnel costs down.

There are two kinds of labor-management relations (労使関係): individual labor-management relations (個別的労使関係) between an individual worker and the employer, and collective labor-management relations (集団的労使関係) between a workers' group (labor union) and the employer.

Labor contracts are concluded between the employer and the individual worker, so individual labor-management relations are normally the premise. However, employers often hold a stronger position than workers, making it difficult for a single worker to demand a wage increase. In such cases workers unite to form a labor union (労働組合) and proceed with negotiation or consultation on an equal footing with the employer; this is collective labor-management relations.

Shunto (春闘) is a representative process of collective labor-management relations: in many companies, labor unions negotiate with employers for improved working conditions toward April of the new fiscal year.

An employer cannot adopt a hard-line stance of refusing all negotiations from a labor union. Refusing a union's request for collective bargaining without just cause is prohibited by law as an unfair labor practice (不当労働行為).
The rights to form a labor union, to negotiate with the employer, and at times to strike are guaranteed by the Constitution of Japan (日本国憲法) and are called the labor three rights (労働三権).

The labor three rights consist of: (1) the right to organize (団結権) — the right to form a labor union; (2) the right to collective bargaining (団体交渉権) — the right of a labor union to negotiate with the employer; and (3) the right to collective action (団体行動権) — the right to engage in disputes and strikes.
If no labor union is organized inside the company, collective bargaining (団体交渉) and strikes (ストライキ) may not feel immediately relevant to managers or HR staff.
Japan’s labor union organization rate has recently hovered at a low level of about 16%.
Joint/general unions (合同労組) that individuals can join across company and industry lines have been growing in presence.
Even when a firm has no enterprise union, labor-management negotiations with a joint union can still arise.
Labor/HR staff should therefore learn the basics of collective labor-management relations (集団的労使関係).

Labor-management relations (労使関係) are coordinated either between an individual worker and an employer (個別的労使関係, individual labor-management relations) or between a labor union and an employer (集団的労使関係, collective labor-management relations).

個別的労使関係 (individual labor-management relations): the relationship between a worker who has concluded a labor contract and the employer (company). Generally the employer holds the stronger position, so negotiations such as wage increases are difficult.
集団的労使関係 (collective labor-management relations): the relationship between a labor union organized by multiple workers and the employer (company).
The Japanese Constitution guarantees the three labor rights (労働三権): 団結権 (right to organize), 団体交渉権 (right to collective bargaining), and 団体行動権 (right to collective action).
Even if no labor union exists at one's own company, a joint labor union (合同労組) can be joined on an individual basis.
Labor unions (労働組合) are organizations that workers form by uniting in order to improve labor conditions such as wages and working hours. Members of a labor union are called 組合員 (union members).
Enterprise unions (企業別組合) are labor unions that workers of a specific company join; this is the most common form of labor union in Japan.

Industry unions (産業別組合) are cross-cutting labor unions joined by workers engaged in the same industry. This form is common in Europe and the United States. Representative Japanese examples include the All Japan Harbor Workers’ Union (全日本港湾労働組合) and the National Federation of Construction Workers’ Unions (全国建設労働組合総連合).

General or community unions (合同労組) are labor unions organized on the principle of individual membership in a given region, going beyond company boundaries. They take various forms, such as being organized by occupation or industry or being limited to a particular region.
When a union’s members are individual workers it is called a unit union (単位組合); when its members are themselves labor unions it is called a federation union (連合組合).

The Japanese Trade Union Confederation (日本労働組合総連合会, abbreviated 連合 or Rengo) was formed in 1989 as the national central organization of labor unions and has approximately 7 million affiliated members.

Industrial federations that constitute Rengo include Denki Rengo (電機連合, electrical manufacturers), UA Zensen (UAゼンセン, textiles, distribution and services), and Jidosha Soren (自動車総連, automobile manufacturers and parts companies).

In many Japanese enterprise unions, a member who is promoted to a managerial or supervisory position leaves the union and becomes a non-member. The purpose is to exclude persons who represent the employer’s interests from participating in the labor union.
Many enterprise unions restrict membership to regular employees (正社員). With the growth of non-regular employment, the question of how far union membership should extend has become a major issue.
Before negotiating with employers (使用者), a labor union must first consolidate the diverse opinions of its members internally.
Labor unions are operated internally through a democratic system.
The highest decision-making body (最高議決機関) of a labor union is the General Assembly (大会).
Larger labor unions may also establish additional bodies such as a representative assembly (代議員会) or central committee (中央委員会).
The executive organ is the Executive Committee (執行委員会), composed of the three officers (三役)—chairperson (委員長), vice-chairperson (副委員長), and secretary-general (書記長)—plus other committee members.
The Executive Committee is responsible for the union’s day-to-day duties based on the policies resolved at the General Assembly.
The relationship between the General Assembly and the Executive Committee is analogous to that between the National Diet (国会, the legislative body) and the executive government (行政府).

Japanese labor unions (労働組合) are organized in a nested hierarchy: national central organizations (全国中央組織) at the top, industrial organizations (産別組織) below them, then corporate-group union federations (企業グループ連合), and finally enterprise-level labor unions (企業別労働組合) at the base.
An example of an industrial organization (産別組織) is UA Zensen, which covers distribution and manufacturing (流通・ME).
Examples of corporate-group union federations include the Hitachi Group Union (日立グループ連合), Fujitsu Labor Union Federation (全富士通労連), and Toshiba Group Union (東芝グループ連合).

Under a corporate-group federation such as Panasonic, individual enterprise unions exist, for example Automotive Systems Labor Union (オートモーティブシステムズ労働組合), Panasonic Energy Labor Union (パナソニックエナジー労働組合), and Panasonic Homes Labor Union (パナソニックホームズ労働組合).
The diagram (図表 073) illustrating this union structure is compiled from Denki Rengo’s explanation of Shunto and the Panasonic Group Labor Union Federation’s list of affiliated organizations.
The national center (ナショナル・センター) of labor unions in Japan is the Japanese Trade Union Confederation, known as Rengo (連合 / 日本労働組合総連合会).
Traditional labor unions primarily focus on collective bargaining (団体交渉) with employers over wage base-up (ベア).
Some labor unions now take on broader roles that include career development and work-style reform (働き方改革).
Mitsui Bussan Labor Union, later rebranded Mitsui People Union (MPU), was organized in 1962 as an enterprise union during the peak of the base-up era.

By 2012 the union’s existence was questioned and dissolution was considered; in 2015 it survived by shifting to a union-shop system (ユニオンショップ制) under which, in principle, all workers must join the union.

After the dissolution crisis, MPU first undertook re-branding to raise member interest: in 2019 it changed its name to the more approachable “Mitsui People Union,” enlisted an external design firm, and thereby transformed into an organization that now attracts high member engagement.
Workers are important stakeholders for a company’s mid- to long-term development; future unions are therefore expected to gather workers’ needs carefully and make them visible to management.
MPU chairman Matsui described this function as “eliminating management’s blind spots” (経営のブラインドポイントをなくすこと).
MPU conducts an engagement (“ease of working”) survey of all approximately 4,000 members, achieving an ~80 % response rate that itself signals high interest.

The survey data are scored with eNPS and analyzed for issues across roughly 120 workplaces; the resulting high-reliability data are used in repeated dialogues with top management, HR, and division heads.

These dialogues have led to concrete HR measures being implemented, including flextime (自由な始業・終業時刻), a system allowing temporary work interruption for childcare during COVID, and, from January 2023, a permit-based broad side-job (副業) system—the first among major general trading companies.
Like MPU, workers can design their own ways of working and personnel policies together with the company through labor unions.
The labor-management relationship required in the coming era is 'labor-management co-creation' (労使共創), which goes beyond traditional 'labor-management cooperation' (労使協調).
Future labor unions analyze and aggregate diverse member needs and implement varied measures (such as career development and work-style reforms) jointly with the company.
Traditional labor unions versus future labor unions differ in stance: traditional unions operate through labor-management confrontation and/or cooperation (労使対立・労使協調).
Main purpose of traditional unions is wage base-up (ベースアップ / ベア) obtained via collective bargaining (団体交渉).
Main purpose of future unions is the overall treatment and conditions of workers, including non-wage aspects.
Union-member needs in traditional unions tend to be highly homogeneous opinions; future unions must handle opinions rich in diversity.
Traditional opinion aggregation relies on workplace discussion meetings (職場懇談会); louder members’ views are more easily reflected.
Future opinion aggregation is data-driven: survey (アンケート) results are visualized first, after which dialogue is emphasized.
Traditional planning role: the union comments on proposals already prepared by management or the HR department.
Future planning role: the union itself also conceives and proposes personnel/HR measures.
The function of labor unions consisting of analyzing and aggregating the diverse needs of union members will become increasingly important in the future.

Labor-management interests are adjusted through individual labor-management relations (個別的労使関係) and collective labor-management relations (集団的労使関係), but when adjustment fails, labor-management disputes (労使紛争) can arise.

Individual labor disputes (個別的労使紛争) are disputes between an individual worker and an employer (company). Civil litigation is often imagined first, but it generally takes a long time until judgment, procedures are public, and it imposes large financial and mental burdens on both labor and management.

Besides civil litigation, many dispute resolution systems are provided by administration (national and prefectural governments), courts, and private organizations. Representative systems include conciliation (あっせん) and labor tribunal (労働審判).

Conciliation (あっせん) is a system in which a fair and neutral third-party labor-issue expert enters between the disputing parties, confirms the main points of both claims, performs adjustment, and promotes discussion to resolve the dispute. It is conducted non-publicly (useful for privacy protection). Resolution often occurs within 2 months (short period). The presented conciliation plan has no coercive force (unlike court mechanisms). Implementing bodies include Prefectural Labor Bureaus (national), Labor Committees (prefectural), bar associations, and social insurance labor consultant associations (private organizations).

Labor tribunal (労働審判) is a mechanism that, in principle, holds hearings within 3 sessions while attempting mediation as appropriate, for rapid resolution. It is conducted non-publicly (like conciliation). Confirmed labor tribunal results or adjustment contents have the same effect as a court settlement (i.e., they have coercive force), unlike conciliation. If an objection is filed against the labor tribunal result, the case transitions to civil litigation.

Collective labor-management disputes (集団的労使紛争) are disputes between a labor union and an employer. When talks between the union and employer do not reach agreement, the administrative agency known as the Labor Committee (労働委員会) is involved in resolution.
Labor-management disputes in Japan can be resolved through systems such as conciliation (あっせん) administered by the Labor Relations Commission (労働委員会).

If an employer refuses collective bargaining (団体交渉) without just cause, or dominates or intervenes in the operations of a labor union (労働組合の運営に支配・介入), the Labor Relations Commission reviews the matter as an unfair labor practice (不当労働行為) and may issue a relief order (救済命令).
Subsequent material (ツボ 076) addresses company-side risks arising from labor-management disputes (労使紛争における会社のリスク).
Individual labor-management disputes in Japan can be resolved through specialized systems such as conciliation (あっせん) and labor tribunals (労働審判) in addition to ordinary civil litigation.

Comparison of individual labor dispute resolution systems (図表 075) covers courts, labor relations commissions, and professional bodies such as bar associations and social insurance labor consultant associations.
Court civil litigation (民事訴訟) is public, has coercive/binding force (強制力がある), typically involves a large financial and psychological burden, and takes longer to resolve.
Labor commission conciliation (あっせん) is non-public, has no coercive force (強制力はない), and is relatively fast (78.2% of cases resolved within 2 months; average around 3 months).

Labor tribunal proceedings (労働審判) are non-public, generally concluded within a small number of sessions (原則 3 回以内), produce a tribunal decision with binding force unless objected to, and if either labor or management files an objection the case migrates to ordinary civil litigation.
Resolutions through lawyer associations, social insurance labor consultant associations, etc., rely on discussion leading to agreement, are non-public, and lack coercive force.
Source material for the comparison is the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare pamphlet “職場での労働関係のトラブルでお困りの方へ”.
Japanese labor dispute procedures of あっせん (conciliation/mediation) or 労働審判 (labor tribunal) typically conclude in about 2–3 months.
These procedures enable relatively rapid dispute resolution compared with ordinary litigation.
Key statement: あっせんや労働審判であれば終結まで2〜3か月程度と迅速な紛争解決が可能です
In Japanese labor-management disputes that reach labor tribunals or civil litigation, employers face two primary categories of risk: monetary risk and reputation (brand-image) risk.

The largest monetary risk is wage back pay (バックペイ). If a dismissal is ruled invalid, the labor contract is treated as having continued from the date of dismissal until the judgment becomes final; the company must therefore pay wages retroactively for that entire period because the worker was prevented from attending work by the employer.

Back-pay liability is not limited to dismissals; it can also arise from the end of a fixed-term employment contract, natural retirement at the expiration of a leave-of-absence period, and similar situations in which the employment relationship is later found to have continued.

Unpaid wages (especially unpaid premium/overtime wages) are a frequent additional point of contention. After 2020 the statute of limitations for wage claims was extended to five years (provisionally three years), substantially increasing companies’ potential financial exposure.
Further monetary risks include claims for damages and consolation money (慰謝料).

Reputation risk is the danger that the company’s brand image will be damaged. If a lawsuit proceeds to judgment without settlement, the matter is typically publicized as a “[Company Name] Case,” making the details of the labor dispute widely known.
Cases involving important labor-law issues may be reported by the mass media and further amplified through social media (SNS).
Non-experts generally find labor-dispute facts difficult to evaluate accurately and tend to perceive the employer as the villain.

From the company’s standpoint, labor disputes should be resolved quickly and amicably. Daily preventive efforts are essential; as soon as a potential dispute is sensed, a specialist labor lawyer should be consulted at the earliest possible moment.
Future labor affairs personnel (労務担当者) require the indispensable ability to appropriately predict risks (リスクを適切に予測する力).

If a labor-management trouble (労使トラブル) escalates into a dispute (紛争化), personnel should raise the resolution (解像度) of worst-case risks that could occur for the company and communicate those risks with the management team (経営陣).
Effective communication of detailed risk assessments to management is a key responsibility when handling potential labor disputes.
In labor-management (労使) disputes, companies face two primary categories of risk: monetary/financial risk (金銭的リスク) and reputational risk (風評リスク).
If a dismissal is ruled invalid, the company may be required to pay wage back pay (バックペイ) covering the relevant period.
Extension of the statute of limitations (消滅時効期間) for wage claims makes unpaid wages more likely to escalate into formal disputes.
Additional financial exposure can include damages claims (損害賠償請求) and consolation/solatium payments (慰謝料).
Civil court procedures, including oral argument and judgment, are public; this publicity can damage a company’s brand image.
Dispute substance is often difficult for non-experts to grasp accurately, producing a strong tendency for the company to be framed as the “villain.”
Reputational harm can take the form of public commentary such as “that Company A case—they got sued; it was written up large in the newspaper.”
When making management decisions (経営判断), one should also raise the resolution (解像度) of labor-management dispute risk (労使紛争リスク), i.e., develop a clearer, more detailed understanding of that risk.

There are two methods to make a disadvantageous change (不利益変更) to labor conditions: (1) changing the work rules / employment regulations (就業規則の変更), and (2) changing labor conditions by agreement (合意).
Even a labor-management agreement cannot change conditions below the standards set by the Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) or the work rules (就業規則); work rules override such agreements.
In a labor dispute, courts strictly examine whether the agreement was based on the worker's own free will (自由意思), not merely whether a consent document exists.
Workers are generally in a weaker bargaining position, so a key issue is whether the structure of the relationship forced them to agree against their will in response to the employer's request.

There is typically an information disparity between employer and worker regarding labor matters; insufficient explanation can later lead to the agreement being held invalid (e.g., the worker claiming they were not told how disadvantageous the change would be).
Simply obtaining a consent form (同意書) is not enough and is a common misconception; it is insufficient especially for important conditions such as wages or retirement benefits.
When changing important labor conditions, the employer must provide detailed information the worker needs to make an informed judgment, not merely abstract concepts or general formulas.

Best practice includes individually simulating the amount of disadvantage before vs. after the change for each worker and giving individual explanations, with a sincere attitude of providing all available information without holding back.
These points apply in contexts such as personnel system revisions (人事制度改定).
When revising a personnel/HR system (人事制度), companies frequently skip the required process of amending the work rules (就業規則) or obtaining individual employee consent.
Distributing explanatory materials to all employees or holding multiple briefing sessions does not replace the prescribed legal process.
A disadvantageous change to working conditions (労働条件の不利益変更) that does not follow the required process is highly likely to be held invalid (無効), creating serious legal risk.
HR system revisions must always be risk-checked from a labor-law perspective; if the change is disadvantageous, the necessary legal procedures must be completed.

In Japanese labor law, disadvantageous changes to working conditions (労働条件の不利益変更) follow a decision path based on whether the workplace has work rules (就業規則) and whether the condition being changed is included in those work rules.

One method is to amend the work rules under Labor Contract Act (労働契約法) Article 10. The change must be reasonable in light of: the degree of disadvantage suffered by workers (労働者の受ける不利益の程度); the necessity of changing the working conditions (労働条件の変更の必要性); the appropriateness of the content of the amended work rules (変更後の就業規則の内容の相当性); and the status of negotiations with labor unions etc. (労働組合等との交渉の状況). Workers must also be notified of / made aware of the amended work rules (周知).
