The alternative method is to obtain individual agreement under Labor Contract Act Article 8. Such a change cannot set conditions below the levels stipulated by the Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) or the existing work rules. The agreement must be based on the worker’s own free will (自ら の自由な意思によるもの). A consent form (同意書) alone is insufficient; the worker must be given detailed information needed to make an informed judgment.
Source material for the framework is the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare document “Points of the Labor Contract Act” (労働契約法のポイント).
When labor conditions are lowered by agreement (合意により労働条件を引き下げる場合), sufficient information provision to workers is essential (労働者に対する十分な情報提供が必須です).

Non-regular employment workers (非正規雇用労働者) are those who work under employment forms with a fixed term, including part-time workers, contract employees (契約社員), dispatched workers (派遣社員), and commissioned workers (嘱託). Regular employment workers (正規雇用労働者) are those without a fixed term, commonly known as seishain (正社員).
The share of non-regular employment workers has been rising year by year and accounts for about 40% of all employees in Japan.

Non-regular workers occupy a weaker position than regular workers in individual labor-management relations. They often lack membership qualifications in enterprise-based labor unions, making it structurally difficult for their views to be reflected in collective labor relations.

Japanese labor law therefore contains various protective measures aimed at improving and stabilizing the status of non-regular workers. Rules on equal pay for equal work (同一労働同一賃金) and on non-renewal of fixed-term contracts (雇止め) serve this purpose.

The unlimited-term conversion rule (無期転換ルール) provides that when a fixed-term labor contract with the same employer has been renewed so that the total period exceeds five years, the worker (e.g., contract employee or part-timer) may apply to convert the contract into an open-ended labor contract.

Timing of the conversion right: for a one-year contract the right arises during the one-year period after the fifth renewal; for a three-year contract it arises during the three-year period after the first renewal.

From 1 April 2024 (Reiwa 6) onward, at each renewal timing when the conversion right arises the employer must explicitly inform the worker that an application for unlimited conversion may be made and must also state the working conditions that will apply after conversion.

A common misunderstanding is that conversion to an unlimited-term contract automatically requires treatment equivalent to that of a regular employee. In principle, all working conditions other than the contract period remain the same as they were under the fixed-term contract.

Many firms have personnel systems, evaluation schemes and wage structures only for regular employees and leave those for non-regular workers undeveloped. Such systems, including pathways for conversion to regular-employee status, should also be established for non-regular workers.
It is desirable to introduce and operate an appropriate personnel system (適切な人事制度の導入・運用).
Organizations are advised to establish a transparent system for converting non-regular workers to regular employee status (透明性のある正社員転換制度).
Nearly 40% of workers are in non-regular employment (非正規雇用), as indicated in Chart 078.

Human capital investment in non-regular workers should be pursued seriously for the sake of improving organizational capability itself, not merely because protective labor policies are being advanced.
The following section (ツボ 079) addresses disguised contracting / bogus contracting (偽装請負).
非正規雇用は、パート、アルバイト、契約社員、派遣社員、嘱託などの期間の定めのある雇用形態の総称である。
図表078は正規雇用と非正規雇用労働者の推移を示し、役員を除く雇用者数と非正規雇用労働者の割合の時系列データを含む。
近年の非正規雇用労働者の割合はおおむね36.7%〜38.3%の範囲で推移している（例: 38.3%、37.2%、36.7%、36.9%、37.3%など）。
役員を除く雇用者数は約5,138万人〜5,689万人の規模で示されている（例: 5,688、5,656、5,662、5,689）。
非正規雇用の内訳例として、パートが1,021万人、アルバイトが453万人、その他が83万人などが挙げられる。
データ出典は厚生労働省「2023年度第1回雇用政策研究会（参考資料集）」である。

For employees on fixed-term employment contracts (有期雇用契約社員), Japanese labor rules create a right to apply for conversion to an indefinite-term contract (無期転換申込権) once the statutory conditions (typically five years of continuous employment) are met.

At the moment that conversion-application right arises, employers are expected to thoroughly and explicitly state the applicable working conditions (労働条件明示) so the employee can make an informed decision.

The page presents this as a practical compliance reminder: 有期雇用契約社員の「無期転換」申込権の発生時の労働条件明示を徹底しましょう (thoroughly implement clear disclosure of labor conditions when the indefinite-conversion application right arises).

Worker dispatch (労働者派遣) is a system in which the dispatching company (派遣元) has workers it employs work under the command and orders of the dispatch destination (派遣先) for the benefit of that destination. There is no employment contract between the dispatched worker and the dispatch destination.
Operating a worker dispatch business requires permission from the Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare.
The Worker Dispatch Act (労働者派遣法) sets various rules for worker dispatch.
Dispatch period restrictions fall into two categories: dispatch-destination workplace unit (派遣先事業所単位) and dispatched-worker individual unit (派遣労働者個人単位).

The period for which workers can be dispatched to the same workplace of the dispatch destination (派遣可能期間) is generally limited to 3 years. To accept dispatch beyond 3 years, the dispatch destination must hear opinions from the majority labor union (or equivalent) of that workplace.

Even if the workplace-unit dispatch period is extended, the same dispatched worker cannot work more than 3 years in the same organizational unit (e.g., a section/課) at the dispatch destination workplace.
In principle, the dispatch destination is prohibited from naming specific dispatched workers, conducting interviews before dispatch work begins, having resumes sent, and similar practices.
A contracting (請負) contract is one in which one party (the contractor/請負者) promises to complete a certain job and the other party (the orderer/注文者) pays remuneration for the result of that work.

Unlike worker dispatch, the orderer is not permitted to give command and orders to employees employed by the contractor. Doing so constitutes disguised contracting (偽装請負) and violates the Worker Dispatch Act.

Example of disguised contracting: An engineer employed by an IT company (contractor) is stationed at a client’s office doing system development under a contracting contract. Ordinary daily conversation between the orderer and the contracting worker is not treated as command/order. However, if the orderer instructs on work sequence and methods regarding the work process, or decides placement of contracting workers or assignment of work to each individual worker, it is judged as disguised contracting.
Distinguishing whether an action constitutes 指揮命令 (command/direction) or コミュニケーション (communication) is difficult in practice.

A key reference for this distinction is the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) document 「労働者派遣事業と請負により行われる事業との区分に関する基準 (37号告示) 関係疑義応答集」 (Q&A collection on the criteria for distinguishing worker dispatch business from contract/請負-based business).
This relates to Japanese labor-law rules separating 労働者派遣 (worker dispatch) from 請負 (contracting) based on the presence or absence of client-side command and control.

In Japanese labor law, a key distinction between worker dispatch (労働者派遣) and contracting (請負) is the presence or absence of command and control (指揮命令). Exercising command and control over workers in a contracting arrangement constitutes disguised contracting (偽装請負) and is a legal violation.

Worker dispatch (労働者派遣契約): The dispatching company (派遣元) employs workers and sends them to work under the command and control of the client company (派遣先). There is no employment relationship between the dispatched worker (派遣労働者) and the client. Operating a worker dispatch business requires permission from the Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働大臣).

Contracting (請負): A contract in which the contractor (請負者) promises to complete a specified job (仕事の完成) and the orderer (注文者) pays remuneration (報酬) in return. The orderer is not permitted to issue command and control instructions to the contractor.
Intended communication (コミュニケーションのつもり) can still be received by the other party as a command or order (指揮命令として受け止められる).
Perception of a message as directive rather than dialogue can occur even when the speaker does not mean it that way.
This mismatch between sender intent and receiver interpretation is a key interpersonal/organizational communication issue.

Cabinet Office estimates there are about 4.62 million 'freelancers' in Japan who run their own businesses without hiring employees. Matching platforms connecting freelancers and companies have been developed, and government promotion of side jobs and dual employment has diversified freelance work.

Telework has shifted much internal and external communication online, blurring the boundary between 'employment' and 'freelance'. Companies must therefore confront the fundamental question of why they employ people at all: what roles (missions) they expect from directly employed workers and what work styles they want, which will substantially change each company's approach to labor management.

In Reiwa 5 (2023), the Freelance and Business Transaction Optimization Act (Freelance New Law) was passed. From a labor-management perspective it requires consideration for freelancers' childcare and nursing-care needs and establishment of consultation systems for harassment. Labor personnel must therefore be properly involved in the use of freelancers.

Traditional labor-management relations discussions were biased toward regular employees. With the spread of work styles not based on employment and the increase in non-regular employment (part-time, dispatch, etc.), the framework of labor-management relations itself must be expanded.

Key concepts for the expanded labor-management relationship are 'differentiation' and 'integration'. Differentiation means designing an optimal portfolio of numbers and ratios for each employment and contract form, based on the 'expected role' assigned to each form; differences in expected roles then determine differences in responsibility and authority. This process must take into account legal issues such as equal pay for equal work and the Worker Dispatch Act versus disguised contracting.
Integration means recognizing that, regardless of employment or contract form, living people are involved; their motivation for work and engagement with the company affect individual performance.

To realize a company's philosophy or purpose (理念 / パーパス), the organization must operate as a "one team" (ワンチーム) that involves and integrates all people regardless of employment form (雇用形態) or contract form (契約形態).
The labor-management relations (労使関係) that labor affairs (労務) must cover have expanded substantially compared with the era when covering only regular employees (正社員) was sufficient.
Future labor-management relations (労使関係) are described as 分化と統合 (differentiation and integration): diverse employment forms and contract types mix together and function as one team (ワンチーム).
Traditional labor relations centered only on regular employees (正社員のみが中心), whereas the future model integrates mixed forms rather than treating regular employees as the sole core.
Mixed forms illustrated include regular employees (正社員), outsourcing/consignment (委託), short-time work (時短), part-time regular employees, external workers (外部), and business outsourcing (業務委託).
The diagram contrasts strategy/planning (戦略・企画) layers with operational work (業務), showing how both regular and non-regular/outsourced workers participate.
Motivation and engagement (モチベーション / エンゲージメント) plus work-execution measures (業務遂行 施策の対象) are to be applied across the mixed workforce rather than only to regular employees.
The framework is adapted from Korn Ferry Japan (ed.), Future of Work 人と組織の論点 (Nikkei, 2022).
The labor-management relationship (労使関係) with personnel who are not engaged under employment contracts (雇用契約によらない人材) is identified as an important future theme.
This points to evolving industrial relations beyond traditional employer-employee contracts, such as with independent contractors, freelancers, or gig workers.
Chapter 8 covers 労使関係 (labor-management relations). Its summary compiles Q&A from key points (ツボ) 071–080 and targeted messages for HR/labor-affairs staff, executives, managers, and all workers.

HR/labor-affairs staff (労務担当者) must especially understand labor-dispute risks (ツボ 076) and the range of resolution methods (ツボ 075). When a matter could become a labor dispute, they must organize and report both the risks and countermeasures to executives.
Reporting only that “this plan has risk” is insufficient. Staff must explain at high resolution the concrete impact on corporate management if monetary risk or reputational (風評) risk materializes.

Executives (経営者) must fulfill their legal, work-rule, and labor-contract obligations toward workers (ツボ 071). Labor-law rules may appear overly detailed from the management side, but an attitude of “a little non-compliance is fine” is mirrored in workers’ own attitudes.

Managers (マネージャー) must develop the ability to manage diverse employment and contract forms (ツボ 080). Future workforces will mix full-time regular employees with non-regular workers, contractors, and side-job talent; these must be integrated as one team while observing the legal cautions in ツボ 078 and 079—a high-difficulty form of management.
Members (従業員) should maintain a strong contract awareness (契約意識) regarding their employment relationship.
A labor contract (労働契約) is the contract concluded between the company and the individual employee (referenced as ツボ 071).
A contract (契約) is an agreement that defines the mutual rights and obligations of both parties.
If one's own obligations are not fulfilled, one cannot claim corresponding rights.
If rights are infringed, the employee must raise their voice appropriately within both individual and collective labor-management relations (個別的・集団的労使関係) (referenced as ツボ 072).
The following Chapter 9 addresses organizational systems or structure (体制).
A good labor-management relationship (よい労使関係) is defined as one in which both parties first fulfill their mutual 'obligations' (義務) and then aim for a 'warm relationship' (あたたかしい関係性).
Labor union interests are adjusted either through individual labor-management relations (個別的労使関係) or collectively between the labor union and the employer (集団的労使関係).
Types of labor unions include enterprise-based unions (企業別組合), industry-based unions (産業別組合), mixed/general unions (合同労組), unit unions (単位組合), and federated unions (連合組合).

A key function related to unions or employee representation is analyzing and aggregating diverse needs, then jointly implementing with the company various measures such as career development and work-style initiatives.
Labor-management disputes (労使紛争) can be resolved by using formal dispute-resolution systems including civil lawsuits (民事訴訟), mediation/conciliation (あっせん), and labor tribunals (労働審判).
Labor disputes carry both monetary/financial risk (金銭的リスク) and reputational risk (風評リスク).
Because Japanese law strictly examines whether an action was based on free will (自由意思), a consent form (同意書) alone is insufficient as evidence of valid agreement.

Regular/permanent employment (正規雇用) is contrasted with non-regular/fixed-term forms such as contract employees (契約社員), dispatched workers (派遣社員), commissioned/entrusted workers (嘱託), and other employment with a defined term.

The legal distinction between worker dispatch (労働者派遣) and contracting/outsourcing (請負) is the presence or absence of command-and-control (指揮命令). Exercising command over workers in a contracting arrangement constitutes disguised contracting (偽装請負) and is a legal violation.

Future labor-management relations are expected to feature both differentiation and integration: diverse employment and contract forms will mix, yet parties will function as a single 'one-team' labor-management relationship (ワンチームとなる労使関係).

Even non-researcher medical practitioners regularly attend academic conferences (学会) to input the latest scientific knowledge into practice, as shown by common clinic notices that the director is closed for conference attendance.

The scientist-practitioner model (科学者-実践者モデル) for clinical psychologists (臨床心理士) holds that they must be both practitioners and scientists and should constantly incorporate the latest scientific research findings into practice.
Practitioners in labor and human resources (労務) should similarly learn more actively from scientific research in personnel and labor fields.
Academic conferences often seem high-threshold and academic, but many allow non-researchers (the general public) to attend as listeners (聴講) simply by paying a participation fee.
In HR/labor-related fields, the Japan Labor Society (日本労務学会) features many practical research themes with presentations that are relatively easy to understand.
After attending and finding a conference interesting, one option is to officially join the academic society.
Example: The author, who has no research background, joined the Labor Theory Society (労務理論学会), which has many social insurance labor consultants (社会保険労務士) as members.
Search online for societies in fields of interest and aim to attend several per year as a listener.

National conferences (全国大会) of academic societies are large annual events held at universities across Japan, offering a chance to travel beyond the capital region and enjoy local food and drinks after attending.
The author aspires to someday post a notice at his own office stating it is closed for academic conference participation.

Labor affairs (労務) business structure should be designed using a business portfolio (業務ポートフォリオ). The horizontal axis is routine/standard tasks (定型業務) that occur daily, monthly, or yearly versus non-routine/sudden tasks (非定型業務) such as mental health (メンタルヘルス) and harassment (ハラスメント) responses. The vertical axis is frequency of occurrence (high vs low).
Three approaches must be balanced: (1) in-house operation (内製) by internal labor staff; (2) outsourcing (アウトソーシング) to external parties; (3) systematization (システム化) via systems that automate work.

High-frequency routine tasks should be shifted to systematization. If the in-house share is too high, labor staff become overwhelmed by routine work and neglect non-routine work such as trouble prevention and incident response. This is especially common in small organizations due to budget constraints. Routine work should be automated so staff can spend time on non-routine work; executive/management support is essential for this shift.

Fully internalized 'all-in-one' work (丸抱え業務) should be outsourced. A common pattern is one labor staff member also handling general affairs and accounting and running all admin work alone. This is dangerous: if that person is absent due to illness, leave, or resignation, all essential work including payroll stops. Outsourcing is used so that work does not halt in an emergency.
Payroll calculation in particular tends to become person-dependent and a black box (ブラックボックス). Outsourcing can be an opportunity to dismantle the black box and organize the work.

The head of the management department should establish a backup capability for at least the minimum labor tasks. Even when outsourcing, a double-check system remains necessary. An attitude of understanding the work together with the person in charge is desirable.
The optimal business structure is always changing.
Business process decisions such as outsourcing versus insourcing are constantly changing and should not be treated as permanent.
Even work that has already been outsourced can swing back toward insourcing (内製化 / 揺り戻し).

Example reasons for re-insourcing: payroll/compensation systems become too complex for the vendor to handle; headcount of labor/HR staff increases and internal capacity appears; IPO preparation requires faster financial closing (決算早期化), forcing rapid insourcing.
Continuously review the company’s business-process portfolio according to its current organizational phase (組織フェーズ).
Upcoming key points (ツボ 082–088) cover three approaches: (1) insourcing (内製), (2) outsourcing (アウトソーシング), (3) systemization (システム化); the next point focuses on insourcing.
業務ポートフォリオから内製・アウトソーシング・システム化のバランスを設計する
労務の業務ポートフォリオ例（図表081）では、発生頻度（高〜低）と業務の定型性（非定型業務から定型業務）を軸にタスクを配置する
発生頻度が高い領域ではシステム化を検討する
非定型業務を定型業務へ寄せる方向性が示される（図表082参照）
ポートフォリオ上の配置により内製・アウトソーシング・システム化の対象を判断するフレームワーク
A labor/HR (労務) staff member taking on all duties creates a dangerous single-point-of-failure state described as 「その人がいないと回らない」 (the organization cannot function without that person).
Concentrating all labor-related operations in one individual is a key-person risk that should be avoided.
In-house (内製) labor operations by internal staff have several organizational patterns; the overall business-system picture is covered separately (ツボ 081).

Pattern ① Regular employees only: labor work handles My Number, salary data, and other sensitive personal information, so only regular (full-time) employees are assigned. Small organizations often cannot staff two or more regulars, producing a one-person setup that easily becomes a black box.

Pattern ② Non-regulars for primary/routine work, regulars for secondary/irregular work: contract, part-time, and dispatched staff (ツボ 078) handle standard clerical operations; regulars handle exceptions. This enables double-checking with two or more people and frees regular-employee capacity for other missions.

A competing policy in some firms is to keep access to salary and HR information as limited as possible; that raises the question of how much work can be given to higher-turnover, fixed-term non-regulars.
Labor functions as an internal service to employees. Highly hospitable staff therefore feel pressure to grant irregular exceptions in order to satisfy worker requests.

Accumulated irregular exceptions make processes hard to manualize, prevent coverage or handover when a staff member is sick, retires, or takes leave, and become a barrier to outsourcing or system introduction—so labor ends up holding back operational transformation.
Outsourcing contracts and system specifications create external pressure toward standardization; pure in-house work lacks that pressure and tends toward a “just work harder” structure.
Well-intentioned irregular accommodations become future operational liabilities and are not beneficial even for the labor staff themselves.
Labor affairs personnel (労務担当者) should adopt the perspective of a "Rule Master" (ルールマスター), as emphasized in Tsubo 009.
Rather than making cases irregular (イレギュラー化する), apply them within the framework of existing rules (既存のルールの枠組み).
Continuously pursue standardization (標準化) and efficiency (効率化) in labor affairs work.
The subsequent section (Tsubo 083) covers public institutions related to labor affairs.
Do not flee from irregular (exception) handling; combine irregular-case response with standardization rather than treating exceptions as one-off heroics.
Master and apply rules (e.g., employment regulations / 就業規則) so that exception handling itself becomes a driver of standardization and efficiency.

Ad-hoc ‘just do your best’ irregular handling may earn thanks from workers but creates a black box: knowledge stays with the individual, cannot be handed over, systematized, or outsourced, and is often framed as ‘this time only.’
The preferred path is rule literacy and dissemination: labor staff explain cases by citing specific articles (‘according to Article X of the work rules…’), so both worker and HR share the same logic.
Standardization unlocked by rule-based handling enables four concrete next steps: manualization, handover systems, IT systemization, and outsourcing.
Standardization is not only operational; it efficiently advances work processes, organizational structure, and strategy together.

Contrast of two postures: (1) laborer and HR struggling without shared rules → gratitude plus black-box risk; (2) both parties using and teaching the rules → transparent, repeatable, scalable response.
Establishing and maintaining employment regulations (就業規則) is a fundamental prerequisite (大前提) for organizational standardization (標準化) and efficiency (効率化).
Key statement: 「就業規則」が整備されていることは、標準化・効率化の大前提となります

Public agencies (役所) involved in labor affairs (労務業務) function as an external 'business system' outside the organization. They may initially feel intimidating, but if you first understand the responsible person and jurisdiction before contacting them, they will generally respond cooperatively. They should be used without hesitation.

Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署): Has authority for on-site inspections and supervisory guidance, which can create a fearful image, but for unclear points related to the Labor Standards Act (労働基準法), Industrial Safety and Health Act (安全衛生法), or Workers' Accident Compensation Insurance Act (労災保険法), contacting the relevant department yields correct legal application and interpretation. There are 321 offices nationwide. Key departments for labor work: 方面課 (various notifications and consultations based on labor standards laws), 安全衛生課 (workplace safety and health matters), and 労災課 (workers' compensation insurance benefits).

Prefectural Labor Bureau (都道府県労働局): Established in all 47 prefectures. The Employment Environment and Equal Opportunity Department (雇用環境・均等部) handles the Equal Employment Opportunity Act (男女雇用機会均等法) and Childcare and Family Care Leave Act (育児・介護休業法). The same department also handles harassment consultations.

Hello Work (ハローワーク): 544 locations nationwide. Handles employment insurance (雇用保険), job placement (職業紹介), and employment measures (雇用対策). Labor-related work includes employment insurance qualification acquisition/loss, issuance of leaving certificates (離職票), job applications, subsidy applications (助成金申請), and disability employment matters. The relationship with labor affairs is very broad.

Japan Health Insurance Association (協会けんぽ): Consists of a headquarters and 47 prefectural branches. Operates medical insurance mainly for small and medium enterprises without their own health insurance associations. Main labor involvement is applications for childbirth-related benefits (出産関連の給付金) and injury/sickness allowances (傷病手当金). Health insurance associations (健康保険組合) are public corporations that large companies or industries operate with government approval, sometimes offering unique welfare services not available through Kyokai Kenpo.

Pension Office (年金事務所): 312 locations nationwide. Handles qualification acquisition and loss procedures for employees' welfare pension insurance (厚生年金保険). Also involved in Kyokai Kenpo health insurance enrollment and premium payment procedures.
Additional procedures (付手続) are also handled by the pension office (年金事務所).
Income tax-related matters (所得税関連) involve collaboration with the tax office (税務署).
Resident tax-related matters (住民税関連) involve collaboration with municipalities (市区町村).
Work is advanced in cooperation with these public institutions (公的機関).
The next key point (ツボ 084) covers consulting experts/professionals (専門家 / 士業).

Public institutions that labor affairs personnel (労務担当者) deal with include the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署), prefectural labor bureaus (都道府県労働局), Hello Work (ハローワーク), Japan Health Insurance Association (協会けんぽ), and Pension Offices (年金事務所).

The Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署) includes a supervision division (方面課) that handles notifications based on the Labor Standards Act (労基法), a safety and health division (安全衛生課) that ensures workplace safety and health, and a workers' compensation division (労災課) that handles workers' accident compensation insurance benefits (労災保険給付).

The Employment Environment and Equal Opportunity Department (雇用環境均等部) covers the Equal Employment Opportunity Act (男女雇用均等法), the Childcare and Family Care Leave Act (育児・介護休業法), and harassment consultations (ハラスメント相談).

Japan Health Insurance Association (協会けんぽ) and health insurance societies (健保組合) operate medical insurance, provide childbirth-related benefits (出産関連の給付金), and process applications for sickness and injury allowances (傷病手当金).
Pension Offices (年金事務所) handle procedures related to Employees' Pension Insurance (厚生年金保険) as well as enrollment in Japan Health Insurance Association health insurance and payment of premiums.
When consulting with a public institution (公的機関), clearly specify which law or ordinance (法令) the consultation concerns.
Connecting with external specialists (士業) is essential for building a labor affairs (労務) work system (業務体制).

Licensed professionals such as lawyers (弁護士), tax accountants (税理士), social insurance labor consultants (社会保険労務士), and administrative scriveners (行政書士) have legally defined exclusive scopes of practice called 独占業務 (monopoly/exclusive business).
独占業務 exists as a protective regulation because each field demands high expertise, preventing unqualified people from harming clients.

Labor law and social insurance matters fall under 社会保険労務士 (Sharoushi). When unsure whom to consult on labor topics, start with a Sharoushi. They can also advise on overall labor management, including creating a comfortable work environment, not only legal or government procedures.
Drafting and filing employment rules (就業規則) and applying for Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare subsidies are exclusive businesses of 社会保険労務士.

Tax matters, especially payroll issues involving income tax (所得税) and resident tax (住民税), are the exclusive domain of 税理士 (Zeirishi). Sharoushi may not legally handle tax consultations; conversely, labor-insurance and social-insurance procedures are exclusive to Sharoushi, so a tax accountant handling them would violate the law.
When introducing new policies, confirmation from both labor and tax perspectives is often required; always consult both a Sharoushi and a Zeirishi.
Lawsuits are handled by lawyers (弁護士). Visa matters are handled by administrative scriveners (行政書士).
In practice, early-stage labor-trouble consultations are typically handled by Sharoushi; if signs of a labor-management dispute appear, the matter may be referred onward (page truncated).
When an issue becomes visible, lawyers are often brought into the project team so that the matter can be handled as a three-party response.
Visa applications (在留資格申請) when hiring foreigners can be handled by administrative scriveners (行政書士) who hold application-agency qualifications (申請取次資格).
The next section (ツボ 085) covers using outsourcing (アウトソーシング) as part of the operational structure.

Japanese specialized professionals (士業) relevant to labor and corporate consultations include 社会保険労務士 (social insurance and labor consultant), 税理士 (certified tax accountant), 弁護士 (lawyer), and 行政書士 (administrative scrivener).
Figure 084 (図表 084) presents consultation contents categorized by each of these professions (士業ごとの相談内容).
Labor/HR staff (労務担当者) commonly face the practical question of which professional to consult for a given issue (誰に相談すればいいのかな?).
専門家の知見をつなぎ専門領域間でのポテンヒットを防ぐことも労務担当者の仕事です (Connecting specialists' knowledge and preventing potential hits/gaps between specialized domains is also part of the labor affairs officer's job.)

The key point of using outsourcing is not to dump everything (丸投げしない). Even an excellent outsourcer can have operational mistakes because people are involved in the business process, so an internal double-check system for outsourced work is essential.

Outsource tasks that labor staff themselves could perform in terms of knowledge and ability but for which they want to reduce required man-hours. Do not outsource work you yourself do not understand, as checks become lax and can lead to serious mistakes.
Representative outsourceable tasks in the labor (労務) field include labor insurance and social insurance procedures, payroll calculation, and various consultation desks.

Assume that mistakes will definitely happen and build mechanisms to prevent them both at the outsourcing destination and internally. Confirm the outsourcer's operational system for performing the entrusted work.

Divide the outsourcer's processing into system processing and manual processing, and write down in advance the possible errors/mistakes for each; this enables differentiated intensity in internal checks.

A hidden disadvantage of outsourcing is that the hands-on feel for personnel information becomes scarce. Labor clerical work is not mere mechanical operation; it contains primary information about workers and the organization.

Example: When labor staff close attendance themselves they may notice mental-health warning signs such as a person recently having many late arrivals/early leaves, or previously stable attendance becoming irregular this month.
Performing payroll calculation yourself also makes it easier to stay alert to issues such as wage balance among workers and total personnel costs.

Even when the same information appears in deliverables from an outsourcing vendor, there is distinct value in personally performing the work so that you come into contact with primary (first-hand) information.
The benefit of moving your own hands and touching primary information is easily overlooked; new staff in charge of outsourced work should therefore try doing that work themselves at least once.
The next section (Tip 086) covers methods for selecting an outsourcing partner.
When outsourcing work that the company itself possesses the knowledge and ability to perform internally, always implement double-checking (ダブルチェック).
Even highly capable outsourcers should be used to handle tasks the company could do itself, specifically to reduce man-hours (工数を下げる).
Typical outsourced HR/labor tasks include: labor insurance (労働保険), social insurance related procedures (社会保険関係の手続), payroll calculation (給与計算), and various consultation windows (各種相談窓口).
Mistakes will occur (ミスは起きる) even with excellent outsourcers.
Risk mitigation: Confirm and understand the business processing process in advance, and write down the contents of possible errors and mistakes beforehand.
Double-check should be performed between the company's internal labor personnel (労務担当者 / 社内業務) and the social insurance BPO outsourcing company (社会保険 BPO 企業).
Delegating (丸投げ / marunage: completely dumping) work or duties that you yourself do not understand leads to missing serious mistakes.
Core principle: Do not fully outsource or hand off business/tasks you lack comprehension of, because you will fail to catch major errors.
Outsourcing (アウトソーシング) means delegating part of a business process to an external party. This section covers how to select an outsourcing partner (utilization of outsourcing is covered in point 085).

Main candidates for outsourcing labor insurance/social insurance procedures and payroll calculation are: (1) social insurance labor consultants (社会保険労務士, sharoshi) and (2) BPO (Business Process Outsourcing) companies.
Sharoshi are suitable for small- to medium-sized companies. Under law, labor insurance and social insurance procedures can be performed as agency work only by a sharoshi (see point 084).
If a company wants payroll calculation and labor/social insurance procedures handled by a single outsourcing partner, a sharoshi is a strong choice.
Few sharoshi can serve large organizations, so as headcount grows it becomes more common to outsource payroll separately to a BPO company.

BPO companies excel at outsourcing for medium- to large-scale organizations. Their scope is not limited to payroll and bonus calculation; they may also propose operational efficiency improvements for the entire HR department.
BPO companies cannot accept labor insurance or social insurance procedures, so those tasks must be kept in-house or separately outsourced to a sharoshi.

Outsourcing in the labor field now extends beyond insurance procedures and payroll. Examples include: employee mental-health consultation windows outsourced to EAP (Employee Assistance Program) companies; external harassment consultation windows using lawyers or sharoshi; health checkups, occupational health, and stress checks related to the Industrial Safety and Health Act; and welfare-benefits agency services.
A wide range of services is offered across virtually all labor-related work (see Figure 086).
Labor staff must manage many different outsourcing partners. Changing vendors or renegotiating terms is cumbersome, so once a service is introduced it is often left unchanged for years.
Labor-related outsourcing services evolve rapidly (日進月歩). Labor staff should keep watching new service trends and periodically review what mix is optimal for their own company.
Evaluate whether operations have been organized into a sourcing system (ソーシング体制).
Outsourcing (アウトソーシング) costs should not be reduced excessively, because doing so is undesirable from the standpoint of maintaining quality.
Always keep track of the appropriate/fair market price of the service.
The following section (ツボ 087) covers systematization of the business/operating system (業務体制「システム化」).

Outsourcing destinations for HR/labor work should be selected from social insurance labor consultants (社会保険労務士) and various BPO companies according to purpose and organization size, with periodic reviews of those choices.
A usage-differentiation approach (アウトソーシング先の使い分け) for outsourcing partners is illustrated in Chart 086, enabling labor staff to concentrate on non-routine work (非定型業務).
Typical outsourced routine HR tasks include agency processing of joining and retirement procedures (入社・退職手続きの代行) and agency processing of health-checkup administrative procedures (健康診断の事務手続きの代行).
Health-checkup management tools (健康診断管理ツール) can be introduced as part of outsourced or supported labor operations.
Labor affairs staff (労務担当者) are positioned to focus on establishing and improving welfare benefits (福利厚生の整備) once routine tasks are outsourced.
Office-employee-oriented services (オフィス従業員向けサービス) include mental-health support (メンタルヘルス).
A cafeteria plan (カフェテリアプラン) lets employees freely choose welfare menus within the range of points granted to them (付与されたポイントの範囲内).
Related employee-support offerings include company cafeteria / meal-subsidy services (社食・食事補助サービス), online counseling via EAP services (EAPサービスによるオンラインカウンセリング), and stress-check tools (ストレスチェックツール).
In HR communities, exchanging information about what work is being outsourced and to which providers or locations is recommended.
Systems are not a "magic wand" (魔法の杖). Introducing a system without practical knowledge does not make operations run correctly; many people wrongly assume that installing a system alone is enough.
A system only automates routine, standardized tasks that people would otherwise process by hand. Wrong initial settings cause all subsequent processing results to be wrong.
Unlike manual work, a system still outputs incorrect results in a seemingly plausible form, which makes errors harder to notice.

Real examples of trouble from running a packaged system on default settings include: working hours being automatically rounded in 15-minute units, and incorrect overtime premium rates. These can unintentionally lead to Labor Standards Act (労基法) violations.

Entrust to a system only those tasks that a labor-affairs staff member could still perform themselves in Excel or other manual work. Do not put on a system any processing that the staff cannot independently recalculate and verify.
If a process cannot be self-verified, hire experienced labor practitioners or use external specialists while the internal team also catches up on the correct processing methods.
When introducing a new system, run old operations and the new system in parallel, confirm that output results match with no discrepancies, and only then fully migrate.
Assume mistakes will occur even if initial settings are done with great care.
For core systems—HR management (人事管理), attendance management (勤怠管理), and payroll calculation (給与計算)—secure a sufficient parallel-run period, typically about 3 to 6 months.
Provide careful, thorough explanations of the change to both workers and managers.
Even an excellent system cannot perform correct business processing unless users (employees and managers) input information accurately without errors.
When introducing a system, promote understanding of operation methods by creating operation manuals, holding system operation briefing sessions, and setting up a help desk.
When explaining system operations, also cover the purpose and background of each operation on the system.
From the perspective of reducing workers' input burden, a system's UI/UX is a very important factor.
Select systems that workers can operate as intuitively as possible.

When introducing a system, three critical points are: (1) correct initial settings based on the company's own situation, (2) a schedule with sufficient leeway that includes parallel operation, and (3) thorough explanations to employees and managers.

If a system's initial settings are wrong, every output result will also be wrong. Initial settings must therefore always be changed to match the company's specific circumstances rather than used as-is.
Run the old operations and the new system in parallel so that output results can be compared and verified. For core-system introductions, build in a buffer of 3–6 months.

Explanations to employees and managers must cover not only how to operate the system but also the purpose and background of the introduction. At the same time, create operation manuals and set up a help desk so that an environment is designed in which employees do not become stuck.
A system cannot do more than the knowledge and abilities that the labor/HR affairs personnel possess (労務担当者が持っている知識・能力以上のことは、システムにはできません).
Systems are limited by the knowledge and capabilities of the people who operate or configure them.

Core systems related to labor affairs (労務業務) are mainly three: a. personnel management system / HR master (人事管理システム / 人事マスタ), b. attendance management system (勤怠管理システム), and c. payroll calculation system (給与計算システム).
System introduction for these labor-affairs cores follows three patterns: one-package type (ワンパッケージ型), individual-package type (個別パッケージ型), and company-specific customization type (個社カスタマイズ型).

One-package type: a single vendor supplies a.b.c. as the same product series (examples: Money Forward MF series; DONUTS Jobcan series). Data linkage between modules is convenient, but each series has strengths and weaknesses and may not meet every in-house requirement.

Individual-package type: a, b, and c are each sourced from a different vendor’s packaged product (examples: SmartHR for personnel, KING OF TIME for attendance, 給与奉行 for payroll). Systems are specialized and relatively inexpensive, but inter-system data linkage is weak.

Company-specific customization type: systems (examples: Workday, COMPANY) are customized or modified to match the firm’s own business rules. HR data can be managed centrally while remaining aligned with the company’s personnel policies; introduction and modification costs are higher, so this pattern is typically used by large organizations.

HRTech expansion has added many non-core systems that labor staff also operate: talent management, health management / stress checks, welfare / cafeteria points, engagement surveys, 1-on-1 / interview management, and others.
When systems are introduced in a finely subdivided, domain-by-domain fashion, data linkage and combinations among those systems must still be verified.

Combining analysis results (e.g., overlaying stress-check results with engagement-survey results rather than viewing each in isolation) yields deeper insight than looking at any single system’s output alone.
Human capital management (人的資本経営) will make the utilization of HR/personnel data (人事データ) more important going forward.
When considering system implementation, do not limit the viewpoint to efficiency of individual operations; take an integrated perspective on how to utilize HR data as a whole.
The next topic (ツボ 089) covers the organizational structure (組織体制) of labor/HR administration (労務).
労務（人事労務）システムの導入パターンは大きく3つに分類される：①ワンパッケージ型、②個別パッケージ型、③個社カスタマイズ型。
個別パッケージ型の特徴：各機能に専門特化したパッケージを組み合わせて導入する。メリットは専門特化により品質が高いことと価格が安価なこと。デメリットはシステム間連携が不得意なこと。
個社カスタマイズ型の特徴：自社のニーズに合わせてシステムをカスタマイズ（またはスクラッチ開発）する。メリットは自社要件への適合とシステム間連携のスムーズさ。デメリットは価格が高額になること。
ワンパッケージ型は複数機能を一つのシステムでカバーするため、システム間連携がスムーズになりやすい。
代表的なサービス例：SmartHR、MFシリーズ（マネーフォワード）、Workday、ジョブカンシリーズ、KING OF TIME、給与奉行。

Labor affairs (労務) organizational structure should be designed according to organization scale: up to ~50 people typically have no dedicated labor department and handle it as part of management functions in an admin department (管理部); around 100 people an HR department (人事部) is established; over 300 people a dedicated labor-function group or section is often created.

Four types of labor organization structures: (1) Executive concurrent type (経営者兼務型) — no dedicated labor staff; the executive handles labor work concurrently; common from founding to under 10 employees.

(2) Admin-department integrated type (管理部一体型) — labor functions sit inside the admin or general-affairs department, with dedicated or concurrent labor staff; common around 50 employees. Advantage: other admin staff (general affairs, accounting) can cover when the labor person is absent (illness, leave, resignation). Disadvantage: labor-work check functions tend to be weak because the department head often comes from a finance/accounting background.

(3) HR-department inclusive type (人事部内包型) — an independent HR department contains function-specific staff for recruitment, talent development, HR planning, labor, etc. Advantage: internal job rotation makes it easier to gain broad experience. Mainly used in medium organizations of 100+ people.

(4) Independent labor-group type (独立労務グループ型) — a distinct labor group or section inside HR with multiple labor staff. In large unionized firms this may be called a labor-administration group (労政グループ) that handles union negotiations. Advantage: mutual work-check systems can be guaranteed. Disadvantage: members’ viewpoint may become biased toward labor functions only.
Another organizational pattern for labor/HR functions (労務機能) is to split them between headquarters HR (本社人事) and business-unit HR (事業部人事).
In manufacturing, this split is often between headquarters HR and factory HR (工場人事).
The following section (ツボ 090) covers the relationship between labor organization structure (組織体制) and roles.
As organizational scale increases, labor (労務) functions undergo functional differentiation (機能分化).
Chart 089 classifies four types of labor organization systems (労務の組織体制の類型) that typically correspond to company size.
Type ① 経営者兼務型 (owner/manager concurrent type): used in small/founding companies (under ~10 employees); the business owner personally handles labor affairs.
Type ② 管理部一体型 (integrated management-department type): typical of medium-sized firms (~50 employees); labor work sits inside a combined administration/management headquarters.
Type ③ 人事部内包型 (contained-within-HR type): common in mid-to-large firms (roughly 100 to under 1,000 employees); a dedicated labor specialist is nested inside the personnel department.
Type ④ 独立労務グループ型 (independent labor-group type): used in large organizations (1,000+ employees); a stand-alone labor group exists with its own resources.
Smaller configurations allow other staff to cover if the labor specialist leaves and keep specialization modest; internal rotation can broaden experience.
Larger, more specialized structures enable mutual cross-checks, greater resources, and bolder labor policies, but division of labor can make viewpoints overly labor-centric.
Even for the same labor affairs / HR personnel (労務担当者), the breadth and depth of experience they can gain differs depending on the organizational structure (組織体制).
労務 (labor affairs) has three indispensable layers of roles: オペレーションエクセレンス (Operation Excellence), ルールマスター (Rule Master), and ストラテジスト (Strategist). None of these roles can be omitted.
These three roles are not all carried by a single labor-affairs staff member. Organizations exist so that roles can be divided; how they are divided changes with 組織体制 (organizational structure).
In the 創業期 (founding/startup stage), the business owner/manager must personally take on all three layers of labor-affairs roles.

In a mid-sized organization that already has an HR department, Operation Excellence and Rule Master are typically assigned to labor-affairs staff, while the Strategist role is assigned to the 人事部長 (HR director).

Pay special attention at the moment organizational structure changes. Even if role division worked well under 管理部一体型 (management-department integrated type), moving to 人事部内包型 (HR-department internal type) as the company scales can create distortions in role assignment.

Venture-company example: the first HR hire is often a recruitment specialist. If that person later becomes HR director, a recruitment professional who is inexperienced in labor affairs suddenly has to manage the labor domain. Result: all three role layers may be dumped onto labor staff (dysfunction) or work may become 属人化・ブラックボックス化 (personalized and black-boxed), making proper management impossible. The same problem arises in large companies if an HR director inexperienced in labor affairs is appointed.
The critical practice is continuous monitoring of whether the three layers of roles still function without gaps after any change in organizational structure.

Strategic HR (戦略人事) requires flexibly changing organizational structure to match strategy and then re-assigning roles. Therefore the next generation of people who can actually carry those roles must already be developed.

Labor-affairs talent development has two directions. One is 役割の深化 (deepening of a role): specializing in a single role and pursuing it to a high level of expertise (e.g., an Operation Excellence specialist).

Role evolution (役割の進化): After the roles of each layer can be fulfilled to a certain extent, the direction is to evolve further to higher layers (from Operation Excellence to Rule Master, and then to Strategist).
Such development cannot be achieved overnight; talent development must be advanced in a planned manner over a medium- to long-term span of about 3–5 years.
The next chapter (Chapter 10) covers labor affairs personnel (労務担当者).
Roles must be assigned in line with the organizational structure; this requires medium- to long-term development of people who can actually fulfill those roles.
Chart 090 presents a failure case of role division caused by an organizational-structure change, contrasting a Management-Department Integrated Type with an HR-Department Inclusive Type.
In the original Management Integrated Type, labor-affairs staff A handled OE and RM while the management-department head C handled ST (Strategist); the arrangement functioned well.

After organizational expansion an HR department was created and former recruiting staff B was appointed HR director; B tried to assume the ST role but lacked labor-affairs experience, so the arrangement failed and A plus management-HQ head C had to keep providing follow-up support.

The decisive cause of failure was that ST talent had never been developed, illustrating that structural change without corresponding capability development produces persistent role-assignment breakdowns.
Key role labels appearing in the example include ST (ストラテジスト / Strategist) and RM (ルールマスター / Rule Master).
労務 (labor/HR management) cannot be accomplished in a single day (一日にしてならず), echoing the proverb that major work is not completed overnight.
人材育成 (human resource / talent development) requires a long-term, settled commitment (腰を据えて取り組む) rather than expecting quick results.

Chapter 9 (体制 / organizational system for labor affairs) summary emphasizes continuous optimization of how labor work is structured, plus role-specific messages for 労務担当者, 経営者, マネージャー, and all working people.

労務担当者 should keep a deliberate balance among 内製 (in-house), アウトソーシング (outsourcing), and システム化 (systemization) (ツボ081), and never stop optimizing and improving efficiency. Time freed by that optimization should be used either to deepen a current role or to evolve into a new role (ツボ090).

経営者 should decide which organization labor affairs belongs in (ツボ089) and how the three layers of labor-affairs roles are fully assigned without gaps (ツボ090). Even if admin looks like a cost center, sufficient investment is required so that labor affairs does not become a bottleneck to business growth.

マネージャー who receive labor-related requests or consultations from subordinates may be tempted to ask the company for irregular exceptions out of consideration. Accumulated irregular handling is a company risk (ツボ082). They should instead take a ルールマスター (rule-master) perspective (ツボ009): map the request onto existing rules and handle it creatively inside that framework.
Members must always consult their supervisor or labor affairs staff (労務担当者) in advance whenever irregular (イレギュラー) events occur regarding labor affairs (労務) or ways of working.
If labor affairs staff can grasp an irregular situation in advance, it may still be possible to respond according to the organization's basic rules.
When irregular labor responses accumulate inside an organization, overall labor-affairs efficiency declines (see ツボ 082).
The next chapter (Chapter 10) examines the role of the labor affairs staff (労務担当者).
Labor affairs (労務) business systems should be designed by balancing in-house production (内製), outsourcing (アウトソーシング), and systemization based on a business portfolio.
In-house labor operations: master and apply rules thoroughly to standardize work and drive efficiency.
Key government bodies for labor matters include the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署), Prefectural Labor Bureaus (都道府県労働局), and Hello Work (ハローワーク).
Experts to consult for labor affairs work: social insurance and labor consultants (社会保険労務士), tax accountants (税理士), lawyers (弁護士), and administrative scriveners (行政書士).
Outsourcing labor operations: even when the company has the knowledge and capability to do the work itself, it can still be outsourced; always perform double-checks.
Selecting outsourcing partners: choose between social insurance and labor consultants and BPO companies according to purpose and organization size, and review the arrangement periodically.
Systematizing labor operations: get the initial setup right, allow ample schedule buffer, and give careful explanations to workers and managers.
Labor system introduction patterns: one-package solutions, individual packages, and company-specific customization.
Labor organization structure: as the organization grows, functions should be differentiated.
Relationship between labor organization structure and roles: assign roles according to the organization structure; this requires mid- to long-term development of people who can carry those roles.

Internal control (内部統制) is originally focused mainly on financial reporting, but its concepts and frameworks can be applied to appropriately monitoring outsourced or IT-systematized labor/HR operations.

The '3-point set' (3点セット) approach involves visualizing business processes using documents and flowcharts, then identifying locations that have risks; this thinking, along with IT control concepts, is useful when constructing or reviewing labor affairs systems and organizational setups.

When considering organizational structure and design, start with foundational inputs on what it means to 'design an organization,' including the meaning of division of labor (分業), standardization (標準化), and hierarchy (ヒエラルキー/階層).

Organizational design involves important viewpoints, frameworks, and cautionary points for organizational reform; such knowledge is relevant not only for labor affairs staff but also for executives and HR leaders conceiving company-wide organizational strategy.

Labor affairs knowledge (労務) is framed as a practical 'weapon' for surviving Japan's 100-year life era, useful from junior employees through management because working careers have repeated peaks and valleys.

A personal case: the author (Kocha) was confident in mental toughness after working extremely hard at a venture company as a new graduate, then developed symptoms close to adjustment disorder (適応障害) after a department transfer eroded work confidence.

Due to ignorance of mental illness, the author initially avoided leave, believing that 'breaking once becomes a habit' and that unpaid leave would stop salary; they barely endured the first episode but later needed a doctor's certificate and formal leave at the next company.

Key facts learned from labor-related books during leave: workers on leave can still receive government allowances; with adjustment disorder, removing negative environmental factors often allows return to the original mental state; recurrence risk is especially high in the first six months after returning to work.
Japan has extensive government systems, allowances, and official materials designed to support workers; the author was surprised by how thoroughly public institutions had prepared these supports.
Labor systems (労務) protect people in any situation, support them through rock-bottom periods caused by failure or hardship, and provide a chance to recover and restart.
The author's own recovery involved facing themselves during leave and later returning to work; that experience is presented as a moment when labor knowledge and systems directly helped.
Four perspectives for the growth and development of labor/HR personnel (労務担当者): (1) results/outcomes (成果), (2) ability (能力), (3) role (役割), and (4) career (キャリア).

Social impact of labor personnel outcomes: Results created by labor/HR staff are not limited to their own organization; they impact society as a whole. Example: internally promoting male parental leave (男性育休) appears as visible company work-friendliness, is then reflected in government statistics as the male parental-leave acquisition rate, and influences other companies. Micro-level (organizational) results naturally ripple outward to the macro (societal) level like waves—this is the 'social impact' (社会的インパクト) of labor personnel work. Labor/HR staff therefore carry significant social meaning and mission.

Ability of labor personnel is understood via the Iceberg Model of Corporate Person Ability (企業人能力の氷山モデル): what is visible above the water (behavior) is only a small part of the iceberg; beneath it lie invisible knowledge, skills, stance, and personality.

Labor personnel fulfill three layers of roles and grow through the experience of producing the outcomes expected at each layer. Operation Excellence outcomes: work is executed without mistakes and quickly according to defined business processes, and those processes are continuously improved. Rule Master outcomes: for individual concrete cases, laws and work rules are complied with while providing smooth consultation and preventing labor troubles. Strategist outcomes: the company's ways of working and rules are strategically transformed in response to the times and changes in the external environment.
Career perspective: a variety of possible futures open up for labor/HR personnel (page text on this point is incomplete).

For realizing business strategy and organizational structure, companies must consider not only 「育成」(development/nurturing of labor staff for company needs) but also 「成長」(personal growth) for the labor affairs staff member's own career; this dual focus is necessary for both the employer (会社/使用者) and the individual.

労務担当者 (labor/HR affairs staff) have diverse future career paths (キャリアパス), including: becoming a specialist who has mastered labor affairs work, becoming a人事責任者 (personnel/HR manager), becoming independent as a社会保険労務士 (certified social insurance and labor consultant), or transferring to BPO or HR systems companies (see related section ツボ 100).
The subsequent section (ツボ 092) covers learning about the成果 (results/achievements) of labor affairs staff.

The iceberg model of corporate personnel capabilities (企業人能力の氷山モデル) is a personnel-assessment framework covering four elements: results/achievements (成果), abilities/competencies (能力), roles (役割), and career (キャリア).
The iceberg model is adapted from Osawa Takeshi, Shiba Hiroyoshi, and Nimura Hideyuki’s Personnel Assessment Handbook (人事アセスメントハンドブック).
A related growth-and-development model for labor/HR personnel (労務担当者の成長・育成モデル) maps progression involving the employer/company (使用者/会社), social impact (社会的インパクト), and career goals (キャリア: 目標).
Within that development model, two named roles appear: Strategist (ストラテジスト, ST) and Rule Master (ルールマスター, RM).
労務 (labor/HR management) is a great profession that can improve not only one's own company but society as a whole (労務は自社だけでなく、社会全体をより良くできる偉大な仕事です).
The results that labor/HR (労務) staff should create ultimately all lead to EX (Employee Experience). EX is the value that employees experience at the company from joining until they leave.

EX is analogous to CX (Customer Experience). CX is the value customers experience while purchasing and using products/services; marketing actively works to improve CX. EX replaces the customer with the employee and is the mindset of continually improving employees' experiences inside the organization.
EX gained attention after Adobe renamed its HR function the 'Employee Experience Team' and Airbnb created the CEEO (Chief Employee Experience Officer) role.

A decline in EX leads to labor troubles and resignations. New hires typically start full of dreams, hope, and motivation; stacked negative experiences after joining lower motivation and engagement, which then produce labor disputes and turnover.

Analogy: a motivated user signs up for an online English conversation service, then hits a complex website, cannot book convenient lesson times, and encounters unkind or unclear instructors. Motivation collapses. The same pattern occurs inside organizations.
Labor/HR staff improve EX in order to raise the energy with which workers produce business results. Continuously improving EX is both their mission and their '成果' (result/achievement).

Concrete EX drivers: payroll calculation errors worsen EX; hospitable handling by labor staff improves it. The UX of HR systems that labor staff select also affects EX. Widespread overwork or harassment constitutes the worst EX.
Labor affairs personnel (労務担当者) have every action connected to Employee Experience (EX) and therefore carry a mission to continuously improve EX.
When measuring the results (成果) of labor affairs personnel, the key question is how much those results have contributed to EX improvement.
The following section (ツボ 093) addresses setting goals for labor affairs personnel.
Improving Employee Experience (EX / エンプロイー・エクスペリエンス) raises the energy of workers who produce business results (事業成果を生み出す労働者のエネルギーを高める).
EX covers the employee journey across stages including joining (入社), immediately after joining (直後), and during employment (就業中).
A common EX failure mode is 入社後放置 (neglecting or leaving employees unattended after they join).
Recurring payroll calculation errors (給与計算のミスが続く) are an EX/operational pain point; the questions posed are how mistakes can be prevented and how the process can be improved.
Labor/HR staff (労務担当者) are the actors expected to prevent continuing mistakes and drive improvement, linking EX quality to employee energy, business outcomes, and resignation (退職) risk.

Labor affairs (労務) staff goal-setting often produces items that are specific but whose significance is hard to see, and that do not show how the organization will improve. Typical examples on goal-management sheets include: execute payroll with zero mistakes (ミス0件); conduct harassment training four times; draft rules for side jobs and concurrent employment.
OKR (Objectives and Key Results) is a practical method for goal management that can be used to rewrite such goals.

Objectives state specifically what should be achieved. They should fulfill the organization’s mission, inspire the labor-affairs person, and prompt action. Objectives do not have to be measurable; set significance by thoroughly considering what is most important now, without first thinking about quantification.

Key Results state how the objective will be achieved and serve as monitoring criteria. They must be measurable and verifiable by a deadline. Once Key Results are set, each person can self-control and advance the work independently.
The practical tip for labor-affairs goal setting is to think through significance (Objectives) first and only then think through the concrete measures (Key Results).
The three example goals can be rewritten as OKRs that correspond to three layers of roles (see related points 007–010).

Good Objectives have three characteristics and two prerequisite conditions (from Tsuboya Kunio, Illustrated Introduction to Goal Management). The first characteristic is: worth making an effort for—even if difficult, the goal feels worth striving for and one wants to realize it.

A valid personal/work goal should meet the criterion of feeling achievable (うまくできると思える): even if it seems difficult, it must be a target the person believes they can accomplish through their own effort.
A valid goal should also meet the criterion of being something one wants to talk about (誰かに語りたくなる): it should be the kind of target that one naturally ends up sharing with surrounding colleagues.

Two premises are required for something to qualify as a proper goal. First, it must be understandable (理解可能である): the wording must be clear enough that anyone who reads it can grasp it, so that colleagues will cheer and superiors will provide support.

Second premise: concentrate on the Circle of Influence (影響の輪に集中する). Goals must concern outcomes that one’s own effort can actually determine. Items that belong only to the Circle of Concern (関心の輪)—weather, economic conditions, decisions of top management, etc.—are unsuitable as goals.
The next section (ツボ 094) will cover the concrete “actions” expected of labor-affairs / HR personnel.
After thoroughly considering significance (意義), set the Objective first, then place specific Key Results (indicators) under it.

OKR example (payroll/admin): Objective — Improve business processes so payroll is executed quickly without mistakes. Key Results: (1) Identify workflows to streamline and obtain approval from related parties and the management director; (2) Identify methods such as outsourcing or systemization and secure management-department budget (rollout next half-year); (3) Create a manual and confirm that designated staff and the management director can perform Excel manual double-checks.

OKR example (harassment/HR): Objective — Reduce harassment-related trouble and resignations. Key Results: (1) Communicate harassment rules (law and disciplinary provisions) plus consultation window company-wide, with understanding-test score of 80% or higher; (2) Deliver harassment training to managers and above, with understanding-test score of 90% or higher; (3) For teams scoring below 3.20 on specified organizational-survey items, interview all members and decide countermeasures with the manager and department head.

OKR example (flexible work/side jobs): Objective — Revise side-job/concurrent-employment rules to enable flexible working styles. Key Results: (1) Estimate social impact of introducing side jobs from external trends and obtain concept approval at the management meeting; (2) Tentatively set rules and start trial operation in two agreeing departments; (3) Capture actual pains and gains from the trial and create a plan for full operation (rollout next half-year).

These are presented as role-specific goal examples (図表 093 役割ごとの目標例) illustrating how to cascade qualitative Objectives into measurable, time-bound Key Results in Japanese corporate HR and administration contexts.
The important thing for achieving results (成果をあげる) is concentration (集中).
Decide what not to do (やらないことを決める) in order to concentrate and produce results.

Labor/HR personnel (労務担当者) must raise sensitive "antennas" (アンテナ) to catch workplace events early, grasp what is happening, and think through its impact on labor operations (労務) so that risks and issues are not overlooked.

Example of antenna use: if news arrives that referral hiring (リファラル採用) will pay a temporary bonus (一時金), immediately consider the effect on payroll calculation (給与計算) and drop it into actual practice.

Example of antenna use: when attendance data (勤怠データ) shows continued absences due to poor health (体調不良による欠勤), quickly communicate with managers about possible mental-health or personal-injury leave (私傷病休職) issues and connect the worker to an occupational-physician (産業医) interview.
Knowledge gaps can be filled by asking specialists, but if events themselves are not detected, risks and challenges will simply be missed.
Build a relationship of trust so that executives consult the labor function; executives are rarely labor experts and typically do not think through operational impact of HR policies.
When consulted from the conception stage of an HR measure (人事施策), labor can surface concerns and discussion points in advance.
Trust is earned by continuously reporting and proposing analysis based on workers’ primary information (労働者の一次情報), the issues derived from it, and concrete solutions (see ツボ 095).

The stance to avoid is listing only "reasons it cannot be done" (できない理由); repeatedly saying a policy is too hard because it burdens labor operations leads to becoming a function that is no longer consulted.
The required stance is "How can we make it possible?" (どうすればできるか?) (see ツボ 098).

Labor work is the "last one mile" (ラストワンマイル) of talent strategy (人材戦略): it implements the company’s personnel systems and delivers them to workers. Last one mile is defined as the final contact point at which goods or services actually reach the recipient.
Even when labor affairs (労務) work is outsourced, communication with executives/managers and workers cannot be outsourced.
Labor affairs should put up 'antennas' to detect risks and issues early and respond to them.
Labor affairs should build a relationship in which management consults them.
These 'actions' by labor affairs improve EX (Employee Experience; see ツボ 092).
The next point (ツボ 095) addresses the trust relationship with management.
Labor affairs personnel (労務担当者) are expected to discover risks and issues early and respond to them.
They should build relationships in which they are consulted by both management (経営者) and workers (労働者).
Figure 094 illustrates actions required of labor affairs personnel, covering employee life events and policy changes.
Typical matters handled include sales incentives (営業インセンティブ), wage-system revisions (賃金制度改定), changes in the number of dependents (扶養家族の人数変更), and relocation (引っ越し).

Employees may receive allowances for qualifying events (e.g., congratulations for life events), should consult specialists about concerns, and submit applications through the labor-affairs system (労務システム).
The labor affairs officer coordinates these processes between employees, the internal system, and external experts.
Always be conscious of both the quality and quantity of communication with managers/executives (経営者) and employees (従業員).
This is presented as a HINT for organizational or management practice.

Labor/HR staff frequently receive idea-based (思いつき) instructions from executives, e.g. copying another company's welfare system or creating new allowances for recruitment PR; this happens directly in SMEs/startups or indirectly via superiors in larger organizations.

HR frustration ('another whim from the president; the field has no such need'; 'upper management doesn't understand anything') is common, but most such mismatches actually stem from insufficient reporting and proposals from the HR side itself.
Count how often labor topics appear on agendas of board meetings, management meetings, or manager meetings; if few, HR's work and results are almost invisible to executives.
HR must proactively submit agenda items to meeting bodies; 'no proposals coming up' is often interpreted by executives as 'they are not doing any work.'

HR is the organizational role closest to workers' primary information (一次情報): attendance data (hours, leave rates), payroll data (total personnel costs, departmental labor-cost trends), and occupational health data (stress-check group analysis, health-checkup abnormality rates).
Analyzing this primary data alone can identify issues with high precision; combining it with surveys can also visualize employee needs.
HR should report analysis results, identified issues, and proposed solutions so they actually reach executives, enabling HR to act ahead of executive instructions.
A practical first step is to insert current-situation analysis reports into regular management-meeting agendas.
Managers issue idea-based instructions solely from a desire to improve the organization (「組織をよくしたい」).
If labor affairs staff (労務担当者) convey a proactive attitude toward solving issues, a trust relationship is built and they can become 'consulted labor affairs' (相談される労務); see ツボ094.
The following section (ツボ096) covers the knowledge required of labor affairs staff.

Labor analysis and executive reporting framework: Use workers' primary (first-hand) information as the basis for analysis, then derive issues and solutions and report/propose them to management (経営者への報告・提案).
Process flow (図表 095): Workers' primary information → analysis results → issue identification (課題特定) → solutions (解決策) → report/proposal to executives.

Key input data types for the analysis include attendance/勤怠 data, average working hours, mental-health problems and turnover, salary/payroll data, leave-acquisition rates, stress-check results, total personnel costs, health-checkup results, labor-cost trends, stress status, occupational-physician interviews, and overall health status.
Example issue identified: Persistent long working hours in Department A, requiring healthy/normalized working hours (時間の健全化).
Example solutions: Departmental work improvement via outsourcing and automation, support for managers, and review of personnel/staffing plans.
Trust relationship (信頼関係) between the labor-affairs officer (労務担当者) and executives is presented as essential for the proposal to be accepted and advanced ("なるほど! 進めよう").
Labor/HR management (労務) is an important matter in corporate management.
Labor/HR issues should be treated as a regular standing agenda item in management meetings and discussed sufficiently.

Labor affairs (労務) staff must treat labor and social insurance laws as the foundation of their work, including the Labor Standards Act (労働基準法), Industrial Safety and Health Act (労働安全衛生法), Workers' Accident Compensation Insurance Act (労災保険法), Employment Insurance Act (雇用保険法), Child Care and Family Care Leave Act (育児・介護休業法), Health Insurance Act (健康保険法), Long-term Care Insurance Act (介護保険法), and Employees' Pension Insurance Act (厚生年金法).

Practical seminars hosted by organizations such as Labor Administration (労務行政), Labor Newspaper Company (労働新聞社), and Japan Laws (日本法令) are recommended; staff should choose sessions close to their own area of responsibility.
Studying for the Social Insurance and Labor Consultant (社会保険労務士 / Sharoshi) exam is an effective way to deepen knowledge of these laws.
Labor and social insurance laws are frequently amended, so knowledge must be continually updated.

For systematic study of labor law, the Tokyo Labor University Course (東京労働大学講座) hosted by the Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training (労働政策研究・研修機構) is recommended; it offers practical lectures by prominent university professors in the labor-law field.
Staff who handle payroll calculation need basic knowledge of taxes, specifically income tax (所得税) and resident tax (住民税).
Recommended qualifications for payroll work include the national FP Skill Test (FP技能検定) and the private Payroll Calculation Practical Ability Test (給与計算実務能力検定試験).

Year-end tax adjustment (年末調整) rules change frequently, so staff should catch up on the latest knowledge through seminars every year (for example, those given by tax accountant and Sharoshi Yasuda Dai).
Labor affairs staff play a supporting role for workers’ lives and health and therefore need knowledge that enables them to handle consultations on a wide range of life events.
Life events that labor staff commonly address include marriage, pregnancy, childbirth, childcare, nursing care, disability, illness, and second-life planning after retirement.

It is unrealistic for any single labor-affairs staff member to have personal experience of every life event; nevertheless, staff should keep their antennae up for everyday lifestyle-related topics so they can better understand the feelings of workers facing those events.

労務担当者 (labor affairs / HR labor specialists) can expand their knowledge and perspective by encountering real-life experiences of involved parties through TV documentaries, magazines, and books, and by seriously listening to the private worries of friends and acquaintances.
The knowledge gained through work as a 労務担当者 also enriches one's own personal life, making it a very fulfilling and rich profession.
The next section (ツボ 097) covers the skills that a 労務担当者 should acquire.
Knowledge of labor and social insurance laws (労働社会保険諸法令), taxes, and life events must be updated with each legal amendment (法改正ごとに知識をアップデート).
Recommended knowledge acquisition methods (知識の習得方法) include attending practical seminars (実務セミナー) that match one's area of responsibility.
For deeper study of labor and social insurance laws, challenge the 社会保険労務士 (Sharoshi / Certified Social Insurance and Labor Consultant) examination.
The ファイナンシャル・プランニング技能検定 (FP技能検定) is a national certification conducted by two organizations: 日本FP協会 (Japan FP Association) and 金融財政事情研究会 (Kinzai).
To study labor law systematically, take the 東京労働大学講座 (Tokyo Labor University lectures) hosted by 労働政策研究・研修機構 (JILPT).
The 給与計算実務能力検定試験 (Payroll Calculation Practical Ability Certification Exam), conducted by 一般財団法人実務能力開発支援協会, is a private certification that recognizes experts in payroll calculation work.
Seminars should be used to update knowledge of rule changes (セミナーでルール変更の知識をアップデート).

Key life events (ライフイベント) requiring related legal, insurance, and tax knowledge include: marriage (結婚), pregnancy and childbirth (妊娠・出産), childcare (育児), caregiving (介護), disability (障害), illness (病気), and post-retirement (定年後).
Labor/HR personnel (労務担当者) have a wide and diverse range of topics they must learn, so learning should be approached in a planned and systematic way.

Labor/HR personnel (労務担当者) should acquire counseling skills because they often serve as the internal consultation window for workers on harassment, childcare/nursing-care leave (育児・介護休業法), and other daily workplace issues.

Few people have received professional training in listening to others’ worries; if labor staff master professional counseling (カウンセリング) for mental concerns, workers can consult with greater peace of mind.
